It collects the oracles, laments and life story of Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, a priest from Anathoth, who preached in Judah from the reign of Josiah until the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem in 587/586 BC. Jeremiah's followers, perhaps including his scribe Baruch, and later editors expanded the book. It warns of judgment for idolatry and promises a new covenant. It survives in two forms: the Hebrew text and a shorter Greek Septuagint version.

The Book of Job is an anonymous book of the Hebrew Bible. It belongs to the Ketuvim (Writings) and is the first of the Poetic Books of the Christian Old Testament. Its language points to composition in the Persian period, though the date is uncertain. A prose prologue and epilogue frame poetic dialogues between the righteous Job, who has lost his wealth, children and health, and his friends, followed by Elihu's speeches and God's reply from the whirlwind. The book's treatment of innocent suffering and divine justice made it a major subject of Jewish and Christian theology and exegesis.

The Book of Joel is a prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible and one of the Twelve Minor Prophets. It names its author as "Joel the son of Pethuel", of whom nothing else is known. Its date is disputed. Many scholars place it in the Persian period, partly because it alludes so often to earlier prophetic texts. Starting from a devastating locust plague, it calls the people to repentance and announces the coming Day of the Lord. It also foretells the outpouring of God's Spirit on all people, a prophecy Peter quotes in his Pentecost sermon in Acts 2.

The Book of Jonah is an anonymous Hebrew narrative and one of the twelve Minor Prophets in the Jewish and Christian Old Testament. It tells of the prophet Jonah, son of Amittai, who flees God's command to preach against Nineveh. A great fish swallows him during a storm. After he is released he preaches, the city repents, and God spares it. Most scholars date the book to the postexilic period. Jesus' "sign of Jonah" led early Christian writers to read Jonah as a type of Christ's death and resurrection.

Joshua is the sixth book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It tells how Joshua son of Nun succeeded Moses and led the Israelites across the Jordan. It narrates their campaigns to conquer Canaan, the division of the land among the twelve tribes, and Joshua's closing call to remain faithful to the Law. Jewish tradition attributes the book to Joshua himself. Modern scholars treat it as part of the Deuteronomistic history, with an early form probably written in the late seventh century BC and completed during or after the Babylonian exile.

Judges is the seventh book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It is anonymous: Jewish tradition attributed it to Samuel, while modern scholars see it as part of the Deuteronomistic history, with the main editing often dated to the 7th century BC and later. It covers the period between Joshua's conquest and the monarchy. The book follows a repeated cycle in which Israel is unfaithful, is oppressed, repents and is rescued by a leader. These leaders include Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah and Samson. Its closing chapters look ahead to the coming of kingship.

Lamentations is a book of the Hebrew Bible made up of five poems mourning the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians in 586 BC. Four are alphabetic acrostics. Tradition ascribes them to the prophet Jeremiah, and in Christian Bibles the book follows his. Most modern scholars reject this authorship but date the poems to shortly after the city's fall. The poems personify Zion as a bereaved widow and present the people's sin as the cause of divine judgment. Jews read the book on Tisha B'Av, and Christians read it during Holy Week.

Leviticus is the third book of the Torah (Pentateuch) and of the Old Testament, traditionally ascribed to Moses. Its anonymous text probably developed over a long period, and many scholars think it reached its present form in the Persian period, though this is disputed. Set at Mount Sinai, it consists mostly of divine instructions given to Moses for the Israelites and the Aaronic priests. These cover sacrifices, priestly ordination, purity laws, the Day of Atonement and the Holiness Code (chapters 17–26). Christian interpreters read its sacrifices and priesthood typologically.

Malachi is the last of the Twelve Minor Prophets and, in Christian Bibles, the final book of the Old Testament. Its author is unknown: "Malachi" means "my messenger" and may not be a personal name, and Jewish tradition identified the writer with Ezra. The book mostly dates from the Persian period, perhaps around 500–450 BC. It is written as disputes between God and the people, and it rebukes careless priests, corrupt sacrifice, divorce and unpaid tithes. Christians long read its promise of a coming messenger and the return of Elijah as foretelling John the Baptist.

The Book of Micah is the sixth of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It is attributed to Micah of Moresheth, a Judean prophet active in the late 8th century BC under kings Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. Its seven chapters alternate oracles of doom against Samaria and Jerusalem with promises of restoration. Micah condemns corrupt leaders and defends the poor. Christians read 5:2 as foretelling the Messiah's birth in Bethlehem. Scholars debate when the book reached its final form, possibly in the Persian or Hellenistic period.

The Book of Nahum is the seventh of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It has three chapters and is attributed to the prophet Nahum the Elkoshite. In vivid poetry it foretells the fall of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, as God's judgement on an oppressor of Judah. Its date is debated. Many place it between the sack of Thebes in 663 BC and Nineveh's fall in 612 BC, though other dates have been proposed. The book survives in the Septuagint, the Peshitta and other ancient versions.

Numbers is the fourth book of the Hebrew Bible and of the Pentateuch, traditionally attributed to Moses. Scholars think it has a long, complex history, and its final form probably comes from a Priestly editing in the early Persian period. It is named after the two censuses of Israel that it records. The book follows the Israelites from Sinai through their wanderings in the wilderness. It tells of their rebellions, the sending of the spies and the Balaam episode, and ends on the plains of Moab before Canaan.

The Book of Obadiah is one of the Twelve Minor Prophets of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. Tradition attributes it to the prophet Obadiah, about whom nothing else is known. It has a single chapter of 21 verses, which makes it the shortest book in the Hebrew Bible. The prophecy announces God's judgment on Edom for its pride and for its hostility toward Judah, and it foretells the restoration of Israel on the day of the Lord. Most scholars date it soon after the fall of Jerusalem in 587/586 BC. Others think it took shape later, during conflicts with the Edomites in the fifth and fourth centuries BC.

The Prayer of Manasseh is a short penitential prayer attributed to Manasseh, king of Judah. According to 2 Chronicles 33, he repented while held captive in Babylon. Most scholars think it was written in Greek, though some argue for a Semitic original. It probably dates from the second or first century BC, and certainly before AD 70. It praises God's mercy and confesses great sin. Early Christian church orders preserve it, and it is found among the Odes in some Greek Bibles. Churches differ on whether it belongs to the canon, and it circulated in Syriac Peshitta tradition.

The Book of Proverbs is a book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament, and a classic example of biblical wisdom literature. Tradition ascribes it to King Solomon. Scholars instead see it as a "collection of collections" from different periods, with the final redaction often placed in the Persian or Hellenistic era. In short sayings and longer discourses it sets wise conduct against folly. It teaches that "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge" and personifies Wisdom as present at creation. Christian writers widely read Proverbs 8 in a Christological sense.

The Book of Psalms, or Psalter, is an anthology of Hebrew religious poetry in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It has 150 psalms in Jewish and Western usage, with a few more in Eastern churches, and is divided into five books. It includes hymns of praise, laments, royal psalms and thanksgivings. Many psalms are traditionally attributed to David, but scholars doubt this. They were composed over several centuries, before and after the Exile. The Psalms were central to Jewish and Christian worship, and early Christian writers commented on them extensively.

The Book of Ruth is a short anonymous Hebrew narrative in the Hebrew Bible. It is one of the Five Megillot in the Writings, while the Greek and Christian canons place it after Judges. The date is uncertain, but many scholars assign it to the Persian period. It tells how Ruth, a Moabite widow, stays loyal to her mother-in-law Naomi, goes with her to Bethlehem and marries their kinsman Boaz. Their son Obed became David's grandfather. Ruth appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, and the book is read in synagogues at Shavuot.

Sirach, also called Ecclesiasticus or the Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach, is a Jewish wisdom book. Jesus ben Sira, a scribe in Jerusalem, wrote it in Hebrew around 196–175 BC. His grandson translated it into Greek in Egypt after 132 BC and added a prologue. The prologue is an early witness to the threefold division of the Hebrew scriptures. The book offers ethical teaching, praise of wisdom and a hymn to Israel's famous ancestors. Judaism excludes it from the Hebrew Bible, but it is in the Septuagint and was widely read in the early Church.

The Song of Songs, also called the Song of Solomon or Canticle of Canticles, is a book of love poetry in the Hebrew Bible. It is one of the five megillot of the Ketuvim. Its superscription links it with Solomon, but its author is unknown. Its date is disputed: estimates range from the monarchic period to the Hellenistic age. In a series of dialogues, a woman and her beloved express their desire for each other. Jewish tradition read it as an allegory of God and Israel. Christian writers such as Origen and Gregory of Nyssa read it as an allegory of Christ and the Church or the soul.

Susanna is an anonymous Jewish narrative in Greek, one of the additions to the Book of Daniel, probably composed in the second or first century BC. Set among the exiles in Babylon, it tells how Susanna, the virtuous wife of Joacim, is falsely accused of adultery by two elders whose advances she refused, and is saved when the young Daniel cross-examines them separately. It survives in the Old Greek and in Theodotion's later revision, which became standard in Christian Bibles, where it is often numbered as Daniel 13.

Tobit is an anonymous Jewish narrative from the Second Temple period, usually dated to the 3rd or early 2nd century BC and probably first written in Aramaic or Hebrew. It tells of the pious, blinded exile Tobit in Nineveh and his son Tobias, who travels guided by the angel Raphael. On the way Tobias frees Sarah from the demon Asmodeus and marries her, and Tobit's sight is restored. The short recension, preserved in Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus, is one of several ancient forms of this deuterocanonical book.

The Wisdom of Solomon, or Book of Wisdom, is a Jewish wisdom book written in Greek, probably by an Alexandrian author. Most scholars date it to the first century BC, though proposed dates vary. It speaks in the voice of Solomon and urges rulers to love righteousness. It praises wisdom as a divine spirit present with God from eternity, defends the immortality of the righteous, and retells the Exodus. It is part of the Septuagint and is counted as deuterocanonical by Catholic and Orthodox churches. Protestants class it among the Apocrypha. It shaped early Christian theology.

The Book of Zechariah is the eleventh of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It is attributed to Zechariah, son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, a prophet active from about 520 BC under the Persian king Darius I. Chapters 1–8 contain eight night visions and oracles urging the returned exiles to repent and rebuild the Temple. Chapters 9–14, often assigned by scholars to later authors, hold oracles about a coming king and the future of Jerusalem. Christian writers frequently read these passages as messianic prophecy.

The Book of Zephaniah (Latin Sophonias) is the ninth of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew Bible, a short prophetic book of three chapters. It is attributed to Zephaniah, who prophesied in the reign of Josiah of Judah (640–609 BC). Many scholars date it to that period, though others think an original core was later expanded. It announces the coming "day of the Lord" as a day of judgement on Judah and the nations, and ends with promises that a humble remnant will be restored. Its imagery inspired the medieval hymn Dies irae.

The Dendermonde Codex, kept at the Benedictine abbey of Saints Peter and Paul in Dendermonde, is a twelfth-century liturgical manuscript with musical notation. It is one of the two main sources for the liturgical songs of Hildegard of Bingen (1098–1179), known as the Symphonia armonie celestium revelationum. Its antiphons and responsories address the Trinity, the Virgin Mary and the saints, and include "O magne pater" and "Ave Maria, o auctrix vitae". The codex was probably prepared at Hildegard's convent of Rupertsberg around 1175. It is the earliest surviving collection of her music.

Einsiedeln, Stiftsbibliothek, Codex 121 is an anonymous Latin liturgical manuscript from the tenth century, generally linked to the Benedictine abbey of Einsiedeln in present-day Switzerland. It is a notated gradual: it contains the sung proper chants of the Mass (introits, graduals, alleluias, offertories with their verses, and communions) for the church year, beginning with Advent. Its melodies are written in finely detailed neumes of the St Gall type. This makes it one of the most important early witnesses to Gregorian chant and a key source for the study of how the chant was performed.

This anonymous Latin liturgical chant book is now kept in the Bibliothèque cantonale jurassienne at Porrentruy, Switzerland, as manuscript 18. It is dated roughly between 800 and 1050. Its contents are the sung proper chants of the Mass, arranged by the church year and starting with the First Sunday of Advent. These include introits, graduals, offertories with their verses, and communions, and each chant is assigned a mode. Added pieces appear as well, among them the Advent processional antiphon "Ecce carissimi dies illa". The manuscript is a witness to the early medieval Gregorian repertory.

Codex 390 of the Abbey Library of Saint Gall is the first of two volumes of the Hartker Antiphoner, a Latin chant book for the Divine Office. It is traditionally linked to Hartker, a monk and recluse of Saint Gall, and dates from around the end of the tenth century. This volume holds the antiphons, responsories and verses of the night and day Offices, starting with the Advent cycle. Its detailed Saint Gall neumes make it one of the earliest and most important witnesses to Gregorian chant and its performance.

This Latin liturgical manuscript is the second volume of the Hartker Antiphoner, a two-volume collection of chants for the monastic Divine Office. It is traditionally linked with Hartker, a monk and recluse of the abbey of St Gall, and dates from around the late tenth century. It runs from Eastertide and Pentecost through the rest of the church year and includes chants for the saints. The antiphons and responsories are written with St Gall neumes. The Hartker Antiphoner is among the earliest and most important fully notated sources for Gregorian chant.

This is an anonymous Latin liturgical manuscript, or fragment of one, held in Prague under the shelfmark VI.E.4c. It contains chants for the Divine Office, such as antiphons, responsories, hymn incipits and versicles. Its texts are indexed by number in the Cantus chant database. The surviving sections cover weekdays of the second week of Lent, with Gospel antiphons on the sons of Zebedee and on Lazarus and the rich man. They also include the Common of Apostles, with the invitatory "Regem apostolorum" and the hymn "Aeterna Christi munera". Its exact date and origin are uncertain.

This anonymous Latin liturgical manuscript is held in the Erzbischöfliche Diözesan- und Dombibliothek, the cathedral and diocesan library of Cologne. It is a chant book for the Divine Office, probably copied between the ninth and eleventh centuries, though its exact date and origin are uncertain. Its contents follow the church year, beginning with the First Sunday of Advent. For Vespers, Lauds and Matins it gives antiphons, responsories, versicles, hymns and the invitatory with Psalm 95, and many chants carry modal assignments. It is a witness to the early medieval Office repertory of Gregorian chant.

This anonymous Latin liturgical book survives in Trier as manuscript 1245/597 of the Stadtbibliothek Weberbach. It is dated to the ninth or early tenth century. It contains chants for the Divine Office arranged by the liturgical year, starting with the First Sunday of Advent. These include antiphons, invitatories and the Matins responsories with their verses, such as "Aspiciens a longe" and "Missus est Gabriel." It is an early witness to the Carolingian-era repertory of Office chant.

This anonymous Latin liturgical manuscript, now held in the Stadtbibliothek Weberbach in Trier, is dated to roughly the ninth or early tenth century. It contains the chants of the Divine Office arranged in the order of the church year, beginning with the First Sunday of Advent. Its entries include antiphons, invitatories, and the great responsories with their verses for Matins, such as "Aspiciens a longe" and "Missus est Gabriel." As an early witness to the Carolingian-era Office repertory in the Frankish lands, it is valuable for studying how the Gregorian chant tradition was transmitted.

The Riesencodex ("giant codex"), now Wiesbaden, Hochschul- und Landesbibliothek RheinMain, Hs. 2, is a large Latin manuscript of the works of Hildegard of Bingen (d. 1179). It is generally thought to have been compiled at her Rupertsberg convent around or shortly after her death. Besides her visionary and other writings, it preserves her liturgical songs, the Symphonia, with musical notation. These include antiphons and responsories such as "O vis aeternitatis", "O magne pater" and "O virtus sapientiae". It is the most comprehensive surviving source for Hildegard's music.

Toledo, Catedral, Archivo y Biblioteca Capitulares, 44.1 is an anonymous Latin liturgical manuscript held in the chapter library of Toledo Cathedral. It is dated roughly to the late tenth or first half of the eleventh century. It is an antiphoner of the Divine Office, giving chants for the liturgical year in order. For each feast it lists the Matins responsories with their verses, beginning with Advent. Many are assigned modes. It is an early witness to the Office chant repertory and to how the Roman liturgy spread in the Iberian Peninsula.

This anonymous Latin liturgical manuscript is held in the chapter archive and library of Toledo Cathedral. It is an office antiphoner containing the sung chants of the Divine Office arranged through the liturgical year, starting with the First Sunday of Advent. The chants include antiphons, responsories with their verses, invitatories and hymns for Vespers and Matins, such as "Missus est Gabriel angelus" and "Aspiciens a longe." Its date and origin are uncertain, but it is usually placed between the ninth and eleventh centuries. It is a witness to the Latin chant repertory used in the Office.

Helsinki, National Library, F.m.I.26 is an anonymous Latin liturgical manuscript fragment containing chants for the Mass. It is dated approximately to between the ninth and the mid-eleventh century. The surviving leaves hold Proper chants from the Gregorian repertory, including introits, graduals with their verses, offertories and communions. These are assigned to days in the first and fourth weeks of Lent and to Easter Sunday, among them the Easter gradual Haec dies. Its exact origin is not recorded. Fragments like this one are evidence of how the chant repertory was transmitted in the early Middle Ages.

Albi, Bibliothèque municipale Rochegude, 44 is an anonymous Latin liturgical manuscript, an antiphoner for the Divine Office, usually dated to the late ninth or early tenth century. It is now held in the municipal library of Albi in southern France. It sets out the chants of the liturgical year, beginning with the First Sunday of Advent. These include the responsories and verses sung at Matins, such as "Aspiciens a longe" and "Missus est Gabriel." As one of the early surviving office antiphoners, it is an important witness to the Frankish form of Gregorian chant.

This is an anonymous Latin liturgical manuscript dated to roughly the tenth century, about 910 to 1010. It is an antiphoner, a book of chants for the Divine Office, and is generally linked to the abbey of Saint-Martial at Limoges in Aquitaine. It gives antiphons, responsories, versicles and invitatories through the church year, opening with the Advent cycle. Many chants appear only as short opening words. It is valued as an early witness to the Office repertory of southern France and to Aquitanian chant practice.

Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, Latin 1090 is an anonymous Latin liturgical manuscript dated broadly to between about 800 and 1050. It contains chants for the Divine Office, the kind of book usually called an antiphoner. The chants are arranged by the liturgical year, beginning with the First Sunday of Advent. They include responsories and verses for Matins, antiphons for Lauds and hymns, mostly drawn from Isaiah and the other prophets. Each chant has its modal assignment. Its origin and the community that used it are not established.

Paris, BnF, Latin 1240 is an anonymous tenth-century Latin liturgical manuscript generally associated with the Abbey of Saint-Martial at Limoges in Aquitaine. It preserves chants for the Mass and the Divine Office, including tropes and Office antiphons and responsories for feasts such as John the Baptist, Peter, Martial of Limoges, and John and Paul. Its chants for Saint Martial reflect the abbey's devotion to its patron. It is an important early witness to Aquitanian chant and to the Saint-Martial musical tradition.

Latin liturgical manuscript held in Paris (Bibliothèque nationale de France, Latin 12601). It is an anonymous medieval source of chants for the Divine Office, roughly dated between the ninth and mid-eleventh centuries. Its contents include invitatories, hymns such as Somno refectis artubus, antiphons, responsories and versicles. They are arranged by liturgical day and Office hour, including the weekday Matins and Lauds of the ordinary season, and there is a section of additions. As a witness to early Office chant, it is catalogued chant by chant in the Cantus index.

Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, nouvelles acquisitions latines 1411, is an anonymous Latin liturgical manuscript containing chants for the Divine Office. It is usually dated to roughly the ninth to eleventh centuries. Its antiphons, responsories and versicles are arranged by feast and by hour: Lauds, Prime, Terce, Sext, None and Vespers. It opens with the office of the Holy Trinity, including "O beata et benedicta et gloriosa trinitas," and continues with the first Sunday of Advent. The manuscript is a witness to the early medieval Latin chant repertory.

This is an anonymous Latin liturgical manuscript held in the Bibliothèque nationale de France as nouvelle acquisition latine 1412, dated approximately to between the ninth and mid-eleventh centuries. It contains chants for the Divine Office, including responsories, verses, antiphons and invitatories, each with its mode. The surviving sequence includes Matins chants for the feast of the Holy Trinity, such as "O beata trinitas", and Vespers and Matins chants for Saint Stephen, the first martyr. Its origin and exact date are not established.

This anonymous Latin liturgical manuscript is kept in the treasury of the Collegiate Church of San Lorenzo in Chiavenna, northern Italy, now the Museo Capitolare, and has no shelfmark. It dates to roughly 950–1050 and contains chants for the Divine Office. These are responsories with their verses for Matins and antiphons for Lauds, arranged through the liturgical year from the First Sunday of Advent. It is evidence of the chant repertory used in the Alpine and Lombard region around the eleventh century.

Vercelli, Biblioteca Capitolare, CLXX is an anonymous Latin liturgical manuscript held in the chapter library of Vercelli in northern Italy. It contains the chants of the Divine Office arranged by the liturgical year, starting with the First Sunday of Advent. These include antiphons, responsories, hymns such as Conditor alme siderum and Verbum supernum prodiens, invitatories and versicles for Vespers, Matins and the other hours. Its date is only roughly established, somewhere between about 800 and 1050. It is a witness to the early medieval Office chant tradition in Italy.

The Xuting Mishisuo jing, or Sutra of Jesus the Messiah, is an anonymous Chinese Christian text of the Church of the East. It is one of the Jingjiao Documents and is usually counted among the oldest of them. It is generally dated to the years after Alopen's mission reached China in 635, though the exact date is uncertain. The text sets out teaching about the invisible, all-present Lord of Heaven, moral precepts and the life of Jesus. It borrows heavily from Buddhist vocabulary. The manuscript is reported to have come from the Mogao Caves at Dunhuang.

The Hymn to the Three Majesties is an anonymous liturgical hymn of the Church of the East in Tang China, the "Brilliant Teaching" (Jingjiao). It was written in Literary Chinese, probably in the eighth or early ninth century, and survives among the manuscripts recovered at Dunhuang. It praises the Trinity: the merciful Father A-lo-hê, the Son Mi-shih-hê, called the Lamb who bears the sins of the world, and the Holy Spirit. It is generally regarded as an adaptation of the Syriac Gloria in excelsis. It is one of the earliest surviving Christian hymns in Chinese.

The Zunjing is an anonymous liturgical text of the Church of the East in China, written in Literary Chinese and dated roughly between the late eighth and tenth centuries. It begins by worshipping the Trinity as Father Aluohe, Son Mishihe and the Holy Spirit. It then honours a list of saints called "spiritual kings", among them John, Luke, Matthew, Mark and Paul. A catalogue of sacred books follows, with titles given in Chinese. This makes it an important witness to the scriptures and veneration of Tang-era Christianity.

The Xi'an Stele inscription is a Literary Chinese text with Syriac additions. It was composed by Jingjing, a monk of the Church of the East whose Syriac name was Adam, and set up in 781 under the Tang dynasty. It opens with a doctrinal eulogy covering the Trinity, creation, the fall and redemption. It then tells the history of the "Luminous Religion" in China from the missionary Alopen's arrival in 635. The stele was buried in the ninth century and found again in 1625. It is the chief witness to early Christianity in China.

The Pilgrimage of Etheria (Peregrinatio or Itinerarium Egeriae) is a Latin travel account by a Christian woman, usually called Egeria, who probably came from Hispania or Gaul. She wrote it as a long letter to a circle of women at home, describing a journey of about 381–384. It survives only in incomplete form. It was once attributed to Silvia of Aquitaine. Egeria describes Sinai, Jerusalem, Egypt and Edessa, and then the liturgical year in Jerusalem. The account is the earliest of its kind and an important source for early Christian worship and for late spoken Latin.

The Gospel of John is the fourth of the canonical Gospels of the New Testament. Tradition attributes it to the apostle John, though modern scholars dispute who wrote it. It is usually dated to about 90–100. It opens with a prologue on the divine Word (Logos) made flesh. It then tells of Jesus' signs, long discourses, farewell teaching to his disciples, passion and resurrection. Its strong emphasis on Christ's divinity made it central to early Trinitarian and Christological debate. Origen, John Chrysostom, Augustine and Cyril of Alexandria all wrote major commentaries on it.

The Gospel according to Luke is the third of the canonical Gospels of the New Testament, written in Greek, probably around 75–90. Tradition attributes it to Luke, companion of Paul, who also wrote the Acts of the Apostles, but the work itself is anonymous. Addressed to Theophilus, it tells of Jesus from the births of John the Baptist and Jesus to the resurrection and ascension. It is noted for its infancy narratives, its parables, and its concern for the poor and outcast.

The Gospel according to Mark is the second book of the New Testament and is generally thought to be the earliest of the four canonical gospels. Most scholars date it to about 65–75. Tradition attributes it to John Mark, a companion of Peter, but the authorship is uncertain. Written in Greek, it is a short, fast-moving account that runs from John the Baptist's preaching through Jesus' ministry in Galilee to his passion in Jerusalem and the empty tomb. Matthew and Luke drew heavily on it. It was soon translated into Latin, Syriac, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian, Georgian and Slavonic.

The Gospel of Matthew is the first book of the New Testament and one of the three Synoptic Gospels. It was written in Greek, probably between about 70 and 100, and is traditionally attributed to the apostle Matthew, although its author is unknown. It opens with Jesus' genealogy from Abraham and goes on to tell of his birth, ministry, teaching, death and resurrection. It includes the Sermon on the Mount and stresses Jesus as the fulfilment of Jewish scripture. In the early Church it was the most widely cited gospel.

This sermon for Holy Wednesday is attributed to John Chrysostom but is not his work. It survives in Church Slavonic and is thought to date from about the late ninth or tenth century. Whether it was written in Slavonic or translated from a Greek original is uncertain. It starts from the Gospel verse in which the Pharisees plot to destroy Jesus for healing a withered hand on the Sabbath. This sermon survives in Church Slavonic under the name of John Chrysostom, but it is not his work and belongs to the large body of writings falsely attributed to him. This sermon for New Sunday, the Sunday after Easter, is falsely attributed to John Chrysostom. It survives in Church Slavonic and is dated roughly to the late ninth or tenth century, although its exact origin is uncertain. The preacher returns to the story of the apostle Thomas, who doubted the Resurrection until he saw and touched the risen Christ and then confessed him as Lord and God. The homily presents Thomas's absence and doubt as part of God's providence and argues that "the disciple's unbelief became the mother of our faith."

This sermon in praise of the apostle Thomas survives in Church Slavonic. It carries a heading that names John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople, as its author, but it is counted among the many works wrongly attributed to him. The Slavonic text is usually dated to roughly the late ninth or tenth century. The title also presents it as a sermon against the Arians. It opens with a run of rhetorical paradoxes: Thomas is dead yet deathless, buried below yet shining above, and his relics are spread across the whole world, which they light like the sun.

This homily for the feast of the Annunciation (25 March) survives in Church Slavonic under the name of John Chrysostom. It is not his work, however, and belongs to the large body of sermons transmitted as Pseudo-Chrysostom. Its origin and date are uncertain, though the Slavonic form is placed roughly in the late ninth or tenth century. It retells the Annunciation as a lively dialogue in which Mary questions and challenges Gabriel. The angel answers with paradoxes about the virgin birth, Christ's divinity and his everlasting Davidic kingdom.

This is a festal sermon for the feast of the Annunciation on 25 March. It is attributed to John Chrysostom, but the attribution is spurious and the real author is unknown. The homily survives in Church Slavonic and was most likely translated from a Greek original in the early Slavonic literary period of the late ninth or tenth century. Written in a rhetorical style built on repetition ("Once again… Gabriel was sent…"), it treats Gabriel's message to Mary as the undoing of the serpent's words to Eve. It presents the Incarnation as a mystery to be proclaimed rather than investigated.

This Church Slavonic homily is attributed to John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople (died 407). It expounds two parables from Matthew 25: the ten virgins awaiting the bridegroom and the talents entrusted to servants. Its heading says it comes from Chrysostom's commentary on the Gospel of Matthew and assigns it to Holy Tuesday, the day these parables are read in Holy Week. It probably reworks material from his Greek homilies on Matthew. The Slavonic version is generally dated to the late ninth or tenth century. It shows how Chrysostom's preaching was adapted for liturgical use among the early Slavs.

This sermon for Holy Thursday survives in Church Slavonic under the name of John Chrysostom but is not his work. It is one of many anonymous homilies wrongly credited to him. It probably dates from the early period of Slavonic literature, roughly the late ninth or tenth century, and it may be a translation of a lost or unidentified Greek original. The preacher sets the coming joy of the Resurrection against the betrayal of Christ. In vivid, rhetorical language he condemns Judas for selling his master. He also attacks the Jewish leaders who paid for the betrayal.

This sermon for Holy Tuesday of Passion Week survives in Church Slavonic under the name of John Chrysostom, but the attribution is not considered authentic. It is thought to date from the early period of Slavonic Christian literature, roughly the late ninth or tenth century. Whether it was translated from a Greek original is uncertain. The preacher opens by comparing himself to a mother who has no milk for her children. He then comments on the Gospel of John's account of the Jewish leaders meeting in council against Jesus and asking, "What shall we do?"

This is a sermon for Great (Holy) Monday on Christ cursing the barren fig tree near Bethany (Matthew 21:18–19). It is attributed in its heading to John Chrysostom, archbishop of Constantinople, but is not his work and belongs to the large body of Pseudo-Chrysostom writings. It survives in Church Slavonic and is thought to date from roughly the late ninth or tenth century. The preacher imagines himself following Christ to witness the withered tree, then explains the miracle and its meaning for the Holy Week liturgy.

This sermon on the raising of Lazarus (John 11) is attributed to John Chrysostom but is not by him. It survives in Church Slavonic and is roughly dated to the late ninth or tenth century; its true author is unknown. The preacher answers opponents who said that Christ's prayer before raising Lazarus proved the Son inferior to the Father. He argues that the prayer was an act of condescension, made for the weakness of the onlookers, and compares it with Christ washing the disciples' feet, including those of Judas.

This sermon on the raising of Lazarus (John 11) is attributed in its heading to John Chrysostom but is not regarded as his work. It survives in Church Slavonic and is usually placed in the early period of Slavonic literature, roughly the late ninth or tenth century. It may be a translation of a lost Greek original, but its origin and author are unknown. The preacher opens with an image of a nursing mother whose milk has dried up. He uses it to explain why his earlier sermon broke off, then takes up the Gospel story again and explains it.

This homily is a Church Slavonic version of part of John Chrysostom's exposition of the Gospel of Matthew. The Greek original is among the homilies on Matthew he preached at Antioch around 390. The Slavonic translation is generally dated to the late ninth or tenth century, the early period of Slavonic literature. It comments on Matthew 27:62–64, where the chief priests and Pharisees ask Pilate to seal Christ's tomb. Chrysostom argues that their precautions unwillingly confirm Christ's death, burial and resurrection, and he praises the disciples' honesty in hiding nothing.

This sermon for Holy Wednesday is attributed in its heading to John Chrysostom, but it is not his work and is assigned to Pseudo-Chrysostom. It survives in Church Slavonic and is roughly dated to the late ninth or tenth century. Whether it was first written in Slavonic or translated from a Greek original is uncertain. It retells the Gospel story of the sinful woman who washed Christ's feet with her tears in the Pharisee's house. It presents her as a teacher of repentance during the Lenten fast and stresses Christ's mercy and love for humankind.

This sermon for Palm Sunday survives in Church Slavonic and is attributed to John Chrysostom, though the attribution is not genuine. It is generally placed in the early period of Slavonic writing, roughly the late ninth or tenth century. Whether it was translated from a Greek original or first written in Slavonic is uncertain. The preacher compares the Gospel miracles to the links of a golden chain and calls all nations to rejoice at Christ's entry into Jerusalem. He presents the feast as a victory song that follows the struggle of the Lenten fast.

This Easter sermon survives in Church Slavonic under the name of John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople, but it is not his work and belongs to the large body of writings falsely attributed to him. Its author is unknown, and it is roughly dated to the late ninth or tenth century. It takes as its text Luke's account of the two disciples walking to Emmaus. In a run of rhetorical exclamations it describes the fear that scattered the apostles after Christ's arrest: Peter's denial, John's flight and Thomas's unbelief. It shows how sermons under Chrysostom's name spread in early Slavonic preaching.

This Easter sermon survives in Church Slavonic and is attributed in its heading to John Chrysostom, archbishop of Constantinople. The attribution is false, so it is counted among the Pseudo-Chrysostom writings. Its author and date are uncertain, and it may be translated from a lost Greek original. It is assigned to the Monday after Easter. The sermon celebrates Christ's resurrection as the defeat of the devil, Hades and death, and argues that death is now called repose and sleep. It draws on the Psalms, Genesis, Job and Paul's cry "Death, where is your sting?"

The Tale of the Soldier is an anonymous edifying narrative in Church Slavonic, dated approximately to the late ninth or tenth century. It is probably a translation or adaptation of a Byzantine Greek model. It is a first-person account by a man who died in sin and saw the torments of the afterlife. Two angels then return him to his body, which is foul and dark next to his shining soul, so that he can repent and warn others. The tale belongs to the early Slavonic literature of visions and moral instruction on death, judgement and repentance.

This short anonymous Church Slavonic hagiographical text gives the prayer said to have been spoken by Pionius, a presbyter of Smyrna who was burned alive for his faith, usually dated to the Decian persecution around 250. Its introduction says the prayer was taken from another writing and that he was weakened by long suspension. Kneeling before the fire, he addresses Christ as the Word, the Father's power and the steward of creation. Its relationship to the Greek Martyrdom of Pionius is uncertain.

This anonymous hagiographical passion, read on 24 March, tells of the martyrdom of Artemon, a priest of Laodicea, during the persecution under Emperor Diocletian. The text opens with an imperial inspection of pagan shrines. Bishop Sisinnius and the priest Artemon smash and burn the idols in the temple of Artemis, and after pagans denounce them the visiting count turns against the Christians gathered in the church. Its heading also calls the saint Artemius. The Church Slavonic version is probably a translation of an earlier Greek passion. It is dated roughly to the late ninth or tenth century.

This anonymous hagiographical account, preserved in Church Slavonic and assigned for reading on 7 March, tells of the bishops martyred at Cherson (Chersonesus) in the Crimea. It is usually dated between the late ninth and tenth centuries. Tradition holds that these bishops were sent to the region around the early fourth century. The account centres on Basil, killed by the pagans of the city, and Capito, who is said to have come unharmed out of a burning furnace. It is an important witness to the early Christian traditions of Cherson, a city later linked to the conversion of Rus'.

This anonymous Church Slavonic hagiographical text is assigned in its heading to 5 March. It tells of the martyrdom of Saint Basiliscus at Comana in Pontus under the emperor Maximian and the governor Agrippa, successor of Asclepiodotus. Basiliscus is held in prison and grieves that he has been called later than his fellow martyrs. Christ appears to him and promises him martyrdom at Comana. The prison doors open and he sets out with his guards to settle his affairs in his home village. The text probably dates from the early Slavonic period and most likely derives from a Greek passion.

This anonymous Church Slavonic passion tells of the martyrdom of Saint Quadratus and his companions, commemorated on 10 March. It probably dates from the late ninth or tenth century. It is set at Nicomedia in Bithynia during the persecution under the emperors Decius and Valerian. Christians from many cities were imprisoned there and pressed to eat sacrificial food. Quadratus, a wealthy and noble believer, bribes the guards so he can care for the prisoners and encourage the fearful, and he himself goes on to confess Christ. The text belongs to the early Slavonic tradition of readings for saints' days.

This anonymous hagiographical account survives in Church Slavonic and is assigned to 23 March. It probably dates from the late ninth or tenth century. It tells of the martyrdom of Saint Dometius and his disciples under the emperor Julian the Apostate (361–363). It opens with a hostile portrait of Julian as a former cleric who had abandoned the faith. At Antioch he persecutes Christians and desecrates the great church built by Constantine, before setting out on campaign against the Persians. It is one of the early Slavonic readings for the commemoration of saints.

This anonymous Church Slavonic hagiographical account of martyrdom is read on 29 March. It tells the story of Jonah and Barachisius, two Christian brothers from the Persian village of Iasa. They were put to death in the persecution under King Shapur II, which the text dates to the eighteenth year of his reign. The brothers went to encourage nine imprisoned Christians, were arrested by the Magi, refused to sacrifice, and were tortured and killed. The Slavonic version belongs to the wider tradition of the Persian martyr acts, which survive in Syriac and Greek.

This anonymous Church Slavonic hagiographical text, read on 26 March, tells the martyrdom of Irenaeus, bishop of Sirmium in Pannonia. He died in the persecution under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, traditionally dated to around 304. It is a version of an older passion narrative and follows the usual form of martyr acts. Irenaeus is arrested and questioned by the governor Probus. He refuses to sacrifice to the gods, is imprisoned and tortured, and stays steadfast in his faith until his execution.

An anonymous hagiographical account of the martyrdom of Paul and his sister Juliana, commemorated on 4 March. It survives in Church Slavonic and is dated roughly to the late ninth or tenth century; it may derive from an earlier Greek passion. According to tradition, the siblings were Christians executed at Ptolemais in Phoenicia under the emperor Aurelian in the 270s. The text sets out their trials before Aurelian in lively dialogue. Paul denounces the emperor's idolatry, and Juliana turns down his flattery and promises, holding to Christ through torture.

This anonymous hagiographical text is a Church Slavonic version of the Greek Martyrdom of Pionius. It tells of the arrest, trial and execution of Pionius, a priest of Smyrna, in the persecution under the emperor Decius around 250. Pionius was arrested together with Sabina, Asclepiades and others, and the account records his speeches to the crowds and his debates with the magistrates. The Greek original presents itself as partly based on Pionius's own writings. It is valued as an early martyr act. The Slavonic translation, read on 12 March, probably dates from the early centuries of Slavonic literature.

The Passion of Sabinus is an anonymous hagiographical account of a martyr's death, read for his commemoration on 13 March. It survives in Church Slavonic and is dated roughly to the late ninth or tenth century, probably drawing on an earlier Greek passion. It is set in Egypt during Diocletian's persecution. Sabinus, a Christian of noble birth and a leading man of his city, hides in a hut outside the city with other believers, devoting himself to fasting and prayer. A beggar betrays him for two gold coins, and his arrest leads to his martyrdom.

This anonymous hagiographical account of martyrdom survives in Church Slavonic and is assigned to the reading for 20 March. It was probably translated from a Greek passion in the early period of Slavonic literature, roughly the late ninth or tenth century. It is set during the persecution of Emperor Decius in the mid-third century. When Fortunatianus, governor of Africa, demands sacrifice to the gods, many townspeople give up their faith, but forty Christians encourage one another to stand firm. Led by Terentius, Africanus and Pompeius, they endure trial and torture before dying as martyrs.

The Passion of Trophimus and Eucarpion is an anonymous hagiographical text in Church Slavonic. It was probably composed or translated between the late ninth and the tenth century and is assigned to 22 March. It tells of two soldiers who serve a governor during an imperial persecution and are known for torturing Christians. On their way to arrest believers, a fiery voice from the air rebukes them and calls them to share the martyrs' lot. They are converted and later suffer martyrdom themselves. The account belongs to early Slavonic collections of saints' readings arranged by calendar day.

This anonymous hagiographical account of the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste is read on their feast day, 9 March. It survives in Church Slavonic and was probably made between the late ninth and tenth centuries, most likely from a Greek passion. It tells how forty Christian soldiers from Cappadocia, serving under the emperor Licinius, refused the governor Agricola's order to sacrifice to the gods. According to the standard tradition, they were then left to freeze on a lake at Sebaste. The account helped spread one of the most widely venerated martyr cults of the early Church.

This anonymous hagiographical passion, preserved in Church Slavonic for the feast of 7 March, celebrates the Forty-Two Martyrs of Amorium. These were Byzantine officers and officials, among them Theodore, Constantine, Theophilus, Callistus and Bassoes, who were captured when the Abbasids sacked Amorium in 838. After years in captivity they refused to convert to Islam and were executed at Samarra in 845. It opens as a sermon praising the martyrs for giving up worldly rank and glory for heavenly reward. Several Greek passions of these martyrs exist, and the Slavonic text probably derives from one of them.

This sermon for Palm Sunday is attributed to Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople in the ninth century, and survives in Church Slavonic. It is unclear whether it was translated from a lost Greek original. The preacher pictures himself in Bethany among the children who greet Christ with "Hosanna in the highest," carrying branches and spreading their garments. He contrasts their simple praise with the hostility of the scribes and teachers who were plotting Christ's death. The homily also deals with the raising of Lazarus, which the Byzantine calendar commemorates on the day before Palm Sunday.

This anonymous martyrdom account in Church Slavonic is set for 15 March, the day Alexander, a priest of Side in Pamphylia, is commemorated. It belongs to the early layer of Slavonic hagiography, probably of the late ninth or tenth century, and was most likely translated from a Greek original. Most of the text is a dialogue between Alexander and the governor Antoninus. Alexander openly confesses that he is a Christian priest and defends the saving death of Christ. He then refuses to sacrifice to the gods, which leads to his trials and martyrdom.

The Life of Aninas the Wonderworker is an anonymous hagiographical account of the venerable Aninas, an ascetic honoured in the Eastern Church as a monk and worker of miracles. It survives in Church Slavonic and is dated roughly to the late ninth or tenth century. It may depend on an earlier Greek original, but that is not certain. In its prologue the author says he wrote at the request of a devout patron, so that the deeds of holy people would teach and encourage readers to live virtuously. The Life then tells of Aninas's ascetic struggles and wonders.

This anonymous Church Slavonic hagiographical text is a short Life of Pope Gregory I (Gregory the Great, c. 540–604), assigned to 11 March in the Slavonic liturgical calendar. It is dated approximately to the late ninth or tenth century. It recalls Gregory's time as abbot of the monastery of Saint Andrew on the Clivus Scauri in Rome, and his mother Silvia. Its opening story shows his generosity to a shipwrecked captain who keeps returning to beg. The text shows how Western saints were honoured in early Slavonic devotion.

This anonymous hagiography tells the story of James (Jacob), a hermit near the city of Porphyrion. He lived for fifteen years in a cave and received the gift of working miracles, but through negligence he fell. He seduced a young woman and then murdered her. His long and severe repentance restores him to holiness. The Life is framed as a lesson on humility and the power of repentance. The legend is set in sixth-century Palestine and circulated widely in Greek, Syriac, Latin and Slavonic. This Slavonic version probably dates from the late ninth or tenth century.

This hagiographical Life of John the Silent (or Hesychast) was written in Greek by the monk Cyril of Scythopolis in the mid-sixth century and later translated into Church Slavonic. It follows John from his birth at Nicopolis in Armenia in 454 to the church and community he founded there. It then describes his brief term as bishop of Colonia and his long life as a recluse at the Great Lavra of Saint Sabbas in Palestine. Cyril knew John personally, which makes the Life an important source for Palestinian monasticism.

This is an anonymous hagiographical life of Isaac, a fourth-century ascetic from the East who settled near Constantinople. It survives in Church Slavonic and is assigned to 21 March. It is probably a translation from a Greek original, though its exact source and date are uncertain. The narrative opens with the conversion of Constantine and the rise of the Arian heresy. It then tells of Isaac's opposition to the Arian emperor Valens, whose death he foretold. Isaac later founded a monastery in the capital, which took its name from his disciple and successor Dalmatius.

This Church Slavonic hagiographical reading for 19 March tells the life of Paul the Simple, an Egyptian hermit of the fourth century. It is taken from the account in the Lausiac History of Palladius of Helenopolis, written around 420, and was later adapted for liturgical reading in the Slavonic tradition. It tells how Paul, an elderly farmer, found his wife was unfaithful and left her. He went to Anthony the Great, who tested his obedience severely before accepting him as a disciple. Paul became known for his innocent simplicity and for his gifts of healing and casting out demons.

The Gospel of John is the fourth of the canonical Gospels of the New Testament. Tradition attributes it to the apostle John, though modern scholars dispute who wrote it. It is usually dated to about 90–100. It opens with a prologue on the divine Word (Logos) made flesh. It then tells of Jesus' signs, long discourses, farewell teaching to his disciples, passion and resurrection. Its strong emphasis on Christ's divinity made it central to early Trinitarian and Christological debate. Origen, John Chrysostom, Augustine and Cyril of Alexandria all wrote major commentaries on it.

The Gospel according to Luke is the third of the canonical Gospels of the New Testament, written in Greek, probably around 75–90. Tradition attributes it to Luke, companion of Paul, who also wrote the Acts of the Apostles, but the work itself is anonymous. Addressed to Theophilus, it tells of Jesus from the births of John the Baptist and Jesus to the resurrection and ascension. It is noted for its infancy narratives, its parables, and its concern for the poor and outcast.

The Gospel according to Mark is the second book of the New Testament and is generally thought to be the earliest of the four canonical gospels. Most scholars date it to about 65–75. Tradition attributes it to John Mark, a companion of Peter, but the authorship is uncertain. Written in Greek, it is a short, fast-moving account that runs from John the Baptist's preaching through Jesus' ministry in Galilee to his passion in Jerusalem and the empty tomb. Matthew and Luke drew heavily on it. It was soon translated into Latin, Syriac, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian, Georgian and Slavonic.

The Gospel of Matthew is the first book of the New Testament and one of the three Synoptic Gospels. It was written in Greek, probably between about 70 and 100, and is traditionally attributed to the apostle Matthew, although its author is unknown. It opens with Jesus' genealogy from Abraham and goes on to tell of his birth, ministry, teaching, death and resurrection. It includes the Sermon on the Mount and stresses Jesus as the fulfilment of Jewish scripture. In the early Church it was the most widely cited gospel.

The Life of Constantine-Cyril is an anonymous Old Church Slavonic hagiography of Constantine the Philosopher (826/7–869). He took the monastic name Cyril shortly before his death in Rome. With the Life of Methodius, it makes up the so-called Pannonian Legends. It was probably written soon after 869, perhaps by Methodius or his disciples. The text tells of Constantine's education in Constantinople, his missions to the Arabs and Khazars, his creation of a Slavic alphabet and the Moravian mission. It is a principal source on the origins of Slavic letters.

The Life of Methodius is an anonymous Church Slavonic hagiography of Methodius (d. 885), archbishop of Moravia and Pannonia and, with his brother Constantine-Cyril, an apostle to the Slavs. Together with the Life of Constantine it is known as the Pannonian Legends. It was probably written soon after his death, around 885–890, possibly by one of his disciples. It covers his early career, the Moravian mission, his conflicts with the Frankish clergy, his papal support and his translation work. It is a key source for Great Moravia and early Slavonic literature.

An Old Irish poem from the ninth century, set in a short prose frame. The frame attributes it to Daniél ua Líathaiti, head (airchinnech) of the monastery of Lismore. He was the soul-friend (anmchara) of a woman who tried to seduce him. In the verses he refuses her, urging her to think of the Last Judgement, the decay of all things and the loss of heaven through sin. He blesses her and sends her home. The prose closes by saying that she followed his guidance for the rest of her life.

A Dé dúilig atat-teoch ("O Creator God, I invoke thee") is a Middle Irish poem on the Psalms. It is attributed to Airbertach mac Coise, a scholar of the monastic school of Ros Ailithir (Roscarbery) in Munster who died in 1016, and is usually dated to about 982. It opens with a personal prayer in which the poet calls Christ his king, his law and his confidant and gives Him body, heart and soul. The poem then turns to the Psalter. It is an example of the verse that Irish monastic scholars wrote in the vernacular to teach biblical learning.

It is an example of the verse that Irish monastic scholars wrote in the vernacular to teach biblical learning.

A Marbáin, a díthrubaig, known in English as "King and Hermit", is an anonymous Old Irish poem usually dated to about the ninth or tenth century. It is a dialogue between Guaire Aidne, the seventh-century king of Connacht, and his half-brother Marbán, a hermit. When Guaire asks why he does not sleep in a bed, Marbán describes his hut in the woods and the animals, birds, springs and wild foods around it. The poem is one of the best-known examples of early Irish nature and hermit poetry.

Adram in Coimdid ("Let us adore the Lord") is a short anonymous Old Irish religious poem, usually dated to the ninth century. It is a hymn of praise that calls on the reader to worship God as the maker of wondrous works. It names parts of creation as signs of his power, beginning with the great bright heaven and its angels and the white-waved sea upon the earth. The poem is a small but typical example of early Irish devotional verse that praises God through nature.

Mór ndrúiss, mór mbáis is a short anonymous saying in Old Irish, probably composed between the seventh and ninth centuries, though its exact date and origin are uncertain. It is a piece of religious gnomic verse that lists lust, folly, frenzy and madness one after another. It then states that because death is certain, the greatest folly is to live against the will of Mary's son, Christ. It is a typical example of the brief, pointed moral verse of early Irish Christianity.

Apgitir Chrábaid ("The Alphabet of Piety") is an Old Irish devotional and ascetic treatise attributed to Colmán maccu Béognae, an early seventh-century Irish monastic founder. The attribution and date are uncertain: estimates run from about 600 to the eighth century. If the early date is right, it is one of the oldest surviving works of Irish prose. It is built from short paired formulas and sets out the virtues of the religious life. It teaches that fear of God leads to repentance, love, keeping the commandments and, in the end, eternal life in heaven.

Baile Bricín (The Vision of Bricín) is an anonymous Old Irish prophetic text, usually dated to around the ninth century. It is set at Tuaim Dreccon (Tomregan), the monastery of the seventh-century abbot Saint Bricín. Kept from church by illness on Easter night, Bricín prays for a messenger from heaven. An angel comes between midnight and matins, opens his eyes to see the heavenly host around the altar, and tells him what lies ahead for Ireland and its churches, including foreign invasion and the persecution of the Church. It belongs to the medieval Irish tradition of visionary prophecy.

Betha Adamnáin is an anonymous Irish prose Life of Adomnán (c. 624–704), abbot of Iona and author of the Life of Columba. It is usually dated to about 956–964. It opens with a Latin and Irish homily on Job's command "Gird up thy loins like a man", praising saints who master the flesh. It then tells episodes from Adomnán's career, especially his dealings with Irish kings. Rather than being a reliable account of the seventh century, it is valued as evidence of the concerns of the tenth-century Columban community.

Bethu Brigte is an anonymous early Irish prose Life of Saint Brigit of Kildare, Ireland's foremost female saint. It is usually dated to the first half of the ninth century and is one of the earliest saints' lives written largely in the Irish language, with passages in Latin. The beginning is lost. It tells of Brigit's birth to an enslaved woman, her upbringing in a druid's household, and the miracles of her life. It is closely related to the Latin Vita Prima of Brigit and is an important witness to her early cult.

Bríathra Flainn Fína maic Ossu is an anonymous Old Irish wisdom text, probably composed between the seventh and ninth centuries. It is attributed to Flann Fína son of Oswiu, the Irish name of Aldfrith, king of Northumbria (d. 705), who was famed for his learning. It is a collection of maxims and gnomic sayings. It praises wisdom, which raises the poor and lowly. It warns that the warrior's life leads to hell without repentance. It belongs to the early Irish tradition of instruction literature.

Cáin Eimíne Báin ("The Law of Eimíne Bán") is an anonymous Old Irish prose text, perhaps composed in the eighth century, though its date is uncertain. It tells how the rulers of Leinster, led by King Bran ua Fáeláin, came to the holy man Eimíne Bán during a plague and asked to take up the religious life. After a night of prayer, Eimíne and his community offered to die in their place, Eimíne himself for Bran. The story serves to justify the privileges and dues claimed by Eimíne's church.

Cenn ard Ádaim ("Adam's lofty head") is an Irish religious poem of the late tenth century, attributed in its own verses to Airbertach mac Coise, scholar of Ros Ailithir (Roscarbery). Those verses describe it as rendered from Latin into Irish. It opens with Adam's creation, naming the lands from which each part of his body was formed and describing God's breath giving him a soul. The poem then turns to the feast of the apostle Thomas, recounting his mission to India and a miracle connected with his preaching there.

Clocán binn ("The Bell") is a short anonymous Old Irish quatrain, usually dated to the ninth century. In four lines the speaker praises a sweet-toned little bell rung on a windy night. He says he would rather go to meet it, answering the call to prayer, than go to meet a foolish or wanton woman. The poem is one of the brief early Irish verses on monastic life. It is often cited as an example of how this verse sets ascetic devotion against worldly temptation in a few compressed, vivid images.

This short anonymous Old Irish poem is put in the mouth of Colum Cille (Columba, d. 597), the Irish monastic founder of Iona. It begins "Colum Cille cecinit" ("Colum Cille sang") and names the places dearest to him: Durrow, Derry, Tír Luigdech, Gartan, Tulach, Tory and Doire Eithne. It ends by preferring Gartan, traditionally his birthplace. The date is uncertain, and the attribution to Columba himself is doubtful. Like other verse ascribed to him, it belongs to the later tradition that linked the saint with places in Ireland.

"Cros Chríst tarsin ngnúis-se" ("Christ's cross over this face") is a short Old Irish protective prayer of the lorica type. It is traditionally attributed to Mugrón, abbot of Iona and successor of Columba, who held office from 965 to 981. The prayer repeats a single formula, calling down the cross of Christ on each part of the body, on every direction, on home, church and altar, and on the speaker's whole life until death. It is a well-known example of Irish devotional poetry built on litany-like repetition and of the tradition of breastplate prayers.

"Día lim fri cach sním" ("God be with me against every trouble") is an anonymous Old Irish protective prayer in verse, usually dated to the ninth century. It belongs to the lorica tradition of Irish devotional poetry. The poem calls on the Trinity and on Christ, Son of Mary, to shield the speaker from demons, sudden death, disease, wounds, thunder, fire, poisonous winds and the judgement of Doomsday. It then invokes saints, disciples, martyrs, confessors, pilgrims and all the righteous as protectors. It is a good example of early medieval Irish vernacular piety.

Dofil aimser laithe mbratha ("The time of Doomsday is approaching") is an anonymous Old Irish poem on the end of the world. Its date is uncertain but is usually placed between the seventh and ninth centuries. In short, heavily rhymed lines it lists the signs of the last age: the earth trembles, truth is drowned, kings and law fail, churches lose their piety, and kin turn against kin. It is a vernacular witness to the apocalyptic and penitential themes of early Irish Christian literature.

"Dúthracar, a Maic Dé bí", known in English as "Manchán's Wish", is a short Old Irish poem. Its heading attributes it to Manchán of Líath (Lemanaghan), a seventh-century saint, but its language points to a much later date, probably the tenth century. The speaker prays to the Son of the living God for a hidden hermitage beside a clear stream and a wood full of birdsong, with a small community of monks, a church and enough food and clothing to live on. It is a well-known example of early Irish hermit poetry.

Eineach úaisle ná gach dán ("Generosity is nobler than any gift") is a short Irish devotional poem in quatrains praising enech, the honour won through generosity and hospitality. It claims that open-handedness covers every fault, even kin-slaying and treachery, and contrasts the generous man, who pleases the King of the elements, with the miser, who is condemned. The closing stanza attributes it to Colum Cille, son of Feidlimid, but this ascription is traditional. The poem's language suggests a later date than the Old Irish period.

The Félire Óengusso is an Old Irish verse martyrology attributed to Óengus mac Óengobann, known as Óengus the Culdee, of the Céli Dé reform movement at Tallaght. Scholars date it to sometime between about 797 and 833, but the exact date is debated. It has a long prologue and epilogue. In between, a quatrain for each day of the year commemorates saints from the wider Church and from Ireland. It draws on the closely related Martyrology of Tallaght. It is the earliest known metrical martyrology in Irish and an important witness to the Old Irish language. Later writers added a Middle Irish preface and glosses.

This short Old Irish prayer is introduced with the words "Fursu cecinit" ("Fursa sang this"). That ascribes it to the Irish monk Fursa (Fursey, died c. 650), who worked as a missionary in East Anglia and Gaul. The ascription is traditional and cannot be confirmed, and the date of the prayer is uncertain. It belongs to the lorica, or protective-prayer, tradition. It asks for God's presence on each part of the body in turn: shoulders, head, forehead, ears, nose, eyes, mouth, hands, feet and heart. It ends with a direction to recite the Creed and the Lord's Prayer.

The Prayer for Tears is an anonymous devotional poem in early Irish, opening "Tucc dam, a Dé móir" ("Grant me, great God"). Its date is uncertain; it is generally placed in the early medieval period. The speaker asks God for a stream of tears to wash the heart and body clean of sin. The poem appeals to the penitent woman who wept over Christ, and to Christ's kingship and cross. It belongs to the Irish ascetic tradition that valued compunction and the "gift of tears" as signs of true repentance.

This is a short anonymous Old Irish devotional text, probably composed between the seventh and ninth centuries, about atoning for sins that are never confessed. In it, Pope Gregory the Great grieves over people's hidden sins and fasts against God until the answer is revealed to him. An angel then prescribes sets of psalms and canticles, with the "Deus in adiutorium" and the Pater noster sung between them. These are presented as commutations (arrae) that cancel every bodily sin except blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. The text reflects early Irish penitential practice.

This is an anonymous Irish-language rendering of the Ecclesiastical History of the English People, completed by Bede of Jarrow in 731. Its date is uncertain, though it has been placed roughly in the ninth century. The surviving text follows Bede's Latin preface closely. It names his informants: Abbot Albinus of Canterbury, the London priest Nothhelm, Bishop Daniel of the West Saxons, the monks of Lastingham and the priest Cyneberht of Lindsey. The version shows that Bede's history was known and translated in early medieval Ireland.

Is mebul dom imrádud ("Shame to my thoughts") is an anonymous Old Irish religious poem, usually dated to the tenth century. The poet confesses that his mind strays while he chants the psalms. It runs off through gatherings and bands of foolish women, through woods and cities, and leaps from earth to heaven quicker than the wind. No fetter, prison or fortress can hold it. The poem closes with a prayer that Christ, through the sevenfold Spirit, will govern the heart. It is valued as a vivid, personal treatment of distraction in prayer, a theme known from monastic spirituality.

Isam aithrech ("I am repentant") is an anonymous Old Irish penitential poem in quatrains, usually placed in the late tenth century. The speaker repents of his wrongdoing and asks Christ to forgive every sin. Like a litany, each stanza calls on something different: the Incarnation, Nativity, Baptism, Crucifixion, Resurrection and Ascension, Christ's coming to judge the race of Adam, and the nine orders of heaven. It then calls on the prophets, martyrs, patriarchs, apostles and holy virgins, and on the Virgin Mary. It is a good example of early Irish private devotional verse.

Ísucán ("Little Jesus") is a short Old Irish devotional poem attributed to Saint Íte of Killeedy, the sixth-century Munster abbess. Its language dates it to around the ninth or tenth century, so the attribution is traditional rather than historical. A brief prose introduction says Christ came to Íte in the form of an infant. In the poem she speaks as his foster-mother, nursing "little Jesus" in her hermitage. She values him above all clerics, riches and the sons of kings, and calls on maidens to sing to him. It is one of the best-known lyrics of early Irish religious poetry.

M’airiuclán hi Túaim Inbir is a short anonymous Old Irish poem from around the late eighth or early ninth century. It is put in the mouth of Suibne Geilt, the mad king-hermit of Irish legend. The speaker praises his small oratory at Túaim Inbir. It is roofed only by the sky with its stars, sun and moon, and it was built by Gobbán, the legendary craftsman, with God as its thatcher. No rain falls on it and no spears are feared there. It is often cited as an example of early Irish hermit poetry and nature poetry.

"M'óenurán im aireclán" ("All alone in my little cell") is an anonymous Old Irish poem, usually dated to around the ninth century. It belongs to the early Irish tradition of hermit poetry. In short rhyming stanzas the speaker wishes for a secluded hut where he can do penance. He describes a hard bed, short sleep, dry bread and water, tears, psalm-singing at every canonical hour, frequent kneeling and study of books, and he hopes Christ will visit him there. The poem closes on a reflection: alone he came into the world, and alone he will leave it.

Molaisse and his sister is a short anonymous Old Irish religious tale, probably written between the ninth and tenth centuries, about Saint Molaise (Laisrén) of Leighlin. His sister becomes pregnant by a young cleric but refuses to name him. Molaise curses her, and she dies without communion and is buried in a bog outside the churchyard. The repentant cleric then does daily penance for her soul, reciting psalms and making prostrations beside her grave. The story shows Irish beliefs about penance and praying for the dead.

Pátraic cecinit ("Patrick sang") is an anonymous Irish prophetic poem placed in the mouth of Saint Patrick. Its date is uncertain. In it, Patrick says it does not matter to him if he never goes into Leinster, because three of its saints will win heaven for its people: Cóemgen (Kevin) of Glendalough, Abbán, and Moling. The poem promises that their monks will be saved. It also foretells that Leinster's rulers will fall into decline and that later clergy will be worthless. The poem shows how Irish writers used Patrick's authority to promote local saints and their churches.

This is a short Irish religious poem headed "Colum Cille cecinit", which attributes it to Columba (Colum Cille), the sixth-century abbot of Iona. Many later Irish verses were credited to him by convention, so the attribution is doubtful. Its language also suggests a date later than the early medieval period. The poem warns that anyone who reviles a cleric or a man in holy orders insults Christ, in whose place the priest stands, and earns hell. It praises the power of a priest's office and Mass and urges respect for the priest who baptized you.

The Rule of Colum Cille is a short Old Irish monastic rule bearing the name of Columba (Colum Cille, d. 597), founder of Iona. The attribution is traditional, and the text is generally thought to be later, possibly connected with the ascetic reform of the Céli Dé. It is addressed to a monk living alone near a principal monastery. In brief precepts it urges stability, obedience to a senior, readiness for red and white martyrdom, and forgiveness, and it divides each day among prayer, work and reading.

The Rule of Mo Chutu of Rahan is an anonymous Old Irish rule in verse, attributed to Mo Chutu (Carthach), the seventh-century founder of Rahan who later founded Lismore. It probably dates from much later than the saint, perhaps between about 800 and 1000. It opens with general precepts: love of God and neighbour, honour for parents and elders, and obedience to one's abbot. Further sections set out the duties of particular ranks, starting with the bishop, who must govern justly, know Scripture and suppress heresy. It is an important witness to early Irish monastic and church discipline.

Saltair na Rann ("The Psalter of Quatrains") is an anonymous Irish religious poem from the late tenth century. Its language falls between Old and Middle Irish. It was once attributed to Óengus the Culdee, but that attribution has been abandoned. Like the Psalter, it has 150 cantos, written in quatrains, plus a few added poems. It retells sacred history from the Creation and the order of the cosmos through the biblical narrative, using apocryphal sources, and ends with the Last Judgement. It is a major monument of early Irish biblical verse.

The Blessing of Generosity is a short anonymous religious poem in Old Irish. Its date is uncertain, though it is generally placed between the seventh and ninth centuries. Speaking directly to a "generous man", it urges him to give the Lord his share, as the Lord gives to him. Food, drink and clothing given in charity will plead for the giver in heaven, but grain, milk and honey stored at home cannot be taken along at death. The poem belongs to the early Irish tradition of verse teaching on almsgiving and the passing nature of worldly wealth.

A short anonymous Irish poem in quatrains addressed to the man who rings a church bell at the canonical hours. It says that the bell's sound is sweet to Christ in every graveyard, refreshes the souls of the wretched and earns the ringer great reward from the King. The hosts of the dead rejoice when it is rung slowly but are displeased by hasty ringing, and demons flee north into the sea at its sound. The poet urges slow, gentle ringing to win God's blessing. Its date is uncertain, and its language may be later than Old Irish.

This short anonymous Old Irish poem is usually dated between the seventh and ninth centuries, though its exact date is uncertain. It gives each mental and emotional faculty a place in the body. Intellect is in the face, memory in the brain, desire in the bowels, anger in the gall, fear in the heart and thought in the kidneys. It then places the soul in the blood, the spirit in the soul and faith in the heart, with Christ in all faith. It shows how early medieval Irish learning combined physiology with Christian teaching about the soul.

A short anonymous Old Irish poem in quatrains, ascribed in its opening line to Adamnán, usually identified with Adomnán, abbot of Iona (died 704). The ascription is traditional, and the poem's date is uncertain, probably between the seventh and ninth centuries. It names three steps that are best for anyone to take: visiting the sick, going on pilgrimage and going to church. It praises the company of a servant of God and warns against heedlessness and life without a rule, urging the reader to give up folly without waiting for old age.

"Tan bím eter mo shruithe" is a short Old Irish poem, usually dated to around the tenth century. Its opening words, "Mo Ling dixit", put it in the mouth of Saint Moling, the seventh-century bishop of Ferns, but the real author is unknown. The speaker says that among his elders he holds back from play, while among merry, foolish company he behaves like the youngest. The poem thus describes adapting oneself to every company, and its English title echoes Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 9:22.

Tiugraind Beccáin ("The last verses of Beccán") is an Old Irish poem in praise of Colum Cille (St Columba), founder of Iona. It is attributed to Beccán mac Luigdech, a seventh-century monk and possibly a hermit linked with Iona. Its exact date is uncertain, with estimates running from about 640 to the 670s. The poem celebrates Columba as the "candle" of Connacht and Alba, praising his ascetic life, his voyages by sea and his learning. With Fo réir Choluimb and Amra Choluim Cille, it is among the earliest surviving vernacular witnesses to devotion to Columba.

This is an anonymous Old Irish treatise on the eight principal vices, probably written in the ninth century. It opens by saying that the elders of Ireland drew from the rules of Scripture a penitential remedy for every sin, great or small. Following the scheme of eight vices handed down from John Cassian, it sets against each vice a healing virtue: gluttony, lust, avarice, envy, anger, worldly sorrow, vainglory and pride. It then lists the offshoots of each vice and their remedies. The work shows how early medieval Irish penitential and ascetic teaching developed in the vernacular.

"Uch, a Dé" ("Alas, O God") is a short anonymous religious lament in early Irish verse. Its date is uncertain; it is usually placed somewhere between the seventh and tenth centuries. The speaker repeats the cry "uch" ("alas") while calling on God and complaining about the weakness of old age. He goes through his failing body part by part: hands, sides, thighs, calves and feet. He says he can no longer walk and fears dying and the coming judgement. The poem belongs to the Irish tradition of personal penitential verse.
