The song defends the Catholic Church as a net holding good and bad fish until the end of the age. It also turns the charge of "traditio", the handing over of the Scriptures during persecution, back on the Donatists. It is valued as an early example of rhythmic Latin verse.

Quaestiones in Heptateuchum (Questions on the Heptateuch) is a Latin exegetical work in seven books by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated to around 419–420. It covers Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua and Judges. Augustine wrote it as working notes while reading these books and comparing Latin manuscripts with the Septuagint. Some problems he only raises, while others he discusses at length. The questions concern textual readings, historical and moral difficulties, and figurative meanings. The work shows his close engagement with the biblical text and his method of inquiry.

The Retractationes (Reconsiderations) is a Latin work in two books by Augustine of Hippo, written around 426–427, near the end of his life. In it Augustine reviews his own writings in roughly the order he wrote them, beginning with the early dialogues composed at Cassiciacum. For each work he explains the circumstances of its writing, corrects or clarifies passages he had come to think mistaken, and gives its opening words. It is unique in ancient literature as an author's critical survey of his own output, and it remains a key source for the chronology of Augustine's works.

The Sermo ad Caesariensis Ecclesiae Plebem is a Latin sermon by Augustine of Hippo. He preached it in 418 to the Catholic congregation of Caesarea in Mauretania, in the presence of Emeritus, the town's Donatist bishop. Augustine reports Emeritus's ambiguous words, "I cannot not want what you want, but I can want what I want," and appeals for Church unity and an end to the schism. The sermon belongs to Augustine's anti-Donatist writings and came before the recorded conference with Emeritus, the Gesta cum Emerito.

The Sermon on Rusticianus the Subdeacon is a Latin sermon attributed to Augustine of Hippo, though its authenticity is doubted and it is often classed as pseudo-Augustinian. It is known only from a seventeenth-century printing, and no manuscript of it is known to survive. Its full title says it concerns a subdeacon named Rusticianus whom the Donatists had rebaptized. The opening is a lament: the preacher grieves with his congregation for a beloved pastor, calls him a father, and hopes the people will give the same affection to his successor.

The Speculum ("Mirror"), opening with the words "Quis ignorat", is a Latin compilation by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated to about 427, late in his life. Augustine separates the ceremonial laws of the Old Testament, which Christians are to understand figuratively rather than observe, from the moral commands that still bind them. He then gathers the passages of the canonical Scriptures that command, forbid or permit conduct, so that readers can see their own lives reflected in them. It should not be confused with the pseudo-Augustinian Speculum known as "Audi Israel".

The Liber de divinis scripturis, also called the pseudo-Augustinian Speculum, is an anonymous Latin collection of biblical testimonia that has come down under the name of Augustine of Hippo but is not his work. It is distinct from his genuine Speculum. Its date and place of origin are uncertain, though it is usually placed in late antiquity. Its 144 chapters arrange scriptural passages under doctrinal and moral headings, such as the one God, the Trinity, penance, almsgiving and humility. It is valued chiefly as a witness to the Old Latin text of the Bible.

The "Letters of Emperors, Popes and Others" is the collection usually known as the Collectio Avellana. It is an anonymous Latin compilation of about 240 documents dating from 367 to 553, made in Rome probably in the mid-sixth century. It brings together letters from emperors and imperial officials, papal correspondence and related texts. It opens with an account of the dispute between Liberius and Felix and the conflicts surrounding Pope Damasus. Many of its documents survive nowhere else. This makes it a key source for church–state relations and the Acacian schism, especially under Pope Hormisdas.

De locis sanctis ("On the Holy Places") is a short Latin description of the Holy Land by Bede, the Northumbrian monk of Monkwearmouth–Jarrow. It was written in the early eighth century. Bede based it mainly on Adomnán of Iona's work of the same title, which recorded the pilgrimage of the Gallic bishop Arculf, and added material from other writers. It begins with the site, walls and gates of Jerusalem. It then covers the places linked to Christ's passion and resurrection and other biblical sites. The book was widely copied and helped shape how medieval readers pictured the Holy Land.

The Consolation of Philosophy is a Latin work in alternating prose and verse by the Roman statesman and philosopher Boethius. He wrote it around 523–524 while imprisoned and awaiting execution under the Ostrogothic king Theodoric. Across five books, Lady Philosophy visits the grieving author. She leads him from complaints against Fortune to reflection on true happiness, the supreme good, providence, fate and free will. It was one of the most widely read books of the Middle Ages. Notker Labeo of St Gall translated it into Old High German with a commentary.

Boethius (c. 480–524) wrote two Latin commentaries on Porphyry's Isagoge, the Neoplatonist introduction to Aristotle's Categories. The first, in two books, is a dialogue between Boethius and his friend Fabius, set on a winter night in the mountains. It explains the Latin translation by Marius Victorinus and opens with the six standard preliminary questions of late-antique commentary. The second, in five books, is based on Boethius's own translation. Both belong to his early logical works, and they shaped medieval discussion of genera, species and the problem of universals.

Boethius (c. 480–524) wrote two Latin commentaries on Porphyry's Isagoge, the Neoplatonist introduction to Aristotle's Categories. The first, in two books, is a dialogue between Boethius and his friend Fabius, set on a winter night in the mountains. It explains the Latin translation by Marius Victorinus and opens with the six standard preliminary questions of late-antique commentary. The second, in five books, is based on Boethius's own translation. Both belong to his early logical works, and they shaped medieval discussion of genera, species and the problem of universals.

The Conferences (Collationes Patrum) is a Latin work by the monk John Cassian, written in southern Gaul in the 420s. It follows his Institutes and consists of twenty-four dialogues, issued in three parts. In them, Egyptian desert fathers, especially the anchorites of Scetis, teach Cassian and his companion Germanus about prayer, discretion, purity of heart and the monastic goal. The Thirteenth Conference's teaching on grace and free will drew criticism from Prosper of Aquitaine. The Rule of Benedict recommends the work, and it became a key channel of Eastern monastic spirituality to the Latin West.

The Institutes (De institutis coenobiorum) is a Latin treatise in twelve books on monastic life by John Cassian. He wrote it in the 420s in southern Gaul at the request of Bishop Castor of Apt, who was founding a monastery. The first four books describe the dress, prayer, psalmody and rules of the monasteries of Egypt and Palestine. The remaining eight books deal with the eight principal vices and their remedies, a scheme that draws on Evagrius Ponticus. Together with Cassian's Conferences, the work helped bring Eastern monastic practice to the Latin West and influenced the Rule of Saint Benedict.

De Incarnatione Domini contra Nestorium is a Latin theological treatise in seven books by the monk John Cassian. He wrote it at Marseille around 429–430, after his Conferences, at the request of the Roman deacon Leo, later Pope Leo I. It was one of the first Western replies to Nestorius of Constantinople. Cassian defends the unity of Christ's person and the title Theotokos, "God-bearer", for Mary, and connects Nestorius's teaching with Pelagianism. He supports his case with Scripture, the creed and earlier Fathers. The work came out shortly before the Council of Ephesus in 431.

De statu animae ("On the Nature of the Soul") is a Latin philosophical and theological treatise in three books by Claudianus Mamertus, a priest of Vienne in Gaul and brother of Bishop Mamertus. It was written around 470 and dedicated to Sidonius Apollinaris. The work answers Faustus of Riez, who had argued that only God is incorporeal and that the human soul is in some sense bodily. Drawing on Augustine and Neoplatonic thought, Claudianus argues that the soul is incorporeal. The treatise is an important witness to philosophical learning in late fifth-century Gaul.

Two Latin letters by Claudianus Mamertus (died c. 473), the Gallo-Roman theologian and priest of Vienne who was the brother of Bishop Mamertus. The first, addressed to Sidonius Apollinaris, gently complains that Sidonius writes to others but has never replied about the books dedicated to him. These were Claudianus's treatise De statu animae. The second, to the Viennese rhetor Sapaudus, laments the decline of learning and eloquence in Gaul. The letters show the literary friendships and classical culture of fifth-century Gaul.

The Instructiones is a Latin didactic poem by Commodian, a Christian poet who said he had converted from paganism. It is usually dated to the mid-third century, though some scholars place it later. It has 80 short poems, nearly all of them acrostics, written in rhythmic hexameters that depend on stress rather than classical quantity. The first part mocks the pagan gods and addresses Jews and heathens. The second deals with Antichrist, the end of the world and the resurrection, and gives advice to Christians, penitents and clergy.

The Carmen Apologeticum is a Latin didactic poem by the Christian poet Commodian, written in rhythmic hexameters that follow word accent rather than classical quantity. It survives in a single manuscript without title or author's name, and was first published by J. B. Pitra in 1852. It is usually dated to the mid-third century, though some scholars place it later. It opens with the poet's account of his conversion from paganism, sets out Christian teaching on God and Christ for pagans and Jews, and ends with a vivid apocalyptic picture of the Antichrist and the end of the world.

Ad Donatum is a short Latin treatise in letter form by Cyprian, bishop of Carthage. It is generally regarded as his earliest surviving work, written soon after his conversion around 246. Set in a garden during the autumn vintage holiday, it is addressed to his friend Donatus. Cyprian describes how the grace of baptism changed him, and he condemns the vices of pagan society, including gladiatorial shows, the theatre, corrupt law courts and political ambition. He urges contempt for the world and devotion to reading and prayer. Its ornate rhetorical style reflects his classical training.

Ad Demetrianum is a Latin apologetic treatise by Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, usually dated around 252, during a time of plague and renewed hostility toward Christians. It answers Demetrianus, a pagan official who blamed war, famine and pestilence on the Christians' refusal to worship the gods. Cyprian argues that the world is declining in its old age. He presents the calamities as divine punishment for pagan unbelief and the unjust persecution of Christians, and urges his opponent to repent. The treatise is an important witness to pagan–Christian tensions in third-century North Africa.

De bono patientiae (On the Advantage of Patience) is a Latin treatise by Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, written around 256. At that time he was in dispute with Pope Stephen of Rome over rebaptising heretics, and he mentions the work in his letter to Jubaianus. It contrasts Christian patience with the patience claimed by the philosophers. Cyprian presents patience as a quality of God himself, shown in Christ and in the righteous of Scripture, and he describes impatience as the source of many sins. The treatise draws on Tertullian's earlier work on the same subject.

De habitu virginum (On the Dress of Virgins) is a Latin treatise by Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, usually dated to around 249, early in his episcopate. Addressed to women who had dedicated their virginity to Christ, it praises discipline and consecrated virginity. It argues that continence requires modest dress and ornament as well as bodily purity, and that wealthy virgins should give their riches to the poor. It also forbids attending weddings and mixed public baths. The work draws on Tertullian and is one of the earliest Latin writings on consecrated virginity.

Latin treatise by Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, written at the request of a certain Fortunatus during a time of persecution. It is dated either to the Decian persecution around 250 or to the Valerian persecution around 257. Cyprian says that the end of the world and the time of Antichrist are near, and he gathers passages of Scripture under a series of headings to strengthen Christians facing trial. They teach the rejection of idolatry, endurance under suffering and the reward of martyrs. The work is an important example of the early Christian collections of biblical testimonies.

Quod idola dii non sint (On the Vanity of Idols) is a short Latin apologetic treatise traditionally attributed to Cyprian, bishop of Carthage (d. 258). Jerome accepted it as his, but some modern scholars question whether Cyprian wrote it. It has three parts. The first argues that the pagan gods were once kings, honoured with worship after their deaths. The second holds that God is one, and the third that salvation comes to believers through Christ. Much of its material is drawn from Minucius Felix's Octavius and Tertullian's Apology.

De Lapsis (On the Lapsed) is a Latin treatise by Cyprian, bishop of Carthage. He wrote it in 251, after the Decian persecution ended and he returned to his see. It praises the confessors who stood firm. It also mourns the many Christians who sacrificed to idols or obtained certificates of compliance, and blames the persecution on lax discipline in the Church. Cyprian requires the lapsed to do real penance and condemns easy reconciliation. The treatise is a key source for the early Church's dispute over penance and readmitting the lapsed.

De mortalitate (On the Mortality) is a Latin pastoral treatise by Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, written around 252 during the epidemic now called the Plague of Cyprian. Cyprian addresses Christians who were frightened by the many deaths. He argues that Christ foretold such afflictions, and that for believers death is a passage to immortality, not something to fear. Citing Job and Tobit, he urges patience. The work is a key witness to how early Christians understood suffering, death and hope in the resurrection.

De Opere et Eleemosynis (On Works and Alms) is a Latin treatise by Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, probably written in the early 250s. It urges Christians to show their faith through good works, especially almsgiving and offerings to the Church. Drawing on many passages of Scripture, Cyprian argues that alms cleanse sins committed after baptism, and he answers wealthy believers who fear that generosity will impoverish their families. It is one of the earliest sustained Christian discussions of charity and of its role in penance and salvation.

On the Unity of the Church is a Latin treatise by Cyprian, bishop of Carthage. He wrote it around 251, after the Decian persecution, when schisms had broken out at Carthage and Rome, the latter led by Novatian. Cyprian argues that the Church is one, founded on Peter, and held together by a single episcopate, so anyone who breaks from it is cut off from salvation. The work contains his famous saying, "He cannot have God for his Father who has not the Church for his mother." Its fourth chapter survives in two versions, and their wording about Peter's primacy has long been debated.

On Jealousy and Envy (De zelo et livore) is a short Latin treatise by Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, written during his episcopate in the 250s. Addressed to his "beloved brethren," it argues that envy is a hidden and underestimated sin that began with the devil. Cyprian draws examples from the Old Testament, presents envy as the root of many other vices, and cites Christ and the apostles against hatred between brothers. He ends by urging love even of enemies, following God's example, and by pointing to the rewards of charity.

This is the collected correspondence of Cyprian, bishop of Carthage. It contains some eighty Latin letters from about 249 to 258, including letters written to him by the Roman clergy, Pope Cornelius, Firmilian of Caesarea and others. The letters document the Decian persecution and Cyprian's withdrawal from Carthage during it. They also cover the dispute over readmitting the lapsed, the Novatianist schism, African church councils, and the controversy with Pope Stephen over rebaptizing heretics. Together they are a major source for third-century church life, discipline and ideas about the church.

The Sententiae episcoporum is the Latin record of the council of North African bishops that met at Carthage under Cyprian on 1 September, usually dated to 256, though some headings give 258. After letters exchanged with Bishop Jubaianus were read, Cyprian and each of the eighty-seven bishops from Africa, Numidia and Mauritania gave a short opinion in turn. All held that heretics joining the Church must be baptized. The record opposed the position of Stephen of Rome and was later debated in Augustine's writings against the Donatists.

Also known as Ad Quirinum, this is a Latin collection of biblical proof-texts by Cyprian, bishop of Carthage (d. 258). He addressed it to his "son" Quirinus, and it is usually dated to around the start of his episcopate, c. 248–249. The first book argues that the Jews fell away from God and lost his favour. The second presents Christ as foretold in the Scriptures. A third book, added later, gathers precepts on Christian conduct. Arranged as short headings followed by quotations, it is an important witness to the Old Latin Bible text used in North Africa.

De Dominica Oratione (On the Lord's Prayer) is a Latin treatise by Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, usually dated to around 252. It draws closely on Tertullian's On Prayer. Cyprian first praises the Lord's Prayer as the most excellent and effective of prayers, given by Christ himself. He then explains its petitions one by one and ends with advice on how and when Christians should pray. It is one of the earliest full commentaries on the Lord's Prayer, and later writers, including Augustine, valued it highly.

The Heptateuchos is a Late Latin biblical epic in verse that retells the first seven books of the Old Testament, Genesis through Judges. It follows the Old Latin translation of the Bible. Its anonymous author is conventionally called Cyprianus Gallus, or Cyprian the Gaul, and probably worked in Gaul around 397–430. The poem was once wrongly credited to Cyprian of Carthage. It seems to have belonged to a larger verse paraphrase of the Old Testament's historical books, but only this part survives. It is an important example of late antique Christian biblical epic.

Ad Novatianum is an anonymous Latin treatise written in the mid-third century, probably in the 250s, by a bishop opposing the Roman schismatic Novatian. It has come down among the works attributed to Cyprian of Carthage, but it is not his. Its author is unknown, and scholars have proposed several candidates, including a Roman bishop. The treatise argues that Christians who lapsed during persecution should not be refused hope of pardon and readmission through penance. It attacks Novatian's rigorism as cruel and schismatic. It is an early witness to the third-century controversy over penance and the lapsed.

Ad Vigilium episcopum de Iudaica incredulitate ("To Bishop Vigilius, on Jewish Unbelief") is a short Latin letter that came down among the spurious works of Cyprian of Carthage. In it a certain Celsus introduces his Latin translation of the Altercatio Iasonis et Papisci, a lost Greek dialogue in which a Jewish Christian argues with a Jew. The letter condemns Jewish refusal to accept Christ and presents the dialogue as a means of persuasion. The author and date are uncertain. Its chief value is as evidence for the lost dialogue.

The Carmina are a group of anonymous Late Latin Christian poems that were transmitted among the works of Cyprian of Carthage (died 258) but were not written by him. Most are in hexameters. The collection opens with a verse paraphrase of Genesis that matches the work of the poet known as Cyprianus Gallus (fl. c. 400). It also includes biblical narrative poems such as those on Sodom and on Jonah. Their authorship and dates are disputed. These poems are examples of early Christian biblical epic.

De bono pudicitiae (On the Good of Chastity) is a short Latin treatise in the form of a pastoral letter. It came down among the spurious works of Cyprian of Carthage but is now generally attributed to Novatian, the Roman presbyter and rival bishop of the mid-third century. The author writes to his congregation while absent from it. He commends chastity as the Church's adornment and treats it in its forms of virginity, continence and marital fidelity, with biblical examples such as Joseph and Susanna. Together with De cibis Judaicis, it shows Novatian's moral teaching and rigorist outlook.

De duplici martyrio ad Fortunatum ("On the Twofold Martyrdom") is a Latin treatise attributed to Cyprian of Carthage. It presents itself as a sequel to Cyprian's genuine exhortation to martyrdom addressed to Fortunatus. It distinguishes two kinds of martyrdom. The first is open witness under persecution and torture. The second is a hidden struggle against temptation and the passions, which demands equal courage. The work first appeared in Erasmus's 1530 edition of Cyprian, and no manuscript has ever been produced. It is widely held to be a sixteenth-century composition, and many scholars attribute it to Erasmus himself.

De laude martyrii (On the Glory of Martyrdom) is an anonymous Latin treatise that came down among the works of Cyprian of Carthage but is not by him. It was probably written in the mid-third century, during a time of persecution. Some scholars, notably Adolf von Harnack, have attributed it to Novatian, though this is disputed. In a rhetorical style, the author explains what martyrdom is, how great it is and what it gains. He urges readers to accept death for Christ gladly and argues that Christ's propitiation crowns martyrs without further purgation.

De montibus Sina et Sion is an anonymous Latin treatise against the Jews. It was passed down among the works of Cyprian of Carthage but is not by him, and it is usually placed in third-century North Africa, though its date is uncertain. It contrasts Mount Sinai, where the Mosaic law was given, with Mount Sion, from which the new law goes forth. Using etymology and figurative readings of Scripture, it treats Sinai as earthly and Sion as heavenly and spiritual, fulfilled in Christ. It matters for its early Latin biblical quotations, its popular Latin style and its archaic Christology.

De Pascha Computus ("On the Reckoning of Easter") is an anonymous Latin treatise that was handed down among works falsely attributed to Cyprian of Carthage. It is usually dated to 243, and probably comes from North Africa. Starting from the Exodus account of the Passover, the author tries to work out the first day of the paschal month. He then sets out a cycle for calculating future dates of the Jewish Passover and Christian Easter. It is one of the earliest surviving Latin works on computing the date of Easter.

De Rebaptismate is an anonymous Latin treatise from the mid-third century. It was probably written around 256, during the controversy over baptism between Cyprian of Carthage and Pope Stephen I of Rome. Opposing Cyprian's position, the author argues that people baptized by heretics in the name of Jesus Christ should not be baptized again when they return to the Church. Instead, the bishop's laying on of hands, which confers the Holy Spirit, is enough. The work was handed down among Cyprian's writings, and its author's identity and place of origin remain unknown.

De Singularitate clericorum ("On the Single Life of the Clergy") is an anonymous Latin treatise once transmitted among the works of Cyprian of Carthage. Its date and authorship are uncertain. It is generally placed in the third or fourth century, probably in North Africa, and some scholars have linked it to a Donatist author. Writing as a pastor to clerics who lived with women, the author forbids the practice, citing a divine revelation and supporting it with Scripture. It is an important witness to early church debates over clerical continence and the custom of "spiritual marriage."

De Spectaculis is a short Latin treatise in the form of a pastoral letter. It was handed down among the works of Cyprian of Carthage, but scholars generally attribute it to Novatian, the Roman presbyter and rival bishop, and date it to the mid-third century. The author warns Christians against attending the circus, theatre and gladiatorial games. He answers people who defended these shows from Scripture by arguing that every such spectacle is devoted to idols. The treatise draws heavily on Tertullian's earlier work of the same name.

De duodecim abusivis saeculi ("On the Twelve Abuses of the World") is an anonymous Latin moral treatise, generally thought to have been written in Ireland in the seventh century. In the Middle Ages it circulated under the names of Cyprian of Carthage and Augustine. It lists twelve kinds of disorder, among them the wise man without works, the old man without religion, the unjust king and the negligent bishop, and gives a short chapter to each. Its account of the just and unjust king had a wide influence on later medieval ideas of Christian kingship.

Oratio II is a Latin prayer falsely attributed to Cyprian of Carthage. Its title presents it as the prayer that Cyprian of Antioch spoke on the day of his martyrdom. Its author and date are unknown. The speaker calls on the God of the patriarchs, prophets, apostles and martyrs, who will come to judge the living and the dead. He asks to be delivered from this mortal world and pleads for forgiveness of his sins. He recalls God's deliverance of Israel from Egypt, of Jonah from the whale and the repentance of Nineveh. It survives with a companion prayer, Oratio I, among the spurious works of Cyprian.

This is a small collection of Latin letters that were falsely attributed to Cyprian of Carthage (died 258) or his correspondents and were handed down with his genuine works. It includes a fragmentary letter from a certain Donatus to Cyprian and a letter supposedly from Pope Cornelius rebuking Cyprian for teaching rebaptism. A third letter, in Cyprian's name, is addressed to the people of Carthage and concerns traditores. The authors and dates are unknown. The letters show how later writers used Cyprian's authority in disputes over baptism and church unity.

De aleatoribus ("On Dice-Players") is an anonymous Latin sermon against gambling. It has come down among works falsely attributed to Cyprian of Carthage. The preacher speaks as a bishop who claims the apostolic office and the "vicarious seat of the Lord," with the power to bind and loose. He warns that dice-playing is idolatrous and morally ruinous, and he quotes Scripture heavily. The date and author are disputed. Adolf von Harnack credited it to Pope Victor I in the late second century, but most scholars place it in the third century or later, probably in Rome or Africa.

Oratio I is an anonymous Latin prayer, the first of two prayers that have come down among the spurious works attributed to Cyprian of Carthage (died 258). Its date and origin are uncertain. It opens with the Greek acclamation "Hagios" repeated three times and calls on the God of the patriarchs, prophets and apostles. It asks that a heart cleansed in baptism be kept pure, firm in faith and safe from the devil's snares. It cites the angel Raphael's defeat of the demon Asmodeus in the Book of Tobit as a model of divine protection.

Adversus Judaeos ("Against the Jews") is a short anonymous Latin sermon that was handed down among works wrongly attributed to Cyprian of Carthage. Its author is unknown. It is usually dated to the third century, and some scholars have linked it to Novatian or his circle. Some regard it as one of the oldest surviving Christian sermons in Latin. It asks its hearers to understand the divine plan spiritually and retells sacred history from Adam and Noah onward. It argues that God's covenant and inheritance, which Israel rejected, have passed to the Gentiles through Christ.

The Carmen ad quendam senatorem is a short anonymous Latin poem in hexameters, transmitted among works falsely attributed to Cyprian of Carthage and usually dated to the late fourth century. It addresses a former consul who had abandoned Christianity for pagan cults. The poet mocks his devotion to the Great Mother, whose priests he ridicules, and his service to Isis, carrying the sistrum and a dog-headed mask. The poem is a valuable witness to the last phase of aristocratic paganism in Rome.

The Pilgrimage of Etheria (Peregrinatio or Itinerarium Egeriae) is a Latin travel account by a Christian woman, usually called Egeria, who probably came from Hispania or Gaul. She wrote it as a long letter to a circle of women at home, describing a journey of about 381–384. It survives only in incomplete form. It was once attributed to Silvia of Aquitaine. Egeria describes Sinai, Jerusalem, Egypt and Edessa, and then the liturgical year in Jerusalem. The account is the earliest of its kind and an important source for early Christian worship and for late spoken Latin.

The Benedictio Cerei is a Latin prose blessing of the paschal candle by Magnus Felix Ennodius (473/474–521), the rhetorician and later bishop of Pavia. It is the first of two such blessings among his rhetorical works and was probably written in the early sixth century, before he became bishop. Composed for the Easter Vigil in the form of a eucharistic preface beginning "Dignum et iustum est", it praises God as creator of the world, of the seasons and of light set apart from darkness. Alongside the Exsultet, it is early evidence for the rite of the paschal candle.

The second of two Latin blessings of the paschal candle written by Magnus Felix Ennodius (d. 521), the rhetorician and later bishop of Pavia. It is a praeconium for the Easter Vigil, opening with the preface formula "Dignum et iustum est", like the better-known Exsultet. In ornate rhetorical prose it praises the Creator and presents the candle's flame as a herald of the coming baptismal water, uniting fire and water as a sign of redemption. It then turns to the creation of humankind from the earth. Such texts show how the Easter liturgy was developing in early sixth-century Italy.

The Carmina are the collected Latin poems of Magnus Felix Ennodius (473/474–521), a Gallo-Roman rhetorician who became bishop of Pavia in 514. They are usually arranged in two books. They range from occasional verse, such as the opening account of a summer journey to the fort of Brigantio in the Alps, to epigrams and hymns in the style of Ambrose. Most were probably written while he was a cleric in Milan. Their dense classical diction makes them an important witness to Christian literary culture in Ostrogothic Italy.

The Dictiones are a collection of Latin speeches by Magnus Felix Ennodius (473/474–521), composed mostly while he was a cleric in Milan, before he became bishop of Pavia in 514. They include ecclesiastical addresses, such as a speech for the anniversary of Laurence, bishop of Milan, as well as school pieces and rhetorical declamations on mythological and legal themes. Written in an ornate, highly mannered style, they show how classical rhetorical education continued in Christian circles in Ostrogothic Italy.

The Life of the Blessed Antony the Monk is a short Latin hagiography by Magnus Felix Ennodius, rhetorician, poet and later bishop of Pavia (died 521). It was written in the early sixth century at the request of Abbot Leontius, who is addressed in the preface. Its subject is not Antony the Great but Antony of Lérins, a monk from Pannonia who ended his life in the monastery of Lérins. Written in Ennodius's ornate rhetorical style, the work matters as evidence for monasticism in Italy and Gaul in late antiquity.

The Panegyric to King Theoderic is a Latin prose speech by Magnus Felix Ennodius, written while he was a deacon at Milan and usually dated to about 507. It praises the Ostrogothic king Theoderic the Great, who ruled Italy. It recounts his upbringing at Constantinople, his campaign against Odoacer, his wars against the Gepids and at Sirmium, and his restoration of peace and prosperity in Italy. Written in Ennodius's ornate rhetorical style, it is a key contemporary source for Theoderic's reign. Scholars disagree on whether it was ever delivered before the king.

This is the work usually called the Paraenesis didascalica, a hortatory letter-treatise by Magnus Felix Ennodius (c. 473–521), the Latin rhetorician and poet who became bishop of Pavia. He wrote it in early sixth-century Italy for two young men, Ambrosius and Beatus, who had asked him for instruction. Moving between prose and verse, it urges devotion to God and love of neighbour, commends Christian virtues, and praises grammar and rhetoric as the proper studies of a cultivated youth. It shows how late Roman education was being brought into Christian life.

The Epistulae are the collected letters of Magnus Felix Ennodius (c. 473–521), a Latin rhetorician who became bishop of Pavia in 514. Nearly three hundred letters survive, arranged in nine books. Most were written in the early sixth century, while Ennodius was a cleric in Milan, and are addressed to senators, churchmen, friends and relatives in Ostrogothic Italy and Gaul. They are written in a highly ornate, mannered prose. Their content is often slight, but they are an important source for the Roman aristocracy under Theodoric and for the Laurentian schism.

The Eucharisticum de vita sua is a short autobiographical thanksgiving by Magnus Felix Ennodius (d. 521), a Latin rhetorician and poet who became bishop of Pavia. He wrote it while a deacon, probably around 511. In prayerful prose he thanks God for curing him of a dangerous fever. He looks back on his youth and his pride in worldly eloquence, and he takes the illness as a call to repentance. It is often compared to Augustine's Confessions and is a valuable source for its author's life in Ostrogothic Italy.

This polemical Latin tract by Magnus Felix Ennodius, later bishop of Pavia, is often called the Libellus pro synodo. It dates from the Laurentian schism in Rome. Ennodius wrote it around 502–503, while he was still a deacon in Milan. It defends the Roman synod of 501–502, often called the Synodus Palmaris, which had refused to judge Pope Symmachus. The tract answers a pamphlet by supporters of the rival claimant Laurentius. It argues that the pope cannot be judged by those beneath him, and it is an important early statement of papal immunity from judgment.

This is a short Latin petition by Magnus Felix Ennodius (c. 473–521), the rhetorician who later became bishop of Pavia. It asks a bishop, addressed as "your beatitude", to free Gerontius, a servant described in the title as Agapitus's. Ennodius says he acquired Gerontius by exchange and praises his loyalty, modesty and integrity. He gives up the service owed to him and asks that the release be recorded in church acts, so that Gerontius may enjoy Roman citizenship. The petition is a polished example of manumission in church (manumissio in ecclesia) in late antique Italy.

This short Latin decree survives among the minor writings of Magnus Felix Ennodius (c. 473–521). He composed it while a deacon in the service of Pope Symmachus, before becoming bishop of Pavia. Its title says it is the order requiring every bishop to keep cellulani, clerics who shared his living quarters and could vouch for his conduct. In ornate rhetorical prose it argues that a holy life outshines slander, but that bishops should still protect themselves against false accusers. It reflects the bitter charges made against clergy during the Laurentian schism.

The Vita Epiphanii is a Latin prose biography of Epiphanius, bishop of Pavia (Ticinum), who died in 496. It was written by Magnus Felix Ennodius, probably in the early sixth century, before he himself became bishop of Pavia in 514. Written in an ornate rhetorical style, it presents Epiphanius as a model bishop and peacemaker. It recounts his diplomatic missions on behalf of Italy, including his efforts to reconcile the emperor Anthemius with Ricimer, his embassy to the Visigothic king Euric, and his work to ransom captives. It is an important source for late fifth-century Italy.

De laude eremi ("In Praise of the Desert") is a Latin letter by Eucherius of Lyon to Hilary, then a monk of Lérins and later bishop of Arles. It is usually dated to about 428. Hilary had gone with his kinsman Honoratus when Honoratus became bishop of Arles, but he then returned to the island monastery. Eucherius praises that choice and celebrates solitude as the place where God has met his people, using biblical examples from Moses to John the Baptist. The letter ends with praise of Lérins. It is a key text of early Gallic monastic spirituality.

Formulae Spiritalis Intellegentiae ("Formulas of Spiritual Understanding") is a Latin handbook of biblical interpretation by Eucherius, bishop of Lyon (d. c. 449). It was written in the first half of the fifth century and addressed to his son Veranus. The preface argues that all of Scripture, Old Testament and New, has an allegorical sense. The book then gives lists of scriptural words and images, arranged by subject, and explains their spiritual meanings. Along with his Instructiones, it became a widely used guide to figurative exegesis in the medieval Latin West.

The Instructiones ad Salonium is a Latin handbook of biblical interpretation in two books by Eucherius of Lyon (c. 380 – c. 449). It is addressed to his son Salonius, who had been brought up from childhood among the monks of Lérins and later became a bishop. The first book answers questions about difficult passages of the Old and New Testaments, drawing on earlier teachers. The second explains Hebrew names and words, liturgical terms and objects. It was widely used as a reference in the medieval West.

The Passio Acaunensium martyrum (Passion of the Martyrs of Agaunum) is a Latin hagiographical account attributed to Eucherius, bishop of Lyon, and written in the mid-fifth century. It tells the story of the Theban Legion, a unit of Christian soldiers summoned from the East to serve the emperor Maximian. The soldiers refused to take part in persecuting Christians and were massacred at Agaunum, now Saint-Maurice in the Valais. Their leaders included Maurice, Exuperius and Candidus. It is the earliest surviving narrative of the legend, and it shaped the widespread cult of Saint Maurice. Historians dispute whether the events happened.

This is a short Latin description of Jerusalem and Judaea, written as a letter to Faustus, a priest of the island monastery of Lérins. It is attributed to Eucherius, bishop of Lyon (d. c. 449), but some scholars doubt that he wrote it, and it probably dates from the fifth century. Drawing on reports and reading rather than a visit, it describes the city's layout, Mount Sion, its gates and Constantine's buildings at Golgotha and the Anastasis. It then covers other sites across Judaea. It is an early source for the topography of the Holy Land and for Christian pilgrimage.

The Life of St Severinus is a Latin hagiography written around 511 by Eugippius, Severinus's disciple and later abbot of the monastery at Castellum Lucullanum near Naples. Eugippius dedicated it, with a prefatory letter, to the deacon Paschasius. It describes the ascetic life, miracles and public work of Severinus (died 482) in the Danubian province of Noricum as Roman rule collapsed there. It also covers his dealings with the Rugians and Odoacer, and the later move of the Roman population and his relics to Italy. It is a key historical source for the end of Roman rule along the Danube.

This Latin dedicatory letter by Eugippius, abbot of the monastery at Castellum Lucullanum near Naples, prefaces his Excerpta ex operibus sancti Augustini, an anthology of passages from Augustine's writings compiled in the early sixth century. It is addressed to Proba, a consecrated virgin who had asked for a copy even though her library already held Augustine's complete works. Eugippius explains why he made the collection, praising Augustine as a doctor honoured by the bishops of Rome and a defender of grace against its opponents.

The Excerpta ex operibus sancti Augustini is a large Latin anthology of passages from the writings of Augustine of Hippo. Eugippius, abbot of the monastery at Castellum Lucullanum near Naples, compiled it in the early sixth century. It opens with a list of chapters, each naming its subject and the work it is drawn from, such as the Confessions, The City of God and On the Trinity. The extracts cover virtues, the passions, the senses, Christ the mediator, time and creation. Cassiodorus recommended the collection, and it was widely copied in the Middle Ages, helping spread Augustine's thought.

The Altercatio Legis inter Simonem Iudaeum et Theophilum Christianum is a Latin dialogue, an anti-Jewish Christian polemic, written in the fifth century. It is attributed to Evagrius, sometimes called Evagrius Gallus, and is dedicated to a certain Valerius. Gennadius of Marseille mentions it. Presented as a debate the author witnessed, it has the Jew Simon and the Christian Theophilus argue over the Hebrew Scriptures. Theophilus uses prophetic texts to defend Christ's divinity, incarnation and crucifixion, and the dialogue ends with Simon's conversion. It belongs to the long tradition of Christian Adversus Iudaeos literature.

De fide contra Manichaeos ("On the Faith, against the Manichaeans") is a short Latin anti-Manichaean treatise. It is attributed to Evodius, bishop of Uzalis in North Africa and a friend of Augustine of Hippo, and was probably written in the early fifth century. The work has come down among Augustine's writings. It opens with a confession of the one God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit. It then argues against Mani's dualism, especially his claim that an unbegotten prince of darkness stands against God, drawing on Scripture and on the Manichaeans' own texts.

De gratia is a Latin treatise in two books by Faustus, bishop of Riez in southern Gaul. He wrote it around 474 at the request of Leontius of Arles, after Gallic councils at Arles and Lyon condemned the predestinarian teaching of the priest Lucidus. Faustus rejects both Pelagius and strict predestination. He argues that divine grace works together with human free will, which is weakened but not destroyed. The work became a key statement of what was later called Semi-Pelagianism, and its positions were rejected at the Council of Orange in 529.

De Spiritu Sancto is a Latin treatise in two books on the divinity of the Holy Spirit. It was long transmitted under the name of Paschasius, a Roman deacon who died around 512, but many scholars now attribute it to Faustus of Riez, the fifth-century bishop in southern Gaul. Taking the Creed as its starting point, it defends the Spirit's full deity and his equality within the Trinity, drawing on Scripture. It is also known for distinguishing belief "in" God from believing the Church, which it holds should be confessed without the preposition "in".

The letters of Faustus, bishop of Riez in southern Gaul (died c. 490), are a small surviving collection of Latin correspondence from the later fifth century. The best known, to the priest Lucidus, urges him to give up a strict predestinarian teaching that excluded human effort, while also condemning Pelagius. Lucidus later retracted at councils held at Arles and Lyon around 473–474. Other letters offer spiritual counsel and discuss doctrinal questions, including the bodily nature of the soul. They are key witnesses to Faustus's so-called Semi-Pelagian theology of grace.

These are Latin sermons attributed to Faustus of Riez (died c. 490), the monk of Lérins who became bishop of Riez in Provence. They are pastoral addresses for church feasts and for monastic and lay audiences, and they urge moral reform and worthy preparation for receiving the Eucharist, for example before Christmas. Which sermons are authentically his is often uncertain. Many survive anonymously or under other names, especially in the Gallic collection known as Eusebius Gallicanus. They are important evidence for preaching in fifth-century Gaul.

De ratione fidei ("On the Account of the Faith") is a short Latin doctrinal treatise attributed to Faustus of Riez, the fifth-century bishop in southern Gaul. It takes the form of questions and answers and responds to objections raised against orthodox teaching. Its opening question asks how to answer those who read "the Father is greater than I" as proof that the Son is lesser in divinity. The answer distinguishes Christ's two births, eternal from the Father and in time from the Virgin Mary, and affirms his one person in two substances, divine and human.

The Diversarum hereseon liber (Book of Various Heresies) is a Latin catalogue of heresies by Filastrius (Philastrius), bishop of Brescia, written in the 380s. It begins with errors that arose before Christ, including Jewish sects, and then covers those that appeared after the Incarnation, some 156 entries in all. Some entries deal with matters of opinion or interpretation that later writers would hardly call heresies. The work is one of the earliest Latin heresiologies. Augustine drew on it in his own De haeresibus.

De errore profanarum religionum ("On the Error of Profane Religions") is a Latin apologetic treatise by Julius Firmicus Maternus, a former astrologer who became a Christian. He wrote it around 346 and dedicated it to the emperors Constantius II and Constans. It attacks pagan worship of the elements and the mystery cults of Isis, Osiris, Cybele and Attis, Mithras and Dionysus. Firmicus presents these cults as demonic imitations of Christian truth and urges the emperors to suppress them. The treatise survives in a single manuscript whose beginning is lost, and it is a valuable source on the late Roman mystery religions.

The Tractatus super Psalmos is a Latin series of homilies on the Psalms by Hilary of Poitiers. It is generally dated to his last years, after he returned from exile in the East around 360. Only part survives, covering selected psalms, including Psalms 1, 53 and 130. Hilary drew heavily on Origen's exegesis. He reads the Psalms mainly as speaking of Christ, and he holds that interpretation begins by asking in whose person the psalmist speaks and whom he addresses. The work is among the earliest substantial Latin commentaries on the Psalter.

The Collectanea Antiariana Parisina, also called the historical fragments (Fragmenta historica), is a collection of documents on the fourth-century Arian controversy associated with Hilary of Poitiers. It survives in two series, A and B, and is usually thought to come from Hilary's lost polemical history directed against the bishops Valens and Ursacius. It includes synodal letters, creeds and correspondence connected with the councils of Serdica, Rimini and Paris. Together with Hilary's own commentary, these documents are an important primary source for the conflicts over Nicene doctrine under Constantius II.

The Fragmenta minora are short passages from lost or partly lost works of Hilary of Poitiers (c. 298 – c. 367), the Latin bishop and opponent of Arianism. They survive only because later writers quoted them. They include a Christological statement from a book addressed to the emperor Constantius II, which says the Son of God made man is God, and excerpts from Hilary's homilies on the Book of Job. The Job excerpts argue that God's mercy turns the devil's attacks into a means of purifying believers.

The Hymni are Latin hymns by Hilary of Poitiers (c. 298–c. 367), bishop and opponent of Arianism. Hilary is generally regarded as the first known author of Latin Christian hymns, and Jerome mentions a "Book of Hymns" by him. Only fragments survive. They include an abecedarian hymn, "Ante saecula qui manes", which praises the Son's eternal birth from the Father in the language of Nicene theology. The hymns are difficult and doctrinal in style, and they come before the more popular hymnody of Ambrose of Milan.

The Liber ad Constantium Imperatorem is a Latin petition from Hilary of Poitiers to the emperor Constantius II, usually called his second book to Constantius. Hilary had been exiled to Phrygia after the Synod of Béziers in 356. He wrote this work around 359–360, apparently at Constantinople. He insists that he is still a bishop in communion with the churches of Gaul. He asks for a public hearing to answer the men who had him exiled and to set out the faith of Nicaea against the Arians. It is an important witness to the Arian controversy in the West.

Hilary of Poitiers wrote a lost polemical and historical work against Valens of Mursa and Ursacius of Singidunum, two leading pro-Arian bishops. Its arrangement into three books has been worked out by modern scholars from surviving fragments, mainly those preserved in the so-called Collectanea antiariana Parisina and the "first book to Constantius." The first book dates from 356 and the second from the winter of 359/360. The books combine Hilary's narrative with documents such as synodal letters from Serdica, creeds and letters of Pope Liberius. Together they are a major source for the Arian controversy in the Latin West.

This Latin text is a petition to Emperor Constantius II from the Western bishops at the Council of Serdica (343/4). It asks him to stop provincial judges from trying clergy and to end the coercion of Catholics by Arian partisans, appealing for freedom of conscience. It survives with a narrative passage by Hilary of Poitiers. It was long known as Hilary's "first book to Constantius", but it is now usually treated as part of his historical anti-Arian dossier, the Collectanea antiariana, an important source for the Arian controversy.

This is a group of Latin writings that have come down under the name of Hilary of Poitiers (c. 298 – c. 367) but are not thought to be his. It opens with a letter to his daughter Abra. In it the writer explains his long absence through an allegory: he travelled far to a beautiful young man, meaning Christ, to ask for a priceless pearl and garment for her. The letter urges her to choose consecrated virginity. Most scholars regard it as a later composition, and Abra's own existence is historically uncertain.

The Tractatus mysteriorum (Treatise on the Mysteries) is a Latin work by Hilary of Poitiers, the fourth-century bishop and opponent of Arianism. It probably dates from his later years, after his exile in the East. The treatise is a typological reading of the Old Testament. It argues that the patriarchs and other figures, from Adam, Noah, Melchizedek and Abraham onward, prefigure Christ's coming, passion and resurrection and the gathering of the Church. It survives incomplete in two books and is an important early Latin example of figural exegesis.

This short Latin letter is attributed to Hilary of Arles (c. 403–449), bishop of Arles and former monk of Lérins, and is addressed to Eucherius, bishop of Lyon. Eucherius had sent Hilary some of his books, and Hilary had to return them quickly because the messenger insisted. He writes that he has read them through only once and admires them. He asks to receive copies of these "institutions", which Eucherius had written to teach his young sons. The letter is a witness to the literary friendship among the monk-bishops of fifth-century Gaul who were connected with Lérins.

De Evangelio is a short Latin poem in hexameters that has come down under the name of Hilary. It is not considered his work, and its real author and date are unknown, though it is generally placed in late antiquity. The poem retells the Gospel story, starting with Christ's birth from the Virgin. It describes creation rejoicing, the serpent's defeat and the Magi's gifts, and it praises Christ with a string of titles drawn from Scripture and doctrine. It belongs to the early Christian tradition of biblical epic.

De Martyrio Maccabaeorum is a short Latin poem in hexameters retelling the martyrdom of the mother and her seven sons under the Syrian king Antiochus, the story told in 2 Maccabees 7. The king first offers the mother wealth and then threatens torture, but she refuses to abandon the law of God and encourages her sons to remain faithful. Its authorship is uncertain. Manuscripts give it to Hilary, and it has also been attributed to Marius Victorinus. It probably dates from late antiquity.

The Metrum in Genesim ad Leonem papam is a short Latin poem retelling the opening chapters of Genesis. Manuscripts attribute it to a Hilary, but its true author is unknown. It has been linked to Hilary of Arles and to Hilary of Poitiers, and it is usually placed in 5th-century Gaul. The poem opens with elegiac couplets addressed to a Pope Leo, who had asked for the work. Hexameters follow, praising the eternal, self-originating Creator and describing how the world was shaped out of formless chaos. It belongs to the late antique tradition of biblical epic.

This is the collected correspondence of Jerome of Stridon. It spans roughly fifty years, from his earliest surviving letter to Innocent (c. 370) until shortly before his death at Bethlehem in 420. The collection also includes letters written to Jerome by correspondents such as Pope Damasus and Augustine of Hippo. The letters deal with ascetic and virginal life, biblical interpretation and the principles of translation, as well as the Origenist controversy and personal disputes. They are polished examples of Latin prose and an important source for the church and society of the late fourth century.

Jerome's Latin commentary on the Book of Jeremiah in six books was his last major work of biblical exegesis. He wrote it in Bethlehem in his final years, roughly 414–420, and dedicated it to his friend Eusebius. It followed his commentaries on the Twelve Prophets, Isaiah, Daniel and Ezekiel. Jerome works from the Hebrew text and its order, sets aside Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah, and explains the literal and spiritual sense. It also contains polemic against Pelagius. Jerome died before finishing it, and the commentary stops at chapter 32.

The Evangeliorum libri quattuor ("Four Books of the Gospels") is a Latin epic poem by Juvencus, a Christian priest from Hispania. He wrote it around 330, during the reign of Constantine. In about 3,200 dactylic hexameters it retells the life of Christ, mainly following Matthew's Gospel, with material drawn from the other evangelists. Its preface contrasts the false tales of Homer and Virgil with the truth of the Gospel. Its diction borrows heavily from Virgil. It is the earliest surviving Latin biblical epic, and it was widely read and imitated in the Middle Ages.

De ave Phoenice (The Phoenix) is a Latin poem in elegiac couplets, usually attributed to the early Christian writer Lactantius (c. 250–c. 325), though his authorship has been questioned. It describes a paradise-like grove of the sun in the far East, free from disease, old age, death and storms. There the phoenix lives, dies and is reborn from its own remains. The poem has no openly Christian content, but many scholars read the bird as a symbol of resurrection and of Christ. It was the main source of the Old English poem The Phoenix.

De Mortibus Persecutorum is a Latin historical and apologetic treatise attributed to Lactantius, the Christian rhetorician and adviser to Constantine. It was written around 315 and addressed to a confessor named Donatus. It argues that the emperors who persecuted Christians, from Nero to Diocletian, Galerius and Maximinus Daia, died miserable deaths as divine punishment. It gives a detailed account of the Great Persecution and of Tetrarchic politics. It also preserves the texts of Galerius's edict of toleration and the so-called Edict of Milan, which makes it a key historical source. Its authorship has occasionally been questioned.

De passione Domini is a short Latin poem that has come down among the works of Lactantius, the Christian apologist of the early fourth century. Its authorship is doubtful, and many scholars consider it a later composition, though its date is uncertain. In the poem Christ speaks to a visitor entering a church. He asks the visitor to pause and remember him, then recounts his incarnation, humble birth, exile in Egypt, poverty, teaching and innocent suffering for human sin. Its aim is to stir devotion and gratitude for the Passion.

De Ira Dei (On the Anger of God) is a Latin treatise by the Christian apologist Lactantius. It is addressed to a certain Donatus and was written after his Divine Institutes, probably in the early fourth century. Lactantius argues against the Epicurean and Stoic view that God feels neither anger nor favour. He holds that God's justified anger against wickedness follows from his goodness and providence, and that without it religion, the fear of God and moral order would collapse. The work is an important early Christian treatment of divine emotion.

De Opificio Dei is a short Latin treatise by the Christian rhetorician Lactantius. It was probably written around 303–304, early in the Diocletianic persecution, and is addressed to his former pupil Demetrianus. It argues for divine providence against the Epicureans by describing the human body, explaining how each part is fitted to its purpose, and by discussing the soul. In its arguments it follows Cicero's De natura deorum. It is generally considered Lactantius's earliest surviving Christian work, and it looks ahead to his Divine Institutes.

The Epitome of the Divine Institutes is a Latin apologetic work by Lactantius (c. 250–c. 325), the North African rhetorician later called the "Christian Cicero". He wrote it some years after his seven-book Divine Institutes, at the request of his brother Pentadius, to whom it is addressed. In a single book it condenses the larger work's argument: it rejects pagan polytheism and the claims of the philosophers, and defends the one true God, Christian justice and worship, the immortality of the soul and the final judgment. It also shows how Lactantius later revised some of his own arguments.

The Divine Institutes (Institutiones Divinae) is a Latin apologetic treatise in seven books by Lactantius, the North African rhetorician who later became an adviser to Constantine. He wrote it between about 303 and 311, during the Great Persecution. Its aim is to show educated pagans that Christianity is reasonable and true. It attacks polytheism and the errors of the philosophers, then sets out Christian teaching on true wisdom, justice, worship and the afterlife. It was the first systematic account of Christian thought in Latin, and its polished Ciceronian style later earned Lactantius the name "Christian Cicero."

The Fragments are a small collection of passages attributed to Lactantius (c. 250–c. 325), the Latin Christian apologist known as the "Christian Cicero." Later writers preserved them from his otherwise lost works. One passage teaches that the passions of the soul, such as fear, love, anger and desire, were implanted by God and lead to virtue when ruled by reason but to vice when unrestrained. Others come from his letters to Probus on the metres of Latin comedy, citing Terence and Plautus. These scraps show the range of his learning, which extended to grammar and literary scholarship.

De non conveniendo cum haereticis ("On Not Associating with Heretics") is a Latin polemical treatise by Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia. He wrote it during his exile in the later 350s, after he refused to condemn Athanasius at the Council of Milan in 355. Addressed directly and abusively to the Arian-leaning emperor Constantius II, it answers the charge that Nicene bishops were enemies of peace and unity. Drawing on many Old Testament examples, it argues that the faithful must keep themselves apart from heretics. Its long scriptural quotations are valuable evidence for the Old Latin Bible.

De non parcendo in Deum delinquentibus ("That Those Who Sin Against God Are Not to Be Spared") is a Latin polemical treatise by Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari. He wrote it during his exile in the late 350s and addressed it directly to Emperor Constantius II. The emperor had complained of being insulted, and Lucifer answers with Old Testament examples, beginning with Moses and the Levites punishing idolatry, to argue that God's servants have always rebuked apostates. In this way he defends his fierce opposition to the emperor's pro-Arian policy.

De Regibus Apostaticis ("On Apostate Kings") is a short Latin polemical treatise by Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia. He wrote it while in exile in the late 350s, after refusing to condemn Athanasius. It is addressed to the Arian emperor Constantius II and rejects his claim that his continued power proved God approved of his faith and his persecution of the Nicene party. Lucifer cites rulers of Israel and Judah, beginning with Gideon, who fell into idolatry or cruelty. God endured them for a time but punished them in the end.

De regibus apostaticis ("On Apostate Kings") is a Latin polemical treatise by Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia. He wrote it in exile around 358–360, after refusing to condemn Athanasius at the Council of Milan in 355. It is addressed directly and abusively to Emperor Constantius II. Using Old Testament examples of kings who abandoned God and were punished, Lucifer argues that the emperor's support for Arianism makes him an apostate. It belongs to a group of pamphlets against Constantius that includes the books On Saint Athanasius.

A small Latin collection of letters to and from Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia (died 370 or 371), a fierce opponent of Arianism. It includes a letter from Lucifer, the presbyter Pancratius and the deacon Hilarius urging Eusebius of Vercelli to come and resist the Arians, probably at the time of the Council of Milan in 355. It also contains letters from Pope Liberius praising Lucifer and his companions in exile for their steadfast faith. The letters record Western Nicene resistance to Constantius II's pro-Arian church policy.

"That We Must Die for the Son of God" is a Latin polemical treatise by Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia. He wrote it in exile, probably around 360, after he refused at the Council of Milan (355) to condemn Athanasius. It is addressed directly and abusively to Emperor Constantius II. Lucifer denounces the emperor's support for Arianism and his use of force against Nicene bishops. He declares that God's servants scorn imperial violence and should welcome martyrdom rather than give up the faith. It is among the last of his pamphlets against Constantius.

De Ecclesia is a short Latin Virgilian cento, a poem built entirely from lines and half-lines of Virgil. It describes a crowded church where men, women and children sing and pray, and then a priest preaches to them. His sermon tells of Christ's coming down from heaven, his birth from a virgin, his rejection and his trial before Pilate. The poem survives in the Latin Anthology. It is sometimes attributed to Mavortius, probably the consul of 527 known for a Virgilian cento on the Judgement of Paris, but the authorship is uncertain.

Octavius is a Latin dialogue defending Christianity, written by Marcus Minucius Felix, a Roman lawyer, probably in the late second or early third century. Its exact date and its relation to Tertullian's Apologeticum are disputed. Set on the beach at Ostia, it records a debate between the pagan Caecilius Natalis and the Christian Octavius Januarius, with Minucius as judge. Caecilius attacks Christian beliefs and rumoured practices, Octavius refutes him, and Caecilius is converted. Its polished Ciceronian style makes it one of the earliest and most elegant works of Latin Christian apologetic.

This Latin polemical treatise by Optatus, bishop of Milevis in Numidia, replies to Parmenian, the Donatist bishop of Carthage. It was first written around 366–367, and a seventh book was added later, probably in the 380s. Optatus traces the North African schism back to accusations of betraying the Scriptures (traditio) during the Diocletianic persecution. He treats the Donatists as schismatics rather than heretics and argues for the unity of the Catholic Church, its communion with the see of Peter, and the validity of sacraments whatever the worthiness of the minister. The work strongly shaped Augustine's later anti-Donatist writings.

This is a dossier of Latin documents from the early Donatist controversy in Roman North Africa, preserved as an appendix to the anti-Donatist treatise of Optatus of Milevis (late fourth century). It includes the acts of the proceedings that cleared Felix of Aptunga, who consecrated Caecilian as bishop of Carthage, of handing over the Scriptures during the Diocletianic persecution. It also includes letters of the emperor Constantine and records of councils. These official records are key evidence for how the schism began and for the early church's dealings with the emperor.

The Commonitorium is a Latin didactic poem by Orientius, a fifth-century Christian poet usually identified with a bishop of Auch in Gaul. It was composed around 430 in elegiac couplets and runs to about 1,036 lines. It is traditionally divided into two books, though the division may be arbitrary. The poem urges the reader to seek eternal life and shows the way to salvation. It warns against sins such as lust, envy, avarice, vanity and drunkenness, and reminds the reader of death, judgement and the rewards of heaven.

The Carmina are a small group of short Latin poems that have come down with the works of Orientius, a fifth-century Christian poet usually identified with the bishop of Auch in Gaul. Whether he actually wrote them is uncertain. They include verses on the Nativity of the Lord, a list of the biblical names and titles of Christ, and a poem on the Trinity, along with other devotional pieces. These verses are much less studied than his Commonitorium, the didactic poem in elegiac couplets that is his best-known work.

The Orationes are short Latin prayer-poems that the manuscript tradition places among the minor pieces attached to the works of Orientius, a fifth-century Christian poet in Gaul known mainly for his Commonitorium. Whether he actually wrote them is doubtful. Written in iambic trimeters, they read like a litany. Angels, the heavenly bodies, the weather, earth, ocean and even the underworld are called on in turn to praise God, and each stanza ends with the refrain "amen sonamus, alleluia dicimus". A closing section warns copyists not to add or remove a single letter.

The Seven Books of History Against the Pagans is a Latin universal history by Paulus Orosius, a priest who was probably from Gallaecia. He wrote it at the request of Augustine of Hippo, to whom it is dedicated, and finished it around 417–418. After Alaric sacked Rome in 410, pagans blamed Christianity for Rome's troubles. Orosius answered them by surveying wars and disasters from Adam to his own day, arguing that earlier ages had suffered worse. The work became one of the most widely read histories of the Middle Ages and was later adapted into Old English.

The Liber Apologeticus is a Latin polemical treatise by Paulus Orosius, the priest and historian from Hispania, written in Palestine in 415 during the Pelagian controversy. Orosius had been sent east by Augustine of Hippo. After a meeting of clergy in Jerusalem under Bishop John, he was accused of teaching that a person cannot be free from sin even with God's help. Addressing his fellow priests, he defends his own orthodoxy and attacks the teachings of Pelagius on grace and free will. He appeals to earlier Fathers such as Cyprian and Hilary.

The Commonitorium is a short Latin memorandum that the Spanish priest Paulus Orosius addressed to Augustine of Hippo, generally dated to about 414, soon after he arrived in Africa from the Iberian Peninsula. It sets out the errors then troubling the Spanish churches: the teachings of the Priscillianists and certain Origenist doctrines, such as the pre-existence of souls and the restoration of all things. Orosius asks Augustine to refute them. It is an important witness to Priscillianism, and it led Augustine to write his reply, Ad Orosium contra Priscillianistas et Origenistas.

The Epigramma is a short Latin poem in hexameters, transmitted under the name of a "Saint Paulinus" and usually ascribed to Paulinus, bishop of Béziers, in the early fifth century. It takes the form of a dialogue set in a monastery. Salmon, a cleric returning to the city where he was brought up, talks with an aged monk about the moral corruption of Christians in Gaul at the time of the barbarian invasions. It survives alongside the Alethia of Claudius Marius Victorius, and an early edition wrongly attributed it to him.

The Carmina are the collected Latin poems of Paulinus of Nola (c. 354–431), the Roman senator who renounced his career for ascetic life and became bishop of Nola in Campania. Written from before his conversion into the early fifth century, they include verse letters to his teacher Ausonius, paraphrases of the Psalms, a wedding poem for Julian of Eclanum, a consolation for a dead child, and a series of annual poems for the feast of Saint Felix of Nola. Together with Prudentius, Paulinus is a major early Latin Christian poet, joining classical form to Christian subjects.

The Epistulae are the surviving Latin letters of Paulinus of Nola (c. 354–431), the Roman senator who gave up his wealth for an ascetic life and later became bishop of Nola. About fifty letters survive, mostly from the 390s onward. Some were sent jointly with his wife Therasia. His correspondents included Sulpicius Severus, Augustine, Jerome and Delphinus of Bordeaux. Written in an ornate style full of scriptural allusion, the letters deal with Christian friendship, renunciation, biblical interpretation and his building work at the shrine of St Felix. They are an important witness to the spread of Western asceticism.

The Eucharisticos ("Thanksgiving") is an autobiographical Latin poem in hexameters with a prose preface. Paulinus of Pella, a grandson of Ausonius, wrote it in old age, around 459. He presents it as a thanksgiving to God, looking back over a long life marked by both prosperity and misfortune. He recalls his youth in Bordeaux, the Gothic occupation of Aquitaine, the siege of Bazas, the loss of his estates, and his turn to a religious life. It is a valuable firsthand witness to aristocratic life in fifth-century Gaul as Roman rule in the West declined.

De Vita Sancti Martini is a Latin verse life of Martin of Tours in six books of hexameters by Paulinus of Périgueux, a Gallic poet of the later fifth century. It is dedicated to Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, in a prose letter. The first five books turn into epic verse the prose writings of Sulpicius Severus on Martin, the Life and the Dialogues. The sixth book draws on an account of posthumous miracles that Perpetuus had sent to Paulinus. The poem is an important witness to the cult of Martin in Gaul.

This short Latin poem in hexameters is by Paulinus of Périgueux, the Gallic poet who wrote a six-book verse Life of Saint Martin in the later fifth century. In it Paulinus thanks Saint Martin for healing his young grandson and the grandson's bride, who had both fallen gravely ill. The cure followed the use of a written record of Martin's miracles sent by Perpetuus, bishop of Tours. The poem is evidence for the cult of Martin at Tours and for the healing power believed to reside in such writings.

De Orantibus ("On Those Who Pray") is a short Latin verse inscription by Paulinus of Périgueux, the fifth-century Gallic poet best known for his hexameter Life of Saint Martin. It is generally linked with the rebuilt basilica of Saint Martin at Tours, completed under Bishop Perpetuus around 470, and was meant to be inscribed there. It speaks to pilgrims lying in prayer, urging them to lift their eyes, seek Martin's heavenly patronage and see the miracles of healing and deliverance worked at his shrine.

The Life and Passion of Cyprian is a Latin hagiographical account of Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, who was martyred in 258. It is attributed to Pontius, a deacon who served under Cyprian and accompanied him into exile. He wrote it shortly after Cyprian's death. It covers Cyprian's conversion, his time as bishop, his work during the plague at Carthage, his exile to Curubis and his execution under Valerian. It is often regarded as the earliest surviving Christian biography in Latin, and it praises its subject in a rhetorical style.

The Acta Proconsularia is a short Latin martyr account recording the trials and execution of Cyprian, bishop of Carthage. It gives his examination by the proconsul Paternus on 30 August 257, which ended in his exile to Curubis. It then covers his second hearing before Galerius Maximus and his beheading on 14 September 258, during the persecution under Valerian and Gallienus. Its author is anonymous, though it is often transmitted alongside the Life of Cyprian by his deacon Pontius. It is among the most important early Latin acts of the martyrs.

The Versus ad gratiam Domini is a short Latin Christian cento attributed to an otherwise unknown poet named Pomponius. It is usually dated to late antiquity, probably the fourth or fifth century, and is sometimes called the Tityrus. Its lines are taken almost entirely from Virgil and put together in a new order. The poem is a pastoral dialogue between Meliboeus and Tityrus, the shepherds of Virgil's First Eclogue. Through their exchange it praises the one almighty God, creator and ruler of all things. It is an example of how Christian writers reused the classical poetic tradition.

The Canons on the Epistles of Paul are a Latin doctrinal index to the fourteen Pauline letters, Hebrews included, attributed to Priscillian, the ascetic bishop of Ávila executed around 385. The author divided the letters into numbered passages and grouped them under ninety short doctrinal statements, or canons. Readers could use them to find scriptural evidence against heretical opponents quickly. The canons survive only in a version revised by a bishop named Peregrinus, who says he removed unorthodox elements. In this form they were copied in many Vulgate manuscripts.

The Eleven Tractates are a collection of Latin treatises that survive in a single fifth- or sixth-century manuscript at Würzburg. The manuscript was discovered in 1885. The tractates come from the ascetic movement of Priscillian, bishop of Ávila, who was executed around 385. Scholars disagree on whether Priscillian wrote them or one of his close followers, such as Instantius. The first three are apologetic: they defend the group's orthodoxy to bishops, condemn heresies and discuss the use of apocryphal books. The rest are homilies and biblical expositions. They are the main surviving writings of the Priscillianist movement.

The Cento is a Latin poem by the Roman aristocrat Faltonia Betitia Proba, probably written in the mid-fourth century after her conversion to Christianity. It is made entirely of lines and half-lines taken from Virgil and rearranged to retell biblical history. It covers the Creation and Fall, then turns at greater length to the life, death, resurrection and ascension of Christ. Some ancient readers criticised it, including perhaps Jerome, but it circulated widely and was used in teaching. It is a key example of the Christian adaptation of classical poetry.

This Latin commentary on the Carmen Paschale (Paschal Song) of Sedulius, the fifth-century Christian poet, is attributed to Remigius of Auxerre, a Carolingian Benedictine teacher who died in 908. It begins with an introduction to the poet. It says Sedulius was a layman trained in worldly learning who turned to God. He wrote the work first in prose and then in verse, and dedicated it to the priest Macedonius. The commentary then works through the poem, explaining individual words, their grammar and their theological sense. It shows how Sedulius's biblical epic was used to teach Latin in Carolingian schools.

This is a Latin translation of nine orations by Gregory of Nazianzus, made by Rufinus of Aquileia around 399–400 at the request of his friend Apronianus. In a dedicatory preface Rufinus praises Gregory as a teacher whose life matched his doctrine. He sketches Gregory's Cappadocian family and his studies at Athens, recounts a dream in which Wisdom and Chastity came to him, and describes his reluctant ordination. The collection opens with Gregory's apologetic oration on his flight from the priesthood. It was the main way Latin readers came to know Gregory's preaching.

The Epistulae are the collected Latin letters of Ruricius (c. 440–c. 510), a Gallo-Roman aristocrat who became bishop of Limoges around 485. They survive in two books and were written in the later fifth and early sixth centuries. Among the recipients are Faustus of Riez, whom the opening letter addresses as a revered teacher, and Sidonius Apollinaris. The letters deal with spiritual advice, friendship, family matters and church affairs. They are a valuable record of the aristocratic and episcopal network of southern Gaul under Visigothic rule.

This is a short Latin letter from Rusticus, a presbyter, to Eucherius, bishop of Lyon (d. c. 450). Rusticus writes that he has had copies made of two volumes Eucherius sent him and has returned them. He praises Eucherius's skill in explaining the riddles of both Testaments through spiritual understanding, which fits Eucherius's exegetical works. He also recalls reading, as a boy, verse inscriptions beneath portraits of orators and poets in a private library, and he quotes lines on Virgil. The letter is a small witness to literary culture and learned friendship in fifth-century Gaul.

De Gubernatione Dei is a Latin treatise in eight books by Salvian, a priest of Marseilles. He wrote it in the 440s and dedicated it to Bishop Salonius. Christians in Gaul were asking why God allowed the barbarian invasions. Salvian answers that God still governs the world and that the Romans' sufferings are a just punishment for their sins. He sets Roman vice, injustice and oppression of the poor against the comparative virtues of Goths, Vandals and other peoples. The work is an important source for society in fifth-century Gaul.
