The letters of Salvian of Marseilles, a fifth-century priest and writer in Roman Gaul, survive as a small collection of nine Latin letters. They show his ties to the monastic circle of Lérins and to leading Gallic churchmen. One letter thanks Eucherius of Lyon for books he wrote to instruct his sons, Salonius and Veranius. Both were once Salvian's pupils and had since become bishops. Another letter defends his treatise Ad Ecclesiam. Together the letters offer rare personal evidence about Salvian and his circle.

The letters of Salvian of Marseilles, a fifth-century priest and writer in Roman Gaul, survive as a small collection of nine Latin letters. They show his ties to the monastic circle of Lérins and to leading Gallic churchmen. One letter thanks Eucherius of Lyon for books he wrote to instruct his sons, Salonius and Veranius. Both were once Salvian's pupils and had since become bishops. Another letter defends his treatise Ad Ecclesiam. Together the letters offer rare personal evidence about Salvian and his circle.

Ad Ecclesiam ("To the Church"), also called Adversus Avaritiam ("Against Avarice"), is a Latin treatise in four books by Salvian, a fifth-century priest of Marseilles. It was issued under the pseudonym "Timothy", which Salvian later explained in a letter to Bishop Salonius. Written as a letter to the whole catholic Church, it attacks the greed of Christians who hold on to their wealth. It urges clergy, ascetics and lay believers to give their property to the Church and the poor, especially in their wills, so that their riches serve their salvation.

This Latin letter was written by Secundinus, a Manichaean hearer living in Rome, to Augustine of Hippo, probably around 405. It is courteous and full of praise for Augustine. In it Secundinus defends Manichaean teaching, especially its account of the struggle between good and evil, and quotes Paul and Mani together. He criticises Augustine's attacks on the sect and urges him to return to the faith he once held. Augustine answered it in his treatise Contra Secundinum Manichaeum. The letter survives among Augustine's works and is a rare surviving statement of Latin Manichaeism in its own words.

A solis ortus cardine is a Latin hymn by the Christian poet Sedulius, author of the Carmen Paschale, written in the first half of the fifth century. It is an abecedarian poem: its twenty-three stanzas of iambic dimeter each begin with a successive letter of the alphabet. It tells the life of Christ from the Incarnation and Nativity through his miracles to the Passion and Resurrection. Parts of it entered the Western liturgy, with the opening stanzas sung at Christmas and the "Hostis Herodes impie" section at Epiphany. It was widely used and translated in later centuries.

The Carmen Paschale ("Paschal Song") is a Latin biblical epic by the Christian poet Sedulius, written in the first half of the fifth century. After a preface in elegiac couplets, its five books of hexameters retell miracles from the Old Testament and then the life, miracles, passion and resurrection of Christ. Sedulius presents the work as a Christian alternative to the falsehoods of pagan poetry. He later made a prose version, the Opus Paschale. The poem was widely read and used as a school text throughout the Middle Ages.

De Verbi Incarnatione ("On the Incarnation of the Word") is a late antique Latin Virgilian cento, a poem built entirely from lines and half-lines borrowed from Virgil. It tells the Christian story of the Incarnation. God the Father takes pity on humankind and sends the Word, and the poem then turns to the Annunciation, Mary's humble consent and the events that follow. It has been copied together with the works of the fifth-century poet Sedulius and is sometimes attributed to him, but his authorship is doubtful. It is an example of the Christian reworking of classical epic.

De Verbi Incarnatione ("On the Incarnation of the Word") is a late antique Latin Virgilian cento, a poem built entirely from lines and half-lines borrowed from Virgil. It tells the Christian story of the Incarnation. God the Father takes pity on humankind and sends the Word, and the poem then turns to the Annunciation, Mary's humble consent and the events that follow. It has been copied together with the works of the fifth-century poet Sedulius and is sometimes attributed to him, but his authorship is doubtful. It is an example of the Christian reworking of classical epic.

This is a Latin prose letter by Sedulius, a Christian poet of the first half of the fifth century, addressed to the presbyter Macedonius. It dedicates his biblical epic, the Carmen Paschale. Sedulius describes turning away from secular literary studies to devote his talent to God. He defends himself against charges of presumption for setting out on the "vast sea" of the paschal mysteries. He also credits the teaching and encouragement of Macedonius and others. A second letter to Macedonius introduces the prose reworking, the Opus Paschale. Both letters are important statements of the aims of early Christian biblical poetry.

This is a Latin prose letter by Sedulius, a Christian poet of the first half of the fifth century, addressed to the presbyter Macedonius. It dedicates his biblical epic, the Carmen Paschale. Sedulius describes turning away from secular literary studies to devote his talent to God. He defends himself against charges of presumption for setting out on the "vast sea" of the paschal mysteries. He also credits the teaching and encouragement of Macedonius and others. A second letter to Macedonius introduces the prose reworking, the Opus Paschale. Both letters are important statements of the aims of early Christian biblical poetry.

Hymnus I, known by its opening words "Cantemus, socii, Domino", is a Latin poem by Sedulius, the Christian poet of the first half of the fifth century best known for the Carmen paschale. It is written in elegiac couplets. Each couplet uses epanalepsis: the opening words of the hexameter come back at the close of the pentameter. The poem moves through the Old Testament from the fall of Lucifer and Adam onward, setting each episode beside its fulfilment in Christ. It is an early, deliberate use of typological interpretation in Latin hymnody.

The Opus Paschale is a Latin prose work by the Christian poet Sedulius, written in the first half of the fifth century. It is his own prose reworking of his Carmen Paschale, a hexameter poem on the miracles of Christ in the Old and New Testaments, culminating in the Passion and Resurrection. Sedulius wrote it in an elaborate rhetorical style, and its preface presents the work as a modest Easter feast. It is an early example of the paired poem and prose version, or opus geminum.

The Chronica, also called the Sacred History, is a Latin universal chronicle in two books by Sulpicius Severus, the Aquitanian writer best known for his Life of Saint Martin of Tours. Written in the early fifth century, it covers events from the creation of the world to the author's own time. It summarises the Old Testament and the life of Christ, then the persecutions, the Arian controversy and the Priscillianist affair, using secular historians to fix dates. Its brief, classical style earned Sulpicius the name "the Christian Sallust." Its accounts of fourth-century church conflicts are a valuable historical source.

The Vita Sancti Martini is a Latin biography of Martin, bishop of Tours, written by the Aquitanian writer Sulpicius Severus, who knew him personally. It was completed around 396–397, apparently while Martin was still alive, and is introduced by a dedicatory letter to Desiderius. It covers Martin's military service, including the famous sharing of his cloak with a beggar, his monastic life, his work as bishop and his many miracles. It became one of the most influential models for later Western hagiography.

The Dialogues are a Latin hagiographical work by Sulpicius Severus, the Aquitanian writer and biographer of Martin of Tours, composed in the early fifth century. Written as conversations between the author, his friend Postumianus, just back from the East, and Gallus, a Gaulish disciple of Martin, they first tell of the monks and hermits of Egypt and the East. They then turn to further miracles and deeds of Martin, presenting him as the equal of the famous Eastern ascetics. The work adds to Sulpicius's earlier Life of Martin and is an important source for early Western monasticism.

The three Latin letters of Sulpicius Severus (c. 363 – c. 425), a Christian writer from Aquitaine, add to his Life of Saint Martin of Tours. The first, to the priest Eusebius, answers a critic who asked why Martin, said to have worked miracles, had himself been put in danger by a fire. The second, to the deacon Aurelius, tells of a vision of Martin and mourns his death in 397. The third, to Bassula, the author's mother-in-law, describes Martin's last days and funeral. Together they form an important part of the early cult of Martin.

The Epistolae Septem, or Doubtful Letters, are seven Latin letters handed down under the name of Sulpicius Severus, the late fourth- and early fifth-century Aquitanian writer and biographer of Martin of Tours. His authorship is doubted or rejected, and the real writer or writers and the date are uncertain. The letters are personal and spiritual. Some are addressed to a woman the writer calls his sister, encouraging ascetic Christian living, renunciation of the world and perseverance in the Lord's precepts. They show the devotional and ascetic correspondence circulating in the Latin West in late antiquity.

Ad Nationes ("To the Nations") is a Latin apologetic treatise in two books by Tertullian of Carthage, written around 197 and addressed to pagan readers. The first book argues that hatred of Christians rests on ignorance. It rebuts the popular charges against them and turns those accusations back on their accusers. The second book attacks pagan religion and draws on Varro's division of theology into physical, mythical and civil kinds. Its material closely parallels Tertullian's more polished Apologeticum from the same year, and it is often regarded as a preliminary version of that work.

Against Hermogenes is a Latin polemical treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, written in the early third century. It attacks Hermogenes, a contemporary painter and Christian teacher who held that God formed the world out of eternal, uncreated matter. Tertullian argues that an eternal matter would be equal to God and so destroy his uniqueness and sovereignty. Working closely through the opening verses of Genesis, he defends the creation of all things out of nothing. The treatise is an important early statement of the doctrine of creatio ex nihilo.

Adversus Marcionem is a Latin polemical treatise in five books by Tertullian of Carthage, written against the teachings of Marcion of Sinope. By the author's own account, it is the third version of the work. Book I refers to the fifteenth year of Septimius Severus, which dates it to about 207–208. Tertullian rejects Marcion's split between a good, unknown God and the Creator, and argues that Christ fulfilled the prophets. He then goes through Marcion's Gospel and his Pauline epistles. Because the work quotes them so closely, it is the main source for reconstructing Marcion's canon.

Against Praxeas (Adversus Praxean) is a Latin theological treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, probably written around 213 during his Montanist period. It attacks the Monarchian teaching of Praxeas, an opponent of the New Prophecy from Asia Minor. Praxeas stressed God's unity so strongly that he identified the Father with the Son and said the Father himself was born and suffered. Tertullian answered that he had "crucified the Father." Against this view, Tertullian defends one divine substance in three persons and uses the term trinitas. The work strongly shaped the language later Western theology used for the Trinity.

Against the Valentinians (Adversus Valentinianos) is a Latin polemical treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, written in the early third century. It attacks the Gnostic school of Valentinus by summarizing and mocking its elaborate myth of the Pleroma, its paired aeons and the fall of Sophia. Tertullian compares the sect's secrecy to the Eleusinian mysteries and ridicules its many-storeyed heavens as a kind of apartment block. He names Justin, Miltiades, Irenaeus and Proculus as his authorities, and the work leans heavily on the first book of Irenaeus's Against Heresies. It is an early Latin witness to Valentinian teaching.

De Anima (On the Soul) is a Latin treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, usually dated to around 210–213, during his Montanist period. It is his longest single work and is often called the first Christian study of the soul. Tertullian follows an earlier dispute with Hermogenes about the soul's origin and argues mainly against the philosophers. He holds that the soul is corporeal and is passed on from parents to children, a view called traducianism. He rejects pre-existence and transmigration. He also discusses sleep, dreams, death and the soul's state before the resurrection, drawing on the physician Soranus.

De Baptismo (On Baptism) is a Latin treatise by Tertullian of Carthage. It is usually dated to around 200, before his turn to Montanism, and is the oldest surviving Christian work devoted to baptism. Tertullian wrote it to answer a woman of the Cainite sect who rejected water baptism. He defends the power of water as God's chosen means and explains the rite. He also discusses John's baptism, martyrdom as a "baptism of blood" and who may baptize. He advises delaying baptism for young children and the unmarried.

De idololatria (On Idolatry) is a Latin moral treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, written in the early third century; its exact date is disputed. It presents idolatry as the chief crime of humanity, one that contains all other sins. It then sets out how far Christians may take part in the life of a pagan society. Tertullian condemns trades that serve idol worship, such as making images, astrology and selling incense. He also rejects pagan festivals and oaths, public office and military service. The work is an important source on early Christian attitudes toward Roman civic and religious life.

De ieiunio adversus psychicos (On Fasting, against the Psychics) is a Latin treatise by Tertullian of Carthage. He wrote it during his Montanist period in the early third century. It defends the stricter fasting of the New Prophecy against the mainstream Christians, whom Tertullian calls "psychics", or merely carnal believers. These practices included xerophagy (eating only dry food), extended station fasts and additional fasts. Tertullian links gluttony with lust and with repeated marriage, and he answers the charge that such fasts were innovations. The treatise is an important witness to early Christian fasting practice and to the conflicts over Montanism.

De Oratione is a short Latin treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, usually dated to about 200, during his early, pre-Montanist period. It is the oldest surviving Christian commentary on the Lord's Prayer. Tertullian explains each petition and calls the prayer a summary of the whole Gospel. He then turns to the practice of prayer: forgiveness and a clean conscience, posture, kneeling, the kiss of peace, fasting on station days, the veiling of virgins and the hours of prayer. The work later shaped Cyprian's treatise on the Lord's Prayer.

De patientia is a short moral treatise by Tertullian of Carthage. It is usually dated to around 200–206, before his turn to Montanism. He opens by admitting that he is unfit to write on patience because he is so impatient himself. He then presents God and Christ as models of patience and traces impatience back to the devil and to the fall of Adam and Eve. The treatise also covers patience under loss, injury and persecution. It is the earliest Christian work devoted to this virtue, and Cyprian drew on it for his own De bono patientiae.

De Pudicitia (On Modesty) is a Latin polemical treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, written in his Montanist period in the early third century. It attacks an edict by a bishop, ironically called "pontifex maximus", which granted forgiveness to penitent adulterers and fornicators. The bishop has traditionally been identified as Callixtus I of Rome, though some scholars suggest Agrippinus of Carthage. Tertullian argues that grave sins such as these cannot be remitted by the Church. The work is an early witness to debates over penance and church authority.

De Carnis Resurrectione is a Latin treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, written in the early third century. It defends the bodily resurrection against Gnostic and Marcionite opponents. These opponents held that the creator of the world was opposed to the supreme God, that the flesh was worthless, and that only the soul would be saved. Tertullian argues from the dignity of the body as God's creation, from the Old Testament prophets and from Paul's letters. It is among the most thorough early Christian treatments of the resurrection of the body.

De Spectaculis (The Shows) is a moral treatise in Latin by Tertullian of Carthage, written between about 197 and 202. It is addressed to catechumens and baptized Christians, and argues that they must not attend the circus, theatre or amphitheatre. Tertullian traces these entertainments back to pagan festivals and idolatry, and says they stir up dangerous passions. He ends by setting the far greater spectacle of Christ's return and the Last Judgement against them. It is an important early witness to Christian attitudes toward Roman public life.

De Testimonio Animae (The Soul's Testimony) is a short Latin apologetic treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, usually dated to about 197–198, soon after his Apologeticum. It expands on that work's idea of the soul as "naturally Christian". Tertullian sets aside learned appeals to philosophers and poets and turns instead to the plain, untaught soul. He argues that its everyday sayings, such as "God grant it" and "God sees", show that people naturally know the one God, demons, and judgment after death. It is an early Christian argument that knowledge of God is natural to every person.

Scorpiace ("Antidote for the Scorpion's Sting") is a Latin treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, written in the early third century; its exact date is disputed. It is aimed at Gnostic teachers, likened to scorpions, who spread their "poison" in times of persecution by telling Christians that martyrdom was needless and that God could not want the death of the innocent. Drawing on the Old and New Testaments, Tertullian argues that God commands and rewards martyrdom and that confessing Christ publicly is a duty. The work is an important early defence of the theology of martyrdom.

Against All Heresies (Adversus omnes haereses) is a short Latin catalogue of thirty-two heresies, long transmitted as an appendix to Tertullian's De praescriptione haereticorum. Scholars agree it is not by Tertullian. Its author and date are uncertain, and Victorinus of Pettau has been suggested. After briefly setting aside Jewish sects such as the Sadducees and Pharisees, it summarizes Christian heresies from Simon Magus onward, including the Gnostic teachers. It is widely thought to depend on Hippolytus's lost Syntagma, which makes it an important witness to early heresiology alongside Philastrius and Epiphanius.

The Carmen de Iona et Ninive, also called De Iona propheta, is a short Latin poem in hexameters retelling the story of the prophet Jonah. It was once transmitted among the works of Tertullian but is not by him. Its author and date are uncertain; some scholars attribute it to Cyprianus Gallus. It opens by recalling the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, then describes how God sent Jonah to warn sinful Nineveh. Jonah tries to flee, fearing that God's mercy will make his prophecy come to nothing. The poem is often grouped with the companion Carmen de Sodoma.

The Carmen de Sodoma (Poem on Sodom) is an anonymous Latin poem in hexameters retelling the destruction of Sodom from Genesis 19. It has come down among works wrongly attributed to Tertullian and Cyprian. Its real author and date are uncertain, though some scholars attribute it to Cyprianus Gallus. The poem notes that after the Flood God promised never again to punish by water. It then describes how Sodom's renewed wickedness was punished by fire, which it presents as a foreshadowing of the final judgment. It is an example of early Latin biblical epic.

De situ terrae sanctae is a short Latin account of the Holy Land written in the early sixth century. A ninth-century manuscript names its author as Theodosius, an archdeacon, possibly from Germany. The work mentions building under Emperor Anastasius I but not under Justinian, so it is dated to about 518–530. It lists routes, distances and holy sites in Jerusalem, Palestine and neighbouring regions, adding biblical associations and local traditions. It is a useful witness to pilgrimage and the sacred places of late antiquity.

De Martyrio Maccabaeorum is a short Latin poem in hexameters retelling the martyrdom of the mother and her seven sons under the Syrian king Antiochus, the story told in 2 Maccabees 7. The king first offers the mother wealth and then threatens torture, but she refuses to abandon the law of God and encourages her sons to remain faithful. Its authorship is uncertain. Manuscripts give it to Hilary, and it has also been attributed to Marius Victorinus. It probably dates from late antiquity.

The Alethia ("Truth") is a Latin biblical epic in hexameters by Claudius Marius Victorius, a fifth-century rhetor of Marseille. It was probably written in the second quarter of the century and is also known as a commentary on Genesis in three books. It opens with a prayer to the triune God, then retells and interprets Genesis from the creation to the destruction of Sodom. Along the way it digresses on divine providence and the origins of human culture. It is a notable example of Christian verse paraphrase in late antique Gaul.

The Alethia ("Truth") is a Latin biblical epic in hexameters by Claudius Marius Victorius, a fifth-century rhetor of Marseille. It was probably written in the second quarter of the century and is also known as a commentary on Genesis in three books. It opens with a prayer to the triune God, then retells and interprets Genesis from the creation to the destruction of Sodom. Along the way it digresses on divine providence and the origins of human culture. It is a notable example of Christian verse paraphrase in late antique Gaul.

The History of the Persecution of the African Province is a Latin history by Victor, bishop of Vita in Byzacena, written in the late 480s. It tells of the suffering of Nicene (catholic) Christians under the Arian Vandal kings Gaiseric and Huneric. It covers events from the Vandal crossing into Africa in 429 to the harsh measures of 483–484, including the exile of clergy and Huneric's edicts. A prologue addresses a disciple of the bishop Diadochus. The work is the main narrative source for religious conflict in Vandal North Africa.

Victorinus, bishop of Poetovio (modern Ptuj, Slovenia), wrote this Latin commentary on the Book of Revelation in the later third century. He died as a martyr around 304. It is the earliest surviving Latin commentary on Revelation and works through the book's visions and symbols in sequence. Victorinus read the visions as recapitulation: the same events are retold in different images, not given in strict chronological order. The commentary openly teaches millennialism. Jerome later produced a revised version that softened its chiliastic passages, and that revision circulated widely.

On the Creation of the World (De fabrica mundi) is a short Latin treatise, surviving only as a fragment, by Victorinus, bishop of Poetovio (modern Ptuj, Slovenia), who was martyred around 304. It reflects on the six days of creation and the seventh day of rest in Genesis. It draws out the symbolism of the number seven and links the days of creation to events in Christ's life. It is an early example of Latin biblical exegesis and of millenarian thought, and is one of the few works by Victorinus to survive.

The Passio septem monachorum is an anonymous Latin martyr narrative. It has come down with Victor of Vita's History of the Vandal Persecution and is traditionally attached to it. It tells how seven Catholic monks, led by the abbot Liberatus, were put to death at Carthage on 2 July in the seventh year of the Arian Vandal king Huneric, around 483. The text begins with the persecution urged on by the Arian bishop Cyrila, describing exiles and forced rebaptism. It is an important witness to Catholic suffering in Vandal Africa and to the martyrs' later cult.

The Notitia provinciarum et civitatum Africae is an anonymous Latin list of the Catholic bishops summoned to Carthage by the Vandal king Huneric to account for their faith at a conference on 1 February 484. It is arranged by province: Proconsularis, Numidia, Byzacena, the two Mauretanias, Tripolitana and Sardinia. It names each bishop's see and often his fate, such as exile, flight or death, and it notes vacant sees. It survives alongside Victor of Vita's History of the Vandal Persecution and is a key source for the church and geography of Roman North Africa.

The Itinerarium Hierosolymitanum ("Jerusalem Itinerary"), also called the Itinerarium Burdigalense ("Bordeaux Itinerary"), is the oldest known Christian travel itinerary. It was written in Latin by an anonymous pilgrim from Burdigala (Bordeaux) and records a journey to the Holy Land in 333–334. Most of it lists road stations, changes of horses and distances via northern Italy, the Danube valley and Constantinople to Jerusalem, with the return through Macedonia, Rome and Milan. Its brief descriptions of Jerusalem and other biblical sites are valuable early evidence for Christian pilgrimage and for the holy places in Constantine's time.

The Breviarius de Hierosolyma, also called the Breviary or Short Description of Jerusalem, is a short anonymous Latin guide for Christian pilgrims. It is generally dated to the late antique period, around the sixth century. It leads the reader through the holy places of the city, beginning with Constantine's basilica and Golgotha and going on to the tomb of Christ. Along the way it lists relics shown to pilgrims, such as the lance, the horn used to anoint David and Solomon's ring. It is an important witness to Jerusalem's sacred topography and to pilgrim devotion before the Islamic conquest.

Against Apion is a two-book apologetic treatise in Greek by the Jewish historian Flavius Josephus. It was written in Rome some time after his Antiquities of the Jews, and so probably after 94 CE. Its Greek title means "On the Antiquity of the Jews". Josephus defends the antiquity of the Jewish people and their law against Greek and Egyptian critics, including Manetho, Chaeremon, Lysimachus and the Alexandrian grammarian Apion. He quotes many lost non-Jewish historians, and later Christian apologists valued the work; Jerome admired its learning.

The St Albans Breviary is a Latin liturgical book containing the Divine Office as it was celebrated at the Benedictine abbey of St Albans in England. It was printed in 1532, shortly before the abbey was dissolved, and records late medieval monastic use rather than a text from the first millennium. Its anonymous compilers drew on much older material. The office opens with Advent and includes antiphons, responsories, collects, lessons and rubrics, along with ancient hymns such as Conditor alme siderum and Verbum supernum prodiens.

The Battle Breviary is an anonymous Latin breviary from the late fifteenth century. A breviary is a liturgical book containing the texts of the Divine Office, the daily cycle of prayer sung or recited by clergy and religious. The book is much later than the early medieval period, but much of what it contains goes back to older chant and lectionary traditions. The opening portion comes from the night office (Matins) of Advent. Its lessons are interspersed with responsories on the Annunciation, such as "Missus est Gabriel angelus", and on waiting for Christ's coming.

The Coldingham Breviary is an anonymous Latin liturgical book of the thirteenth century. It is associated with the Benedictine priory of Coldingham in Berwickshire, in south-east Scotland, which was a dependency of Durham. A breviary gathers the texts needed for the Divine Office across the church year: antiphons, responsories, hymns, versicles, collects and lessons. This one opens with the Advent offices, including the responsory "Aspiciens a longe" and commemorations of the Virgin Mary. It is valuable evidence for monastic liturgy and chant in medieval Scotland and northern England.

The Chertsey Breviary is an anonymous Latin breviary made in England around 1320 and associated with the Benedictine abbey of Chertsey in Surrey. A breviary gathers the texts needed for the daily Divine Office. This one includes antiphons, responsories, versicles, hymns, collects and Gospel readings, with rubrics for the hours such as Prime, Lauds and Vespers. The book is late medieval, but much of its content is far older. Hymns such as "Aurora iam spargit polum" and "O lux beata" belong to the first-millennium Latin liturgical tradition.

The Ely Breviary-Missal is an anonymous Latin liturgical book from the thirteenth century, associated with Ely in eastern England. As a breviary-missal, it puts texts for the Divine Office and for the Mass together in one volume. It follows the liturgical year from Advent. The opening gives Vespers for the start of Advent, with antiphons, responsories, versicles, collects and hymns such as Conditor alme siderum and Verbum supernum prodiens, plus a commemoration of the Virgin Mary. It is a witness to English liturgical practice in the high Middle Ages.

The Evesham Breviary is an anonymous Latin liturgical book from the thirteenth century, associated with the Benedictine abbey of Evesham in Worcestershire, England. A breviary gathers the texts needed for the Divine Office, the cycle of daily prayer hours. These include antiphons, responsories, hymns, versicles, collects and rubrics. The text begins with Vespers at the start of Advent and includes a daily commemoration of the Virgin Mary. It is valuable evidence for how monks in medieval England celebrated the Office according to local use.

The Gloucester Diurnal is an anonymous Latin liturgical book associated with Gloucester in England and dated between the twelfth and fifteenth centuries. A diurnal holds the day hours of the Divine Office, without the night office of Matins. It begins with Advent: responsories, the hymn Conditor alme siderum and the Magnificat antiphon at Vespers, followed by antiphons for Prime, Terce and Sext. These draw on Isaiah, Jeremiah, Romans and the Annunciation narrative. It is evidence for medieval English monastic or cathedral practice of the Office.

The Hyde Breviary is an anonymous Latin monastic breviary associated with Hyde Abbey, the Benedictine house at Winchester, and dates from the late thirteenth or early fourteenth century. It sets out the Divine Office through the liturgical year, starting with Vespers of the first Sunday of Advent. It gives antiphons, psalm cues, hymns such as Conditor alme siderum, versicles, responsories, collects and rubrics for the night and day hours. It is valuable evidence for medieval English Benedictine liturgy, much of it inherited from older Anglo-Saxon and continental monastic practice.

The Muchelney Breviary is an anonymous Latin liturgical book from the thirteenth century, associated with the Benedictine abbey of Muchelney in Somerset, England. A breviary sets out the texts of the Divine Office, the daily round of monastic prayer. This one gives antiphons, responsories, versicles, hymns, psalm cues and lessons arranged through the church year. It opens with the night office of Advent, which includes the hymns Conditor alme siderum and Verbum supernum prodiens. It is a valuable witness to the liturgical practice of an English monastery in the Middle Ages.

The Peterborough Antiphoner is an anonymous Latin liturgical book. Its title links it to Peterborough in England and dates it to the fourteenth century. An antiphoner contains the sung parts of the Divine Office: the antiphons, responsories and versicles used at Matins, Lauds, the Little Hours and Vespers through the church year. The surviving text begins with chants for Advent, including the responsory "Videbunt gentes" and the "O sapientia" antiphon. The book itself is late medieval, but much of its chant repertory goes back to the early Middle Ages.

The Winchcombe Breviary-Missal is an anonymous Latin liturgical book from about 1140, associated with the Benedictine abbey of Winchcombe in Gloucestershire, England. It combines texts for the Divine Office with those for the Mass and follows the liturgical year. It opens with Advent, giving the chapter, responsories, versicles and antiphons for Vespers and Matins, together with hymns such as Conditor alme siderum and Verbum supernum prodiens. It is valuable evidence for the monastic liturgy of twelfth-century England.

The Worcester Antiphoner is an anonymous Latin liturgical collection of chants for the Divine Office. It is associated with the Benedictine cathedral priory of Worcester in England and dates from the thirteenth or early fourteenth century. It sets out the sung parts of the monastic hours through the church year, mainly responsories with their verses and antiphons, beginning with Advent texts on the Incarnation and the coming of the Saviour. Much of the chant repertory is far older than the compilation itself. It is an important witness to the medieval English monastic liturgy and its music.

The Book of Psalms, or Psalter, is an anthology of Hebrew religious poetry in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It has 150 psalms in Jewish and Western usage, with a few more in Eastern churches, and is divided into five books. It includes hymns of praise, laments, royal psalms and thanksgivings. Many psalms are traditionally attributed to David, but scholars doubt this. They were composed over several centuries, before and after the Exile. The Psalms were central to Jewish and Christian worship, and early Christian writers commented on them extensively.

The Didache, or Teaching of the Twelve Apostles, is a short anonymous Christian treatise in Koine Greek. Most scholars date it to the late first century, though some place it in the second. It opens with the "Two Ways" of life and death, a moral teaching probably adapted from a Jewish source. It then gives instructions on baptism, fasting, the Lord's Prayer and the Eucharist, and on church order, covering itinerant apostles and prophets as well as local bishops and deacons. It is the earliest known church order and an important witness to early Christian practice.

On the Solitaries is a Syriac admonition addressed to solitary monks and attributed to Mar Abraham of Nathpar, an East Syriac monastic writer usually placed in the late sixth or seventh century. He wrote it at the request of a disciple, and it explains why some people are called to anticipate the life of the world to come through monastic withdrawal. The treatise is set out under headings. These cover who should take up the solitary life, with what thoughts and deeds to begin it, how to persevere in it, and how to face temptations and spiritual battles.

The Acts of Thomas is an anonymous apocryphal narrative, probably composed in Syriac in the early third century, likely at Edessa. It survives in Syriac and Greek versions, and scholars disagree about which is closer to the original. It tells how the apostle Judas Thomas was sold as a carpenter to the Indian king Gundaphoros, how he preached and worked miracles in India, and how he was martyred. It strongly favours sexual renunciation and includes liturgical prayers and celebrated poems, notably the Hymn of the Pearl. It is the chief source for the tradition of Thomas's mission to India.

On Divine Providence is a set of Syriac discourses by Antony of Tagrit, a monk of the Syriac Orthodox tradition usually known as Antony the Rhetor and generally dated to around the ninth century. The work is written for fellow believers troubled by questions about God's providence. It argues that providence works for good and restrains people from sin without forcing their free will, while leaving the deepest mysteries of divine knowledge unexplored. It is a notable example of later Syriac philosophical theology and of its author's rhetorical style.

The Demonstrations (Taḥwyātā) are twenty-three Syriac prose treatises by Aphrahat, the "Persian Sage," written in the Sasanian Empire between 337 and 345. Prefaced by a letter from an inquirer asking about the faith, the first twenty-two are arranged as an alphabetical acrostic. They address faith, love, fasting, prayer, humility, the "sons of the covenant," Passover, circumcision and the sabbath, often in debate with Jewish practice, and the persecution under Shapur II. They are the earliest major surviving works of Syriac Christianity, largely untouched by Greek theological influence.

This is a cycle of Syriac hymns (madroshe) by Balai, a poet active at Qenneshrin (Chalcis) in the early fifth century. They praise Acacius, the long-lived bishop of Beroea (Aleppo), who died around 436–437. The poet asks the bishop to intercede for him on his feast day. He then praises Acacius's chastity, his teaching, his care for the weak and his warnings to the rich. The hymns are among the few surviving works securely attributed to Balai and show early fifth-century Syriac praise poetry for church leaders.

This Syriac hymn (madrasha) is by Balai, a chorepiscopus and poet active at Qenneshrin (Chalcis) in northern Syria in the early fifth century. He wrote it for the dedication of a newly built church in that city. It praises those who built the church as a dwelling for God and calls the sanctuary heaven on earth, where priests take the place of the angelic Watchers. It reflects on how God is wholly above yet wholly present below, far from those who pry and near to those who love and believe. It is an important early example of Syriac liturgical poetry about sacred space.

The Book of the Laws of Countries is a Syriac philosophical dialogue from the early third century, among the oldest surviving original works of Syriac literature. It records the teaching of Bardaisan of Edessa and is traditionally credited to his disciple Philip rather than to Bardaisan himself. Bardaisan answers the questions of a pupil, Avida, on human free will, nature and fate. To show that the stars do not determine human conduct, he surveys the differing laws and customs of many peoples. Eusebius quoted parts of it in Greek.

This short Syriac letter was written by Barlaha, a recluse living in the precinct of Mar Elisha, to Simeon, abbot of the monastery of Beth Licinius on the Black Mountain near Antioch. Barlaha responds to news brought by the deacon Damian, who had come with ten leaves containing the introduction to a Greek commentary on the Psalms, and he urges that the whole commentary be translated into Syriac. The letter's date is uncertain. It sheds light on how Greek exegesis reached Syriac-speaking monastic communities.

The Book of the Cause of All Causes, also called the Book on the Knowledge (or Acknowledgement) of Truth, is an anonymous Syriac encyclopedic treatise. It was written sometime between the tenth and twelfth centuries, and its exact date and authorship are uncertain. Addressed to "all the peoples under heaven", it sets out a systematic account of how truth is known and argues for God's existence, unity, attributes, names and providence. It then turns to creation and the ordering of the world. It is a notable late witness to Syriac Christian philosophical and scientific learning.

The Chronicle of Edessa is an anonymous Syriac history of the city of Edessa, generally dated to about 540–550. Its manuscript title is "Histories of Events in Brief." In short dated entries, it covers the period from the founding of the kingdom of Osrhoene in 133/132 BC to 540. It draws mainly on Edessan royal archives and church records and is considered historically reliable. Its account of the Daisan flood of 201 mentions a Christian church building and is one of the earliest pieces of evidence for Christianity in Edessa. Only an abridged version survives.

This anonymous Syriac chronicle was written around 506–507 by an eyewitness living at Edessa, at the request of Sergius, a priest and abbot. It records the disasters that struck Edessa, Amida and Mesopotamia, including locusts, famine, plague and earthquake, and above all the Roman–Persian war of 502–506. It survives only because it was copied into the Chronicle of Zuqnin, and its old attribution to Joshua the Stylite is now rejected. It is one of the earliest and most reliable histories in Syriac and is admired for how it analyses causes.

The Chronicle of Zuqnin is an anonymous Syriac world chronicle finished around 775 by a monk of the Zuqnin monastery near Amida, on the upper Tigris. It was once wrongly attributed to Dionysius of Tel Mahre, and its author is sometimes identified as Joshua the Stylite. In four parts, it runs from the creation to the year 1087 of the Seleucid era (775/76). It draws on the Bible, John of Ephesus and other sources, and it preserves otherwise lost texts such as the Revelation of the Magi. Its eyewitness account of life under early Abbasid rule is especially valuable.

This anonymous apocryphal narrative tells of the death, or "departure", of the apostle John at Ephesus. It is a Syriac version of the account known in Greek as the Metastasis, which closes the apocryphal Acts of John. On a Sunday, John urges the assembled brethren to stay faithful and celebrates the Eucharist. He then has a grave dug, prays, and lies down in it to die in peace. Its date of composition is uncertain, perhaps the fourth or fifth century. It shaped later traditions about John's end.

The Disputation between the Apostle Peter and Nero is an anonymous Syriac apocryphal text. Its date is uncertain, but it was probably composed between the fifth and seventh centuries. It opens with an allegorical prologue: the world is a stormy sea, the twelve apostles are ships carrying great wealth, the devil is the king of the sea who stirs up the waves, and the kingdom is the harbour where they find rest. It then presents the Emperor Nero as the devil's willing servant in opposing Peter's preaching.

The Teaching of Addai is an anonymous Syriac narrative, usually dated to around 400, though estimates range from the fourth to the early fifth century. It develops the legend of King Abgar of Edessa, an earlier form of which Eusebius records. Abgar writes to Jesus and receives a reply. After the Ascension, the apostle Addai heals the king, preaches and converts the city. The work also contains the Protonike legend of the finding of the Cross. It is a key source for how the Edessene church understood its own apostolic origins.

The Carmina Nisibena ("Nisibene Hymns") are a collection of Syriac madrāšê, or teaching hymns, by Ephrem the Syrian, written between about 350 and 373. About 77 of them survive. The early hymns deal with Nisibis, Ephrem's home city, and its sieges by the Persian king Shapur II. They pray for deliverance from the floodwaters turned against the city walls and praise its bishops. Other hymns concern Edessa and Harran. The later hymns dramatise Christ's descent into Sheol and his contest with Death and Satan. The collection is valuable both as poetry and as a historical source.

The Hymns on the Nativity are a cycle of Syriac madrāšê, or teaching hymns, by Ephrem the Syrian. He was a deacon and poet who worked at Nisibis and later at Edessa, and he composed these hymns in the mid-fourth century. They celebrate the birth of Christ as the fulfilment of the prophets, kings and types of the Old Testament. They dwell on paradoxes such as the Creator becoming an infant and on the Virgin Mary's role. They are among the best-known works of early Syriac poetry and incarnational theology.

The Prose Refutations are a group of polemical discourses in Syriac by Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373), the deacon and theologian of Nisibis and Edessa. They are aimed at the three main rival teachings of his region: Mani, Marcion and Bardaisan. The first discourse is a letter to a certain Hypatius. In it Ephrem argues against dualist ideas about light and darkness, matter and the body, and defends free will and the goodness of creation. The work is a rare example of Ephrem's prose. It is also an important witness to early Manichaean, Marcionite and Bardaisanite thought.

This letter was sent by the Christian communities of Vienne and Lyon (Lugdunum) in Gaul to the churches of Asia and Phrygia. It gives an eyewitness account of the persecution of about 177, under Marcus Aurelius. It describes mob violence, trials and the deaths of martyrs such as the aged bishop Pothinus and the slave woman Blandina. Its author is unknown, though some have suggested Irenaeus. The letter survives only in the excerpts Eusebius of Caesarea quoted in Book 5 of his Ecclesiastical History. It is one of the most important early Christian martyr accounts.

The Theophania, or "Divine Manifestation", is an apologetic treatise in five books by Eusebius of Caesarea. It was probably written in the later years of his life, though its exact date is disputed. The Greek original survives only in fragments, but a complete early Syriac translation is extant. The work argues against atheism and polytheism and presents the divine Word as creator and governor of the world. It then treats the incarnation, Christ's teaching and miracles, and the fulfilment of prophecy. Much of its material overlaps with Eusebius's Demonstratio Evangelica and his oration in praise of Constantine.

The Exhortation of the Apostle Peter is an anonymous Syriac apocryphal discourse on admonition, attributed to the apostle Peter. Its date is uncertain; it is generally placed between the fourth and sixth centuries. Speaking to a crowd that has gathered for instruction, Peter warns his hearers not to become attached to worldly things but to be ready for death. He illustrates the point with a parable about two servants banished by their master: one puts down roots in exile, while the other turns his earnings into a gold crown engraved with images of his master and his master's son.

The History of John, the Son of Zebedee is an anonymous Syriac apocryphal narrative about the apostle John, probably composed in the fifth century. It tells how, after Pentecost, the apostles dispersed to preach and John went to Ephesus, where he preached, worked wonders, baptised and turned the city from pagan worship to Christianity. Its heading claims Eusebius of Caesarea as author and says it was translated from a Greek book, but this attribution is not credited. The work is a witness to Syriac traditions about John and his Ephesian ministry.

The History of Karka d-Beth Slokh is an anonymous Syriac work from the Church of the East. It is usually placed among the Persian martyr acts and dated roughly to the late sixth or early seventh century. It tells the history of Karka d-Beth Slokh, the city now generally identified with Kirkuk, beginning with a legendary founding by the Assyrian king Sardana in the time of Jonah. It then follows the city's Christian community and its martyrs under the Sasanian kings. The work matters as a source for local church history and for how Syriac Christians in Mesopotamia saw their own past.

The Acts of Andrew and Matthias is an anonymous apocryphal narrative about two apostles in a "city of the man-eaters." Matthias, sent there by lot, is blinded, drugged and imprisoned by cannibals. Andrew is miraculously carried to the city to rescue him, then endures torture and finally converts the inhabitants. Reads like an adventurous romance rather than history, it was once thought part of the lost Acts of Andrew but probably began as an independent tradition. Its date and original language are uncertain; Greek is likely, and versions survive in Syriac and other languages.

The History of Philip, the Apostle and Evangelist is an anonymous Syriac apocryphal narrative, probably composed between the fifth and seventh centuries; its exact date is uncertain. It tells how Christ appears to Philip in a night vision at Jerusalem and sends him to preach in "Carthage, which is in Azotus." There he drives out Satan's power and converts the city through wonders and preaching. The work blends Philip the Apostle with Philip the Evangelist of Acts, and it reflects the Syriac tradition of legendary apostolic acts.

The History of Mar Qardagh is an anonymous Syriac martyr legend of the Church of the East, probably composed in the early seventh century in northern Mesopotamia, near Arbela. Set in the reign of the Sasanian king Shapur II, it tells of Qardagh, a Persian noble and governor descended from Nimrod. The hermit ʿAbdishoʿ converts him to Christianity, and he is then martyred by stoning. Drawing on Persian epic ideals of the warrior and hunter, it is an important source for Christian identity and culture in the late Sasanian Empire.

The Acts of Paul and Thecla is an anonymous apocryphal narrative, originally written in Greek in the second century as part of the larger Acts of Paul. It also circulated on its own, and versions survive in Syriac and other languages. It tells how Thecla, a young woman of Iconium, hears Paul preach on chastity, breaks off her engagement, and survives two attempts to execute her before becoming an itinerant teacher. The text includes a well-known physical description of Paul and was the foundation of Thecla's widespread cult.

The Hymn of the Soul, also called the Hymn of the Pearl, is an anonymous Syriac poem preserved in the apocryphal Acts of Thomas. In that work the apostle Judas Thomas sings it while in prison in India. A prince is sent from his father's kingdom in the East to Egypt to bring back a pearl guarded by a serpent. He forgets his mission, is woken by a letter, and returns to receive his glorious robe. The poem is widely read as an allegory of the soul. It may be older than the Acts, and some have linked it to Bardaisan of Edessa, though its authorship is unknown.

This short apologetic discourse survives in Syriac and is attributed to Ambrose, described as a leading man of Greece who became a Christian, faced the outcry of his fellow senators, and fled. It is a version of the Greek Oratio ad Graecos (Discourse to the Greeks), traditionally but doubtfully ascribed to Justin Martyr. Its date and authorship are uncertain, perhaps the second or third century. The speaker explains why he left paganism, mocks the immoral gods and heroes of Homer and Greek myth, and urges the Greeks to turn to the divine Word.

On the End Times is a Syriac metrical homily (memra) attributed to Isaac of Antioch, a fifth-century Syriac poet whose death the Chronicle of Edessa places around 451–452. Writing is ascribed to several authors named Isaac, so which one wrote it is uncertain. In the poem, a personified Truth wakes the speaker and orders him to announce that the last times have come. It points to Scripture, the prophets, the apostles and the decay of nature as signs of the end. It urges readers to repent and seek refuge in God against Satan and an evil earthly ruler.

The First Part of Isaac of Nineveh's writings is a collection of Syriac discourses on monastic life, asceticism and prayer. It was composed in the late seventh century by the Church of the East bishop also known as Isaac the Syrian or Isaac of Qatar. It opens by calling the fear of God the beginning of virtue, and it teaches withdrawal from worldly affairs, meditation on Scripture, patient endurance, humility and stillness. It was translated into Greek early on and later into many other languages, and it became one of the most widely read ascetic works in Eastern Christianity.

The Letters are a collection of more than one hundred Syriac letters by Ishoʿyahb III of Adiabene, Patriarch of the Church of the East from 649 to 659. They are traditionally arranged by the stages of his career: as bishop of Nineveh, as metropolitan of Adiabene, and as catholicos. Written to clergy, monks and laypeople, they deal with church discipline, doctrinal disputes and pastoral affairs. They include letters to the Christians of Beth Qatraye. The collection is an important witness to Christian life in the earliest decades of Islamic rule.

The Memre are the verse homilies of Jacob of Serugh (c. 451–521), the Syriac poet-theologian who became bishop of Batnan in 519. Most are written in the twelve-syllable metre associated with him. They cover biblical narratives, feasts, saints and moral exhortation, as in the opening homily on admonition, which presents praise of God as humanity's duty to its Creator. Jacob is said to have composed 763 works. Around 400 survive, and they were copied widely across the Syriac churches.

This saint's life of Peter the Iberian (c. 417–491) was written by his disciple John Rufus, an anti-Chalcedonian priest who may have become bishop of Maiuma. It was composed in Greek around the end of the fifth century and survives only in a Syriac translation. It follows Peter's life as a Georgian royal prince, a hostage at the court in Constantinople, a monk and monastery founder in Palestine, and bishop of Maiuma near Gaza. It is an important source for Palestinian monasticism and for early opposition to the Council of Chalcedon.

The Plerophoriae ("Assurances") is an anti-Chalcedonian collection of anecdotes by John Rufus, a priest of Antioch, disciple of Peter the Iberian and bishop of Maiuma near Gaza. It was written in the early sixth century, probably in Greek, and survives in a Syriac version. It gathers visions, revelations and miraculous testimonies, many of them told by Peter the Iberian, that present the Council of Chalcedon (451) and the doctrine of two natures in Christ as condemned by God. It is a key witness to early miaphysite piety and to Palestinian monastic opposition to Chalcedon.

The Dialogue on the Soul is a Syriac treatise attributed to John the Solitary, often identified with John of Apamea, a fifth-century ascetic writer. It is framed as a conversation in which two disciples, Eutropius and Eusebius, visit John in his cell and question him. Among the topics are why the soul was placed in the human body, and how the passions of body, soul and spirit differ. The work sets out John's threefold scheme of the spiritual life and shows the influence of Evagrius Ponticus. It is an important early witness to Syriac ascetic and mystical thought.

On Prayer is a short Syriac treatise on spiritual contemplation (theoria) in prayer, associated with Joseph Hazzaya, an 8th-century monk and mystic of the Church of the East. The manuscript heading attributes it to "Mar Abdisho". Several of Joseph's writings circulated under the name Abdisho, which was also the name of his brother, so the authorship is uncertain. The work describes how monks who have purified their hearts of the passions are drawn in prayer beyond the senses. It speaks of a "fiery movement" of the indwelling Holy Spirit, received at baptism, which transforms the soul into its own likeness.

The Julian Romance is an anonymous Syriac prose narrative giving a fictionalized, Christian account of the reign of the emperor Julian the Apostate. It was written sometime between Julian's death in 363 and the sixth century, probably at Edessa. It has three parts: Julian's accession and persecution of Christians, his conflict with Eusebius of Rome, and, in the form of a letter, his Persian campaign, death and the accession of the Christian Jovian. It is one of the major narrative works of Syriac literature, and an Arabic adaptation existed by the tenth century.

The Book of Steps (Syriac Ktaba d-Masqata, Latin Liber Graduum) is an anonymous Syriac treatise of thirty discourses (memre). It was probably written in the late fourth or early fifth century by an author living in the Sasanian Empire, who addressed it to his own Christian community. It separates the "upright", who keep the lesser commandments, from the "perfect", who follow the greater commandments of renunciation and celibacy. It also describes the visible church as working alongside a heavenly church. It is an important witness to early Syriac asceticism and spirituality.

The Life of Jacob of Serugh is an anonymous Syriac hagiography of Jacob of Serugh (c. 451–521), the Miaphysite poet, homilist and late in life bishop of Batnan. Its date is uncertain but is usually placed between the mid-sixth and seventh centuries. It opens by calling itself "another account" of the saint. It tells of his birth to a barren mother after prayer at a shrine, and of a childhood miracle in which he received divine inspiration at the Eucharist. It then follows his upbringing in Hawra, his hymn-writing as a visiting priest and his time as bishop.

The Life of Rabbula is an anonymous Syriac hagiography of Rabbula, bishop of Edessa from about 411 to 435/6. It was written by an unnamed member of the Edessene church, probably within a few decades of his death. It praises him as an ascetic champion of the faith. The work follows his conversion and ascetic life, then his time as bishop: his care for the poor, his strict discipline of clergy and monks, and his struggles against heretics and civil rulers. It is an important witness to Christianity in Edessa in the early fifth century.

This Syriac letter of moral advice was written by Mara bar Serapion, a philosopher of Stoic outlook from Samosata, to his young son Serapion. Mara apparently wrote it as a captive after the Romans annexed his city in AD 72. Its date is uncertain and is placed anywhere from shortly after 73 to the late second century. In urging the boy to pursue wisdom, the letter cites the unjust treatment of Socrates, Pythagoras and "the wise king" of the Jews. That last phrase is often read as an early non-Christian reference to Jesus.

This is a short anonymous Syriac martyr act, one of the Acts of the Persian Martyrs, which record Christians who died in the persecution under the Sasanian king Shapur II. It tells how Jacob, priest of the village of Tel Shlila, and his sister Mary, a "daughter of the covenant" (a consecrated woman), were arrested in the seventh year of the persecution. On the orders of Narses Tamshapur they were flogged for refusing to eat blood. A Christian layman named Mahdad then beheaded them at Tel Dara on the Great Zab, on 17 Adar.

An anonymous Syriac hagiography, one of the Persian martyr acts, about Miles, bishop of Susa, and his companions Aborsam the priest and Sinai the deacon. They were executed by the Sasanian authorities in 340 or 341, at the start of the persecution under Shapur II. The account opens with a rhetorical prologue in praise of the martyrs. Its date is uncertain. Sozomen summarized a Syriac account of Miles in the fifth century, but the fuller surviving Acts have been dated as late as the end of the sixth century.

The Memre on Joseph are a cycle of verse homilies (mēmrē) in Syriac by Jacob of Serugh (c. 451–521), the poet-theologian and late bishop of Batnan. They are written in the twelve-syllable metre linked with Jacob, and they retell the story of the patriarch Joseph from Genesis in a series of discourses. The first opens with a prayer to Christ as the source of all beauty. Jacob presents Joseph's beauty and virtue as a reflection of Christ, which fits the Syriac tradition of reading Old Testament figures as types of Christ.

On the Soul is a Syriac theological treatise by Moses bar Kepha (died 903), a Syriac Orthodox bishop and one of the most celebrated writers of his church in the ninth century. It begins by setting out the many senses of the word "soul" in Scripture and in ordinary usage. It can mean the divine nature, the whole human person, the body, the blood, or the life-giving power in plants. It then discusses the nature of the human soul. The work draws on earlier Greek patristic and philosophical thought, and it is a valuable witness to Syriac Christian anthropology.

The Memre are the verse homilies of Narsai (c. 399 – c. 502), a leading poet-theologian of the Church of the East who taught at the School of Edessa and later headed the School of Nisibis. About eighty-one survive. They are metrical sermons on biblical themes, feasts and doctrine. Many were linked to the liturgical year, for example a discourse on the revelations to Abraham for the first Sunday of the Annunciation. They reflect the exegetical tradition of Theodore of Mopsuestia and rank among the major works of classical Syriac preaching, alongside those of Jacob of Serugh.

The Bazaar (or Book) of Heracleides is a theological and autobiographical apology attributed to Nestorius, the archbishop of Constantinople deposed at the Council of Ephesus in 431. He wrote it in exile late in his life, around 451–452. The Greek original is lost, and the work survives only in a Syriac translation preserved by the Church of the East and rediscovered in the nineteenth century. In it Nestorius defends his Christology against Cyril of Alexandria and recounts the events of his condemnation. The work has prompted scholars to reassess his actual teaching.

The Odes of Solomon are a collection of 42 early Christian hymns. Their author is unknown, and the attribution to King Solomon is traditional, not historical. Most scholars date them to the late first or early second century, though some place them later. Whether they were first written in Greek or Syriac is also debated. The poems are lyrical and mystical. They celebrate union with the Lord through love, the gift of the Spirit, salvation and immortality, and each ends with "Hallelujah." They are among the oldest surviving Christian hymnbooks, and they share notable affinities with the Gospel of John.

This anonymous Syriac collection of letters is attributed to correspondence with Papa bar Aggai, bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon in the early fourth century, who is traditionally regarded as the first catholicos of the Church of the East. Writers such as Eusebius, called "patriarch of the Romans", and Judas Cyriacus of Jerusalem praise Papa and send gifts from Constantine and his mother. The letters are spurious and were probably composed between the sixth and eighth centuries. They likely served to support the dignity and apostolic standing of the see of Seleucia-Ctesiphon.

The Ascetic Discourses are a collection of thirteen Syriac discourses on the Christian and monastic life by Philoxenus of Mabbug (died 523), the Miaphysite bishop of Hierapolis. They were written in the late fifth or early sixth century, though the exact date is uncertain. The work sets out a gradual path of discipleship that starts from faith and simplicity and moves through the fear of God and renunciation of the world. It then turns to the struggle against gluttony and fornication, with spiritual love and perfection as the goal. It is among the most important works of early Syriac spirituality.

The Clementine Homilies are a Greek Christian romance in twenty books, falsely attributed to Clement of Rome and probably composed in the fourth century. Clement narrates his youthful search for truth, his conversion, and his travels with the apostle Peter. The work records Peter's discourses and his debates with Simon Magus, and ends with the reunion of Clement's scattered family. It is prefaced by letters of Peter and Clement to James. With the Recognitions, it is one of two surviving reworkings of a lost earlier source and is valuable evidence for Jewish-Christian thought.

The Recognitions is a fourth-century Christian romance falsely attributed to Clement of Rome. It is one of two surviving versions of the Pseudo-Clementine writings, alongside the Clementine Homilies. It tells of Clement's conversion, his travels with the apostle Peter, Peter's debates with Simon Magus, and how Clement was reunited with his scattered family. The Greek original is lost. The text survives complete in Rufinus of Aquileia's Latin translation of about 406, and in part in an early Syriac version. It is an important source for Jewish-Christian traditions.

The Admonitions to Monks is a short set of disciplinary rules in Syriac attributed to Rabbula, bishop of Edessa (Urhay) from about 411 to 435/6. It governs life in the monasteries of his diocese. Its numbered precepts ban women from entering monasteries and limit monks' contact with villages and lay households to an appointed "Visitor". They also forbid drinking wine and restrict ascetic practices such as wearing long hair, iron chains or hair garments outside the monastery. The text is important evidence for early Syrian monasticism and for Rabbula's efforts to bring it under church discipline.

This polemical Syriac letter by Simeon of Beth Arsham, the early sixth-century Miaphysite bishop known as the "Persian Debater", sets out a hostile history of the Nestorian heresy and how it reached Persia. Simeon traces the belief that Christ was a mere man to Annas, Caiaphas and the Jews who rejected him, and then to Simon Magus. The chain continues through later teachers to Barsauma of Nisibis, the late fifth-century bishop who promoted Dyophysite doctrine in the Church of the East. The letter is an important witness to the Miaphysite–Nestorian conflict in the Persian Empire.

This is a Syriac prefatory letter by Simeon, abbot of the monastery of Mary, Mother of God, in Beth Liqnis. It is addressed to the priest Barlaha (Barlahe), a recluse living in the enclosure of Mar Elisha of Markabta. Simeon replies to Barlaha's repeated requests, carried by the deacon Damian, that he translate a book from Greek into Syriac. He professes himself unfit for the task but credits Barlaha's prayers with giving him the strength to attempt it. The letter's exact date and the identity of the translated work are uncertain.

The Testament of Adam is an anonymous Christian pseudepigraphon, preserved mainly in Syriac, in which Adam speaks to his son Seth. Its date is uncertain, but it is usually placed between the third and fifth centuries. It has three parts. The first is a horarium listing the worship offered by each creature at each hour of the night and day. The second is a prophecy of the Flood and of Christ's incarnation. The third describes the hierarchy of the angels. Versions also exist in Arabic, Ethiopic, Armenian and Georgian.

This Syriac treatise explains the feast of Christ's birth in the flesh. It was written by Thomas of Edessa (died c. 540), a theologian of the Church of the East, at the request of Mar Moses. Its chapters ask why the feast is celebrated and what benefits came through Christ. They also explain why God was revealed through a human being born of a virgin, and why the conception took place in Nisan. Reflecting the theology of Theodore of Mopsuestia, it is among the oldest surviving examples of the ʿelltā, or "cause", genre of feast explanations.

Against the Manichaeans is a polemical treatise in four books by Titus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia (died c. 378), written in Greek probably in the 360s or 370s. The Greek original survives only in part. The complete work is preserved in an early Syriac translation, attested in a manuscript of 411. Titus rejects Mani's doctrine of an eternal evil principle opposed to God. He defends divine providence and human free will as the source of sin, arguing first from reason and then from Scripture. It is a major early Christian source on Manichaean teaching.

The Travels of Peter is an anonymous Christian apocryphal narrative that survives in Syriac. Its date is uncertain, though it is generally placed somewhere between the fifth and eighth centuries. It tells of the apostle Simon Peter preaching baptism and the true faith from city to city. In its opening episode Peter meets a demon waiting to kill a newborn child, raises the dead infant to life and questions the demon about its attacks on children. That episode connects the text with traditions of protecting mothers and infants from demons. It is distinct from the Greek Pseudo-Clementine "Circuits of Peter."

The Sententiae episcoporum is the Latin record of the council of North African bishops that met at Carthage under Cyprian on 1 September, usually dated to 256, though some headings give 258. After letters exchanged with Bishop Jubaianus were read, Cyprian and each of the eighty-seven bishops from Africa, Numidia and Mauritania gave a short opinion in turn. All held that heretics joining the Church must be baptized. The record opposed the position of Stephen of Rome and was later debated in Augustine's writings against the Donatists.

This text records a synod held in the baptistery of the great church of Constantinople on 29 September 394, dated by the consulship of Arcadius and Honorius. Nectarius of Constantinople presided, and Theophilus of Alexandria attended. The bishops heard a dispute between Bagadius and Agapius over the see of Bostra. Bagadius had been deposed by only two bishops, and the synod ruled that a bishop may not be deposed by two or three bishops but only by a larger synod of the province. The record survives through the Byzantine canonist Balsamon.

The acts and decrees of the Second Council of Constantinople, the fifth ecumenical council, which Emperor Justinian I convoked. It met under Patriarch Eutychius of Constantinople from 5 May to 2 June 553. Justinian's letter to the assembled bishops opens the record. The council confirmed his condemnation of the Three Chapters: the person and writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia, certain writings of Theodoret of Cyrrhus against Cyril of Alexandria, and the letter of Ibas of Edessa. Its anathemas reaffirmed Chalcedonian Christology against Nestorianism and upheld Mary's title Theotokos.

The acts and decrees of the Third Council of Constantinople, counted as the Sixth Ecumenical Council, were produced when the council met in 680–681 under Emperor Constantine IV. The council received the letters of Pope Agatho and his Roman synod, presented by papal legates. It condemned monoenergism and monothelitism, which taught that Christ had a single operation and will. Against them it defined that Christ has two natural wills and two energies, divine and human. It anathematized the leading monothelite figures, including Sergius, Pyrrhus, Cyrus of Alexandria and Pope Honorius.
