"Dirt" is a Coptic sermon or treatise by Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt. It is a moral exhortation that survives in fragments. Its surviving portion warns those who refuse to repent and urges them to turn to God. It contrasts obedient and disobedient children, using Jacob and Esau as examples: God, like a parent, blesses the child who submits to the church as mother and excludes the quarrelsome one from the inheritance. Its exact date and its place within Shenoute's writings are uncertain.

This is a Coptic text by Shenoute of Atripe (d. 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt. Its short title, "Errs", seems to come from its wording about everyone going astray. The surviving section reflects on wrongdoing throughout the whole earth and holds that God remains true even when every mouth speaks lies. It considers the image of a drawn sword, which human sin has called forth, and contrasts it with the avenging sword in the prophets. It shows Shenoute's typical style of heavily scriptural moral preaching.

A Coptic text known as "House", attributed to Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), the abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt and the most important author of early Coptic literature. It is a moral exhortation in Shenoute's typically forceful rhetorical style. It mourns the sins of the community, quoting Isaiah's words about the mother's certificate of divorce. It sets the praise that heaven, earth, sea and all creation give to God against human beings, who bless him with words alone while insulting him through ungodly and unnatural acts. Its exact date and place within Shenoute's writings are uncertain.

"Listen" is a Coptic text by Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt, written for his monastic community. The opening survives only in fragments. In it Shenoute sharply rebukes members of the community who expect God to forgive defiling deeds committed after they have received instruction. He asks whether he can rightly gather or offer the offering with impure people who have not given up their wrongdoing. The work shows Shenoute's severe concern for purity and discipline within the monastery.

A Coptic sermon or discourse attributed to Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt and one of the major writers of Coptic literature. The text speaks directly to the devil, the "instigator of evil" and "unclean spirit." It charges him with setting every vice against its matching virtue and attacking people through dreams and sinful passions. It also contrasts his weakness with the power of God in those who stay watchful and do good. Its exact date and original context are uncertain.

Seeks is a Coptic work by Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt, so it was written sometime in the late fourth or fifth century. It is preserved in fragments. The surviving opening is a moral exhortation built on Christ's saying that the people of Nineveh will rise at the judgment and condemn this generation. Shenoute warns that the saints, martyrs and apostles, who will sit in judgment, will condemn people and angels who turned toward evil when they should have resisted Satan. The work's exact place among Shenoute's writings is uncertain.

"Thundered" is a Coptic treatise by Shenoute of Atripe (d. 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt. Like many of his writings, it is known by a short title taken from its opening words. Shenoute wrote it in Sahidic Coptic as a polemic against heretics and pagans. He sets the righteous, called friends of God like Abraham and the apostles, against heretics, whom he calls friends of Satan who fill books with abominable words. He condemns pagan sacrifice and ungodly kings, and warns that unbelievers will share the devil's punishment.

This is a fragmentary Coptic text attributed to Shenoute of Atripe (d. 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt. Its exact identity and its place among his writings are uncertain, and its date is unknown beyond his lifetime. The surviving portion is a prophetic warning about the last days. It lists the vices that the ungodly, men and women alike, will no longer count as sins, and condemns sexual immorality, idleness and luxury. It also warns that Satan will rise against those who fail to put these passions to death.

An untitled Coptic text attributed to Shenoute of Atripe, abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt, who died in 465. It has not been assigned to any of his known Canons or Discourses. Like much of Shenoute's writing, it survives only in fragments. The surviving opening strings together verses, mostly from the Psalms, about shame, reproach, mockery and persecution suffered by the righteous and by God's anointed. It then begins to discuss "the proof of their love". Its occasion and full argument are unknown.

Witness is a Coptic work by Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt and the most important writer of Sahidic Coptic literature. Its exact date is not known. In the surviving portion Shenoute sharply rebukes a group he accuses of secret wrongdoing "in these synagogues", in hidden corners and inside houses. He charges them with defiling the temple of God and grieving his Spirit, and warns them of judgment. He draws heavily on biblical language, which is typical of his forceful prophetic style of moral admonition.

This Coptic encomium is a festal sermon in praise of the archangel Michael. It is attributed to Theodosius I, the Miaphysite patriarch of Alexandria who died in 566, though the attribution is uncertain, as with many Coptic homilies circulating under famous names. The preacher recalls Michael's victory over the devil, who was bound and cast into the lake of fire. He then invites his hearers to a royal banquet given by Michael, where patriarchs, prophets, apostles and martyrs take their places first. The work is evidence for the strong devotion to Michael in Egyptian Christianity.

The Apologia altera prophetae David (Second Apology for the Prophet David) is a Latin sermon handed down among the works of Ambrose, bishop of Milan (c. 339–397), though scholars have long questioned whether he wrote it. It takes as its starting point the title of Psalm 50 (51), which tells of Nathan's visit after David's sin with Bathsheba, and the Gospel story of the woman taken in adultery. It defends David's public confession and Christ's pardon against readers who might take either as approval of sin. It treats repentance, humility and divine mercy.

The Apology of the Prophet David is a Latin exegetical treatise by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, dedicated to the emperor Theodosius I. Its date is uncertain; some scholars link it to the emperor's penance after the massacre at Thessalonica in 390. It defends David's sins of adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah by reading the story in 2 Samuel and Psalm 50 (51). It presents David as a model of repentance, humility and penance for rulers who sin.

De Noe (On Noah), sometimes called De Noe et arca, is an exegetical treatise by Ambrose, bishop of Milan (c. 339–397). It comments on the Genesis account of Noah, the ark and the flood, and presents Noah, whose name it explains as "just" or "rest", as a model of righteousness for all to imitate. Its exact date is uncertain. Ambrose drew heavily on Philo of Alexandria's Questions on Genesis and read the narrative allegorically and morally. It belongs with his other treatises on Old Testament patriarchs, such as De Abraham and De Isaac.

The Explanatio Psalmorum XII is a Latin commentary by Ambrose, bishop of Milan (c. 339–397), on twelve psalms: Psalms 1, 35–40, 43, 45, 47, 48 and 61. Most of it seems to come from sermons preached in his last years and later revised. Ambrose's biographer Paulinus says he was still working on Psalm 43 when he died, and that commentary is unfinished. The opening exposition praises the psalms and introduces the theme of delight in God. Throughout, Ambrose reads the psalms morally and in relation to Christ, following the allegorical tradition of Origen and other Greek writers.

The Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam is a Latin commentary on the Gospel of Luke by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, in ten books. It was compiled in the late 380s, largely from sermons he had preached, and it is his longest exegetical work. It opens by presenting Luke's Gospel as a historical narrative, then works through the text, reading it in literal, moral and allegorical senses, much influenced by Origen. It is one of the most important Latin Gospel commentaries of the fourth century.

The Expositio Psalmi CXVIII is a Latin commentary by Ambrose, bishop of Milan (c. 339–397), on Psalm 118 (Psalm 119 in Hebrew numbering), the long alphabetic psalm in praise of God's law. It grew out of his preaching and is generally dated to the late 380s. After a prologue, it moves through the psalm's twenty-two eight-verse sections, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, in a matching series of sermons. Drawing partly on Origen, Ambrose reads the psalm as a guide to the moral and spiritual life. It is the longest of his exegetical works.

The Exameron (Hexameron) is an exegetical work by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, usually dated between 386 and 390. It is a commentary in six books on the six days of creation in Genesis, and it grew out of sermons preached over several days, probably during Holy Week. Ambrose begins by rejecting the philosophers' accounts of the eternity of matter and the world. He draws heavily on Basil of Caesarea's Greek homilies on the Hexaemeron, mixing natural history with moral and spiritual teaching. Through it, Greek creation exegesis reached the Latin West.

The Questions on the Old and New Testament is a Latin collection of short treatises in question-and-answer form. It was handed down among the works of Augustine, but it is now generally assigned to the anonymous Roman writer known as Ambrosiaster, who also wrote a commentary on Paul's epistles. It was composed in the later fourth century and survives in several recensions, including this one of 127 questions. It covers the nature of God, difficult biblical passages and doctrinal questions. It also argues against pagans, Jews and heretics, and it is valuable evidence for Roman Christianity of its time.

Adnotationes in Iob (Notes on Job) is a set of brief Latin comments on the Book of Job by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated to around 399–400. It works through the biblical text phrase by phrase, offering short explanations that are often allegorical and moral. In his Retractationes, Augustine says the notes had been written in the margins of his copy of Job and were collected into a book by others. He doubted they should count as his work, since they were obscure and the copies were corrupt.

The Breviculus Collationis cum Donatistis is a Latin summary by Augustine of Hippo of the Conference of Carthage, held in 411. By order of Emperor Honorius, Catholic and Donatist bishops met there to debate before the imperial tribune and notary Marcellinus, who acted as judge. Augustine wrote it soon after the conference. He condensed the long official record of its three sessions and keyed his summary to the record's numbered sections so readers could find each point. He presented the proceedings from the Catholic side, which won the judgment. The work is a key source for the Donatist controversy.

Contra Adimantum (Against Adimantus) is an anti-Manichaean treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written in the mid-390s while he was a presbyter at Hippo. Adimantus, a disciple of Mani, had written a work setting passages of the Old Testament against passages of the New to show that the two contradict each other. Augustine takes up these pairings in turn, beginning with the creation account in Genesis. He argues that the two Testaments agree, and he defends the unity of Scripture and of the God who inspired both.

Contra Cresconium (Against Cresconius) is an anti-Donatist treatise in four books by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated to about 405–406. Cresconius, a Donatist layman and grammarian, had published a rebuttal of Augustine's earlier reply to Petilian, the Donatist bishop of Cirta. Augustine answers him point by point. He defends the validity of baptism given outside the Donatist communion and rejects the practice of rebaptism. He also turns the Donatists' own handling of the Maximianist schism against them. The work is a major source for Augustine's thinking on the Church and the sacraments.

This is a Latin pastoral letter by Augustine of Hippo to the Catholic faithful in his care, written during his controversy with the Donatists in Roman North Africa around the early 400s. He had already replied to a fragment of a letter by Petilian, the Donatist bishop of Constantine (Cirta). Once he obtained the complete letter, which was widely read, he answered it point by point, as if in a face-to-face debate. The work belongs to his writings against Petilian and defends Catholic unity against Donatist claims.

Against the Letter of Parmenian is an anti-Donatist treatise in three books by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated to around 400. It answers a letter in which Parmenian, the Donatist bishop of Carthage who had died some years before, criticised the Donatist writer Tyconius. Tyconius had argued that no one's sin could cancel God's promise of a church spread throughout the world. Augustine defends this universal church and argues that it contains both good and bad members until the final judgment. He also argues that a sacrament does not depend on the holiness of the minister who performs it.

Contra Gaudentium Donatistarum Episcopum is a polemical treatise in two books by Augustine of Hippo, written around 420. Gaudentius, Donatist bishop of Thamugadi, had threatened to burn himself and his followers inside his church rather than submit to the imperial laws enforcing Church unity. Those laws were being carried out by the tribune Dulcitius. Augustine quotes and refutes, point by point, the two letters Gaudentius sent to Dulcitius. The second book answers Gaudentius's reply to the first. The work is one of Augustine's last anti-Donatist writings and deals with martyrdom, suicide and the use of state coercion.

Contra partem Donati post gesta, also known as Ad Donatistas post collationem, is a Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written around 412. It followed the Conference of Carthage of 411, where Catholic and Donatist bishops debated before the imperial commissioner Marcellinus, who decided for the Catholics. Augustine addresses ordinary Donatists directly and urges them to stop following their bishops. He answers the claim that the judge had been bribed and uses the conference records to show that the Donatist case had been refuted.

Contra Secundinum Manichaeum is a Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated around 405–406. It answers a letter from Secundinus, a Manichaean auditor from Rome, who had written to Augustine with respect but criticised his departure from the sect and urged him to return. Augustine replies courteously but firmly, defending the Catholic faith and attacking Manichaean dualism and its teaching on the two natures and the origin of evil. In his Retractationes Augustine judged it the best of his writings against the Manichaeans.

Contra Felicem (Against Felix) is a Latin work in two books by Augustine of Hippo. It records a public debate held at Hippo Regius in December 404 between Augustine and Felix, a Manichaean teacher. The discussion starts from Mani's Letter of the Foundation and covers the authority of Mani's writings, the nature of God and the origin of evil. At the end Felix gives way and anathematizes Mani. The work is valuable both as anti-Manichaean polemic and as a near-verbatim record of an ancient debate.

De Genesi ad litteram (The Literal Meaning of Genesis) is an exegetical commentary in twelve books by Augustine of Hippo, probably completed around 415. It reads the opening chapters of Genesis as an account of what actually happened, not only as allegory. Books 1–5 treat the days of creation, books 6–11 the second creation narrative and the Garden of Eden, and book 12 Paul's ascent to the "third heaven" of 2 Corinthians 12. It was Augustine's second attempt at a literal interpretation of Genesis.

Locutiones in Heptateuchum (Expressions in the Heptateuch) is a Latin exegetical work in seven books by Augustine of Hippo, written around 419–420 alongside his Quaestiones in Heptateuchum. It goes through Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua and Judges. Augustine collects phrases in the Old Latin Bible that reflect Hebrew or Greek idiom rather than normal Latin usage, and he compares variant Latin manuscripts with the Greek Septuagint. The work shows his concern with biblical language and with sound interpretation of the literal text.

Quaestiones in Heptateuchum (Questions on the Heptateuch) is a Latin exegetical work in seven books by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated to around 419–420. It covers Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua and Judges. Augustine wrote it as working notes while reading these books and comparing Latin manuscripts with the Septuagint. Some problems he only raises, while others he discusses at length. The questions concern textual readings, historical and moral difficulties, and figurative meanings. The work shows his close engagement with the biblical text and his method of inquiry.

The Retractationes (Reconsiderations) is a Latin work in two books by Augustine of Hippo, written around 426–427, near the end of his life. In it Augustine reviews his own writings in roughly the order he wrote them, beginning with the early dialogues composed at Cassiciacum. For each work he explains the circumstances of its writing, corrects or clarifies passages he had come to think mistaken, and gives its opening words. It is unique in ancient literature as an author's critical survey of his own output, and it remains a key source for the chronology of Augustine's works.

The "Letters of Emperors, Popes and Others" is the collection usually known as the Collectio Avellana. It is an anonymous Latin compilation of about 240 documents dating from 367 to 553, made in Rome probably in the mid-sixth century. It brings together letters from emperors and imperial officials, papal correspondence and related texts. It opens with an account of the dispute between Liberius and Felix and the conflicts surrounding Pope Damasus. Many of its documents survive nowhere else. This makes it a key source for church–state relations and the Acacian schism, especially under Pope Hormisdas.

De statu animae ("On the Nature of the Soul") is a Latin philosophical and theological treatise in three books by Claudianus Mamertus, a priest of Vienne in Gaul and brother of Bishop Mamertus. It was written around 470 and dedicated to Sidonius Apollinaris. The work answers Faustus of Riez, who had argued that only God is incorporeal and that the human soul is in some sense bodily. Drawing on Augustine and Neoplatonic thought, Claudianus argues that the soul is incorporeal. The treatise is an important witness to philosophical learning in late fifth-century Gaul.

The Heptateuchos is a Late Latin biblical epic in verse that retells the first seven books of the Old Testament, Genesis through Judges. It follows the Old Latin translation of the Bible. Its anonymous author is conventionally called Cyprianus Gallus, or Cyprian the Gaul, and probably worked in Gaul around 397–430. The poem was once wrongly credited to Cyprian of Carthage. It seems to have belonged to a larger verse paraphrase of the Old Testament's historical books, but only this part survives. It is an important example of late antique Christian biblical epic.

De Singularitate clericorum ("On the Single Life of the Clergy") is an anonymous Latin treatise once transmitted among the works of Cyprian of Carthage. Its date and authorship are uncertain. It is generally placed in the third or fourth century, probably in North Africa, and some scholars have linked it to a Donatist author. Writing as a pastor to clerics who lived with women, the author forbids the practice, citing a divine revelation and supporting it with Scripture. It is an important witness to early church debates over clerical continence and the custom of "spiritual marriage."

The Carmina are the collected Latin poems of Magnus Felix Ennodius (473/474–521), a Gallo-Roman rhetorician who became bishop of Pavia in 514. They are usually arranged in two books. They range from occasional verse, such as the opening account of a summer journey to the fort of Brigantio in the Alps, to epigrams and hymns in the style of Ambrose. Most were probably written while he was a cleric in Milan. Their dense classical diction makes them an important witness to Christian literary culture in Ostrogothic Italy.

The Dictiones are a collection of Latin speeches by Magnus Felix Ennodius (473/474–521), composed mostly while he was a cleric in Milan, before he became bishop of Pavia in 514. They include ecclesiastical addresses, such as a speech for the anniversary of Laurence, bishop of Milan, as well as school pieces and rhetorical declamations on mythological and legal themes. Written in an ornate, highly mannered style, they show how classical rhetorical education continued in Christian circles in Ostrogothic Italy.

The Epistulae are the collected letters of Magnus Felix Ennodius (c. 473–521), a Latin rhetorician who became bishop of Pavia in 514. Nearly three hundred letters survive, arranged in nine books. Most were written in the early sixth century, while Ennodius was a cleric in Milan, and are addressed to senators, churchmen, friends and relatives in Ostrogothic Italy and Gaul. They are written in a highly ornate, mannered prose. Their content is often slight, but they are an important source for the Roman aristocracy under Theodoric and for the Laurentian schism.

This polemical Latin tract by Magnus Felix Ennodius, later bishop of Pavia, is often called the Libellus pro synodo. It dates from the Laurentian schism in Rome. Ennodius wrote it around 502–503, while he was still a deacon in Milan. It defends the Roman synod of 501–502, often called the Synodus Palmaris, which had refused to judge Pope Symmachus. The tract answers a pamphlet by supporters of the rival claimant Laurentius. It argues that the pope cannot be judged by those beneath him, and it is an important early statement of papal immunity from judgment.

Formulae Spiritalis Intellegentiae ("Formulas of Spiritual Understanding") is a Latin handbook of biblical interpretation by Eucherius, bishop of Lyon (d. c. 449). It was written in the first half of the fifth century and addressed to his son Veranus. The preface argues that all of Scripture, Old Testament and New, has an allegorical sense. The book then gives lists of scriptural words and images, arranged by subject, and explains their spiritual meanings. Along with his Instructiones, it became a widely used guide to figurative exegesis in the medieval Latin West.

The Instructiones ad Salonium is a Latin handbook of biblical interpretation in two books by Eucherius of Lyon (c. 380 – c. 449). It is addressed to his son Salonius, who had been brought up from childhood among the monks of Lérins and later became a bishop. The first book answers questions about difficult passages of the Old and New Testaments, drawing on earlier teachers. The second explains Hebrew names and words, liturgical terms and objects. It was widely used as a reference in the medieval West.

De fide contra Manichaeos ("On the Faith, against the Manichaeans") is a short Latin anti-Manichaean treatise. It is attributed to Evodius, bishop of Uzalis in North Africa and a friend of Augustine of Hippo, and was probably written in the early fifth century. The work has come down among Augustine's writings. It opens with a confession of the one God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit. It then argues against Mani's dualism, especially his claim that an unbegotten prince of darkness stands against God, drawing on Scripture and on the Manichaeans' own texts.

De gratia is a Latin treatise in two books by Faustus, bishop of Riez in southern Gaul. He wrote it around 474 at the request of Leontius of Arles, after Gallic councils at Arles and Lyon condemned the predestinarian teaching of the priest Lucidus. Faustus rejects both Pelagius and strict predestination. He argues that divine grace works together with human free will, which is weakened but not destroyed. The work became a key statement of what was later called Semi-Pelagianism, and its positions were rejected at the Council of Orange in 529.

De Spiritu Sancto is a Latin treatise in two books on the divinity of the Holy Spirit. It was long transmitted under the name of Paschasius, a Roman deacon who died around 512, but many scholars now attribute it to Faustus of Riez, the fifth-century bishop in southern Gaul. Taking the Creed as its starting point, it defends the Spirit's full deity and his equality within the Trinity, drawing on Scripture. It is also known for distinguishing belief "in" God from believing the Church, which it holds should be confessed without the preposition "in".

The letters of Faustus, bishop of Riez in southern Gaul (died c. 490), are a small surviving collection of Latin correspondence from the later fifth century. The best known, to the priest Lucidus, urges him to give up a strict predestinarian teaching that excluded human effort, while also condemning Pelagius. Lucidus later retracted at councils held at Arles and Lyon around 473–474. Other letters offer spiritual counsel and discuss doctrinal questions, including the bodily nature of the soul. They are key witnesses to Faustus's so-called Semi-Pelagian theology of grace.

These are Latin sermons attributed to Faustus of Riez (died c. 490), the monk of Lérins who became bishop of Riez in Provence. They are pastoral addresses for church feasts and for monastic and lay audiences, and they urge moral reform and worthy preparation for receiving the Eucharist, for example before Christmas. Which sermons are authentically his is often uncertain. Many survive anonymously or under other names, especially in the Gallic collection known as Eusebius Gallicanus. They are important evidence for preaching in fifth-century Gaul.

The Diversarum hereseon liber (Book of Various Heresies) is a Latin catalogue of heresies by Filastrius (Philastrius), bishop of Brescia, written in the 380s. It begins with errors that arose before Christ, including Jewish sects, and then covers those that appeared after the Incarnation, some 156 entries in all. Some entries deal with matters of opinion or interpretation that later writers would hardly call heresies. The work is one of the earliest Latin heresiologies. Augustine drew on it in his own De haeresibus.

De errore profanarum religionum ("On the Error of Profane Religions") is a Latin apologetic treatise by Julius Firmicus Maternus, a former astrologer who became a Christian. He wrote it around 346 and dedicated it to the emperors Constantius II and Constans. It attacks pagan worship of the elements and the mystery cults of Isis, Osiris, Cybele and Attis, Mithras and Dionysus. Firmicus presents these cults as demonic imitations of Christian truth and urges the emperors to suppress them. The treatise survives in a single manuscript whose beginning is lost, and it is a valuable source on the late Roman mystery religions.

The Collectanea Antiariana Parisina, also called the historical fragments (Fragmenta historica), is a collection of documents on the fourth-century Arian controversy associated with Hilary of Poitiers. It survives in two series, A and B, and is usually thought to come from Hilary's lost polemical history directed against the bishops Valens and Ursacius. It includes synodal letters, creeds and correspondence connected with the councils of Serdica, Rimini and Paris. Together with Hilary's own commentary, these documents are an important primary source for the conflicts over Nicene doctrine under Constantius II.

The Tractatus mysteriorum (Treatise on the Mysteries) is a Latin work by Hilary of Poitiers, the fourth-century bishop and opponent of Arianism. It probably dates from his later years, after his exile in the East. The treatise is a typological reading of the Old Testament. It argues that the patriarchs and other figures, from Adam, Noah, Melchizedek and Abraham onward, prefigure Christ's coming, passion and resurrection and the gathering of the Church. It survives incomplete in two books and is an important early Latin example of figural exegesis.

Jerome's Latin commentary on the Book of Jeremiah in six books was his last major work of biblical exegesis. He wrote it in Bethlehem in his final years, roughly 414–420, and dedicated it to his friend Eusebius. It followed his commentaries on the Twelve Prophets, Isaiah, Daniel and Ezekiel. Jerome works from the Hebrew text and its order, sets aside Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah, and explains the literal and spiritual sense. It also contains polemic against Pelagius. Jerome died before finishing it, and the commentary stops at chapter 32.

The Evangeliorum libri quattuor ("Four Books of the Gospels") is a Latin epic poem by Juvencus, a Christian priest from Hispania. He wrote it around 330, during the reign of Constantine. In about 3,200 dactylic hexameters it retells the life of Christ, mainly following Matthew's Gospel, with material drawn from the other evangelists. Its preface contrasts the false tales of Homer and Virgil with the truth of the Gospel. Its diction borrows heavily from Virgil. It is the earliest surviving Latin biblical epic, and it was widely read and imitated in the Middle Ages.

De non conveniendo cum haereticis ("On Not Associating with Heretics") is a Latin polemical treatise by Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia. He wrote it during his exile in the later 350s, after he refused to condemn Athanasius at the Council of Milan in 355. Addressed directly and abusively to the Arian-leaning emperor Constantius II, it answers the charge that Nicene bishops were enemies of peace and unity. Drawing on many Old Testament examples, it argues that the faithful must keep themselves apart from heretics. Its long scriptural quotations are valuable evidence for the Old Latin Bible.

De non parcendo in Deum delinquentibus ("That Those Who Sin Against God Are Not to Be Spared") is a Latin polemical treatise by Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari. He wrote it during his exile in the late 350s and addressed it directly to Emperor Constantius II. The emperor had complained of being insulted, and Lucifer answers with Old Testament examples, beginning with Moses and the Levites punishing idolatry, to argue that God's servants have always rebuked apostates. In this way he defends his fierce opposition to the emperor's pro-Arian policy.

De Regibus Apostaticis ("On Apostate Kings") is a short Latin polemical treatise by Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia. He wrote it while in exile in the late 350s, after refusing to condemn Athanasius. It is addressed to the Arian emperor Constantius II and rejects his claim that his continued power proved God approved of his faith and his persecution of the Nicene party. Lucifer cites rulers of Israel and Judah, beginning with Gideon, who fell into idolatry or cruelty. God endured them for a time but punished them in the end.

De regibus apostaticis ("On Apostate Kings") is a Latin polemical treatise by Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia. He wrote it in exile around 358–360, after refusing to condemn Athanasius at the Council of Milan in 355. It is addressed directly and abusively to Emperor Constantius II. Using Old Testament examples of kings who abandoned God and were punished, Lucifer argues that the emperor's support for Arianism makes him an apostate. It belongs to a group of pamphlets against Constantius that includes the books On Saint Athanasius.

"That We Must Die for the Son of God" is a Latin polemical treatise by Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia. He wrote it in exile, probably around 360, after he refused at the Council of Milan (355) to condemn Athanasius. It is addressed directly and abusively to Emperor Constantius II. Lucifer denounces the emperor's support for Arianism and his use of force against Nicene bishops. He declares that God's servants scorn imperial violence and should welcome martyrdom rather than give up the faith. It is among the last of his pamphlets against Constantius.

The Seven Books of History Against the Pagans is a Latin universal history by Paulus Orosius, a priest who was probably from Gallaecia. He wrote it at the request of Augustine of Hippo, to whom it is dedicated, and finished it around 417–418. After Alaric sacked Rome in 410, pagans blamed Christianity for Rome's troubles. Orosius answered them by surveying wars and disasters from Adam to his own day, arguing that earlier ages had suffered worse. The work became one of the most widely read histories of the Middle Ages and was later adapted into Old English.

The Liber Apologeticus is a Latin polemical treatise by Paulus Orosius, the priest and historian from Hispania, written in Palestine in 415 during the Pelagian controversy. Orosius had been sent east by Augustine of Hippo. After a meeting of clergy in Jerusalem under Bishop John, he was accused of teaching that a person cannot be free from sin even with God's help. Addressing his fellow priests, he defends his own orthodoxy and attacks the teachings of Pelagius on grace and free will. He appeals to earlier Fathers such as Cyprian and Hilary.

The Carmina are the collected Latin poems of Paulinus of Nola (c. 354–431), the Roman senator who renounced his career for ascetic life and became bishop of Nola in Campania. Written from before his conversion into the early fifth century, they include verse letters to his teacher Ausonius, paraphrases of the Psalms, a wedding poem for Julian of Eclanum, a consolation for a dead child, and a series of annual poems for the feast of Saint Felix of Nola. Together with Prudentius, Paulinus is a major early Latin Christian poet, joining classical form to Christian subjects.

The Epistulae are the surviving Latin letters of Paulinus of Nola (c. 354–431), the Roman senator who gave up his wealth for an ascetic life and later became bishop of Nola. About fifty letters survive, mostly from the 390s onward. Some were sent jointly with his wife Therasia. His correspondents included Sulpicius Severus, Augustine, Jerome and Delphinus of Bordeaux. Written in an ornate style full of scriptural allusion, the letters deal with Christian friendship, renunciation, biblical interpretation and his building work at the shrine of St Felix. They are an important witness to the spread of Western asceticism.

De Vita Sancti Martini is a Latin verse life of Martin of Tours in six books of hexameters by Paulinus of Périgueux, a Gallic poet of the later fifth century. It is dedicated to Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, in a prose letter. The first five books turn into epic verse the prose writings of Sulpicius Severus on Martin, the Life and the Dialogues. The sixth book draws on an account of posthumous miracles that Perpetuus had sent to Paulinus. The poem is an important witness to the cult of Martin in Gaul.

The Eleven Tractates are a collection of Latin treatises that survive in a single fifth- or sixth-century manuscript at Würzburg. The manuscript was discovered in 1885. The tractates come from the ascetic movement of Priscillian, bishop of Ávila, who was executed around 385. Scholars disagree on whether Priscillian wrote them or one of his close followers, such as Instantius. The first three are apologetic: they defend the group's orthodoxy to bishops, condemn heresies and discuss the use of apocryphal books. The rest are homilies and biblical expositions. They are the main surviving writings of the Priscillianist movement.

This Latin commentary on the Carmen Paschale (Paschal Song) of Sedulius, the fifth-century Christian poet, is attributed to Remigius of Auxerre, a Carolingian Benedictine teacher who died in 908. It begins with an introduction to the poet. It says Sedulius was a layman trained in worldly learning who turned to God. He wrote the work first in prose and then in verse, and dedicated it to the priest Macedonius. The commentary then works through the poem, explaining individual words, their grammar and their theological sense. It shows how Sedulius's biblical epic was used to teach Latin in Carolingian schools.

The Epistulae are the collected Latin letters of Ruricius (c. 440–c. 510), a Gallo-Roman aristocrat who became bishop of Limoges around 485. They survive in two books and were written in the later fifth and early sixth centuries. Among the recipients are Faustus of Riez, whom the opening letter addresses as a revered teacher, and Sidonius Apollinaris. The letters deal with spiritual advice, friendship, family matters and church affairs. They are a valuable record of the aristocratic and episcopal network of southern Gaul under Visigothic rule.

The Alethia ("Truth") is a Latin biblical epic in hexameters by Claudius Marius Victorius, a fifth-century rhetor of Marseille. It was probably written in the second quarter of the century and is also known as a commentary on Genesis in three books. It opens with a prayer to the triune God, then retells and interprets Genesis from the creation to the destruction of Sodom. Along the way it digresses on divine providence and the origins of human culture. It is a notable example of Christian verse paraphrase in late antique Gaul.

The History of the Persecution of the African Province is a Latin history by Victor, bishop of Vita in Byzacena, written in the late 480s. It tells of the suffering of Nicene (catholic) Christians under the Arian Vandal kings Gaiseric and Huneric. It covers events from the Vandal crossing into Africa in 429 to the harsh measures of 483–484, including the exile of clergy and Huneric's edicts. A prologue addresses a disciple of the bishop Diadochus. The work is the main narrative source for religious conflict in Vandal North Africa.

On the Solitaries is a Syriac admonition addressed to solitary monks and attributed to Mar Abraham of Nathpar, an East Syriac monastic writer usually placed in the late sixth or seventh century. He wrote it at the request of a disciple, and it explains why some people are called to anticipate the life of the world to come through monastic withdrawal. The treatise is set out under headings. These cover who should take up the solitary life, with what thoughts and deeds to begin it, how to persevere in it, and how to face temptations and spiritual battles.

On Divine Providence is a set of Syriac discourses by Antony of Tagrit, a monk of the Syriac Orthodox tradition usually known as Antony the Rhetor and generally dated to around the ninth century. The work is written for fellow believers troubled by questions about God's providence. It argues that providence works for good and restrains people from sin without forcing their free will, while leaving the deepest mysteries of divine knowledge unexplored. It is a notable example of later Syriac philosophical theology and of its author's rhetorical style.

This is a cycle of Syriac hymns (madroshe) by Balai, a poet active at Qenneshrin (Chalcis) in the early fifth century. They praise Acacius, the long-lived bishop of Beroea (Aleppo), who died around 436–437. The poet asks the bishop to intercede for him on his feast day. He then praises Acacius's chastity, his teaching, his care for the weak and his warnings to the rich. The hymns are among the few surviving works securely attributed to Balai and show early fifth-century Syriac praise poetry for church leaders.

This Syriac hymn (madrasha) is by Balai, a chorepiscopus and poet active at Qenneshrin (Chalcis) in northern Syria in the early fifth century. He wrote it for the dedication of a newly built church in that city. It praises those who built the church as a dwelling for God and calls the sanctuary heaven on earth, where priests take the place of the angelic Watchers. It reflects on how God is wholly above yet wholly present below, far from those who pry and near to those who love and believe. It is an important early example of Syriac liturgical poetry about sacred space.

This short Syriac letter was written by Barlaha, a recluse living in the precinct of Mar Elisha, to Simeon, abbot of the monastery of Beth Licinius on the Black Mountain near Antioch. Barlaha responds to news brought by the deacon Damian, who had come with ten leaves containing the introduction to a Greek commentary on the Psalms, and he urges that the whole commentary be translated into Syriac. The letter's date is uncertain. It sheds light on how Greek exegesis reached Syriac-speaking monastic communities.

The Book of the Cause of All Causes, also called the Book on the Knowledge (or Acknowledgement) of Truth, is an anonymous Syriac encyclopedic treatise. It was written sometime between the tenth and twelfth centuries, and its exact date and authorship are uncertain. Addressed to "all the peoples under heaven", it sets out a systematic account of how truth is known and argues for God's existence, unity, attributes, names and providence. It then turns to creation and the ordering of the world. It is a notable late witness to Syriac Christian philosophical and scientific learning.

The Chronicle of Edessa is an anonymous Syriac history of the city of Edessa, generally dated to about 540–550. Its manuscript title is "Histories of Events in Brief." In short dated entries, it covers the period from the founding of the kingdom of Osrhoene in 133/132 BC to 540. It draws mainly on Edessan royal archives and church records and is considered historically reliable. Its account of the Daisan flood of 201 mentions a Christian church building and is one of the earliest pieces of evidence for Christianity in Edessa. Only an abridged version survives.

This anonymous Syriac chronicle was written around 506–507 by an eyewitness living at Edessa, at the request of Sergius, a priest and abbot. It records the disasters that struck Edessa, Amida and Mesopotamia, including locusts, famine, plague and earthquake, and above all the Roman–Persian war of 502–506. It survives only because it was copied into the Chronicle of Zuqnin, and its old attribution to Joshua the Stylite is now rejected. It is one of the earliest and most reliable histories in Syriac and is admired for how it analyses causes.

The Chronicle of Zuqnin is an anonymous Syriac world chronicle finished around 775 by a monk of the Zuqnin monastery near Amida, on the upper Tigris. It was once wrongly attributed to Dionysius of Tel Mahre, and its author is sometimes identified as Joshua the Stylite. In four parts, it runs from the creation to the year 1087 of the Seleucid era (775/76). It draws on the Bible, John of Ephesus and other sources, and it preserves otherwise lost texts such as the Revelation of the Magi. Its eyewitness account of life under early Abbasid rule is especially valuable.

This anonymous apocryphal narrative tells of the death, or "departure", of the apostle John at Ephesus. It is a Syriac version of the account known in Greek as the Metastasis, which closes the apocryphal Acts of John. On a Sunday, John urges the assembled brethren to stay faithful and celebrates the Eucharist. He then has a grave dug, prays, and lies down in it to die in peace. Its date of composition is uncertain, perhaps the fourth or fifth century. It shaped later traditions about John's end.

The Disputation between the Apostle Peter and Nero is an anonymous Syriac apocryphal text. Its date is uncertain, but it was probably composed between the fifth and seventh centuries. It opens with an allegorical prologue: the world is a stormy sea, the twelve apostles are ships carrying great wealth, the devil is the king of the sea who stirs up the waves, and the kingdom is the harbour where they find rest. It then presents the Emperor Nero as the devil's willing servant in opposing Peter's preaching.

The Prose Refutations are a group of polemical discourses in Syriac by Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373), the deacon and theologian of Nisibis and Edessa. They are aimed at the three main rival teachings of his region: Mani, Marcion and Bardaisan. The first discourse is a letter to a certain Hypatius. In it Ephrem argues against dualist ideas about light and darkness, matter and the body, and defends free will and the goodness of creation. The work is a rare example of Ephrem's prose. It is also an important witness to early Manichaean, Marcionite and Bardaisanite thought.

The Exhortation of the Apostle Peter is an anonymous Syriac apocryphal discourse on admonition, attributed to the apostle Peter. Its date is uncertain; it is generally placed between the fourth and sixth centuries. Speaking to a crowd that has gathered for instruction, Peter warns his hearers not to become attached to worldly things but to be ready for death. He illustrates the point with a parable about two servants banished by their master: one puts down roots in exile, while the other turns his earnings into a gold crown engraved with images of his master and his master's son.

The History of John, the Son of Zebedee is an anonymous Syriac apocryphal narrative about the apostle John, probably composed in the fifth century. It tells how, after Pentecost, the apostles dispersed to preach and John went to Ephesus, where he preached, worked wonders, baptised and turned the city from pagan worship to Christianity. Its heading claims Eusebius of Caesarea as author and says it was translated from a Greek book, but this attribution is not credited. The work is a witness to Syriac traditions about John and his Ephesian ministry.

The History of Karka d-Beth Slokh is an anonymous Syriac work from the Church of the East. It is usually placed among the Persian martyr acts and dated roughly to the late sixth or early seventh century. It tells the history of Karka d-Beth Slokh, the city now generally identified with Kirkuk, beginning with a legendary founding by the Assyrian king Sardana in the time of Jonah. It then follows the city's Christian community and its martyrs under the Sasanian kings. The work matters as a source for local church history and for how Syriac Christians in Mesopotamia saw their own past.

The History of Philip, the Apostle and Evangelist is an anonymous Syriac apocryphal narrative, probably composed between the fifth and seventh centuries; its exact date is uncertain. It tells how Christ appears to Philip in a night vision at Jerusalem and sends him to preach in "Carthage, which is in Azotus." There he drives out Satan's power and converts the city through wonders and preaching. The work blends Philip the Apostle with Philip the Evangelist of Acts, and it reflects the Syriac tradition of legendary apostolic acts.

The History of Mar Qardagh is an anonymous Syriac martyr legend of the Church of the East, probably composed in the early seventh century in northern Mesopotamia, near Arbela. Set in the reign of the Sasanian king Shapur II, it tells of Qardagh, a Persian noble and governor descended from Nimrod. The hermit ʿAbdishoʿ converts him to Christianity, and he is then martyred by stoning. Drawing on Persian epic ideals of the warrior and hunter, it is an important source for Christian identity and culture in the late Sasanian Empire.

The Hymn of the Soul, also called the Hymn of the Pearl, is an anonymous Syriac poem preserved in the apocryphal Acts of Thomas. In that work the apostle Judas Thomas sings it while in prison in India. A prince is sent from his father's kingdom in the East to Egypt to bring back a pearl guarded by a serpent. He forgets his mission, is woken by a letter, and returns to receive his glorious robe. The poem is widely read as an allegory of the soul. It may be older than the Acts, and some have linked it to Bardaisan of Edessa, though its authorship is unknown.

On the End Times is a Syriac metrical homily (memra) attributed to Isaac of Antioch, a fifth-century Syriac poet whose death the Chronicle of Edessa places around 451–452. Writing is ascribed to several authors named Isaac, so which one wrote it is uncertain. In the poem, a personified Truth wakes the speaker and orders him to announce that the last times have come. It points to Scripture, the prophets, the apostles and the decay of nature as signs of the end. It urges readers to repent and seek refuge in God against Satan and an evil earthly ruler.

The First Part of Isaac of Nineveh's writings is a collection of Syriac discourses on monastic life, asceticism and prayer. It was composed in the late seventh century by the Church of the East bishop also known as Isaac the Syrian or Isaac of Qatar. It opens by calling the fear of God the beginning of virtue, and it teaches withdrawal from worldly affairs, meditation on Scripture, patient endurance, humility and stillness. It was translated into Greek early on and later into many other languages, and it became one of the most widely read ascetic works in Eastern Christianity.

The Letters are a collection of more than one hundred Syriac letters by Ishoʿyahb III of Adiabene, Patriarch of the Church of the East from 649 to 659. They are traditionally arranged by the stages of his career: as bishop of Nineveh, as metropolitan of Adiabene, and as catholicos. Written to clergy, monks and laypeople, they deal with church discipline, doctrinal disputes and pastoral affairs. They include letters to the Christians of Beth Qatraye. The collection is an important witness to Christian life in the earliest decades of Islamic rule.

The Memre are the verse homilies of Jacob of Serugh (c. 451–521), the Syriac poet-theologian who became bishop of Batnan in 519. Most are written in the twelve-syllable metre associated with him. They cover biblical narratives, feasts, saints and moral exhortation, as in the opening homily on admonition, which presents praise of God as humanity's duty to its Creator. Jacob is said to have composed 763 works. Around 400 survive, and they were copied widely across the Syriac churches.

This saint's life of Peter the Iberian (c. 417–491) was written by his disciple John Rufus, an anti-Chalcedonian priest who may have become bishop of Maiuma. It was composed in Greek around the end of the fifth century and survives only in a Syriac translation. It follows Peter's life as a Georgian royal prince, a hostage at the court in Constantinople, a monk and monastery founder in Palestine, and bishop of Maiuma near Gaza. It is an important source for Palestinian monasticism and for early opposition to the Council of Chalcedon.

The Plerophoriae ("Assurances") is an anti-Chalcedonian collection of anecdotes by John Rufus, a priest of Antioch, disciple of Peter the Iberian and bishop of Maiuma near Gaza. It was written in the early sixth century, probably in Greek, and survives in a Syriac version. It gathers visions, revelations and miraculous testimonies, many of them told by Peter the Iberian, that present the Council of Chalcedon (451) and the doctrine of two natures in Christ as condemned by God. It is a key witness to early miaphysite piety and to Palestinian monastic opposition to Chalcedon.

The Dialogue on the Soul is a Syriac treatise attributed to John the Solitary, often identified with John of Apamea, a fifth-century ascetic writer. It is framed as a conversation in which two disciples, Eutropius and Eusebius, visit John in his cell and question him. Among the topics are why the soul was placed in the human body, and how the passions of body, soul and spirit differ. The work sets out John's threefold scheme of the spiritual life and shows the influence of Evagrius Ponticus. It is an important early witness to Syriac ascetic and mystical thought.

On Prayer is a short Syriac treatise on spiritual contemplation (theoria) in prayer, associated with Joseph Hazzaya, an 8th-century monk and mystic of the Church of the East. The manuscript heading attributes it to "Mar Abdisho". Several of Joseph's writings circulated under the name Abdisho, which was also the name of his brother, so the authorship is uncertain. The work describes how monks who have purified their hearts of the passions are drawn in prayer beyond the senses. It speaks of a "fiery movement" of the indwelling Holy Spirit, received at baptism, which transforms the soul into its own likeness.

The Julian Romance is an anonymous Syriac prose narrative giving a fictionalized, Christian account of the reign of the emperor Julian the Apostate. It was written sometime between Julian's death in 363 and the sixth century, probably at Edessa. It has three parts: Julian's accession and persecution of Christians, his conflict with Eusebius of Rome, and, in the form of a letter, his Persian campaign, death and the accession of the Christian Jovian. It is one of the major narrative works of Syriac literature, and an Arabic adaptation existed by the tenth century.

The Book of Steps (Syriac Ktaba d-Masqata, Latin Liber Graduum) is an anonymous Syriac treatise of thirty discourses (memre). It was probably written in the late fourth or early fifth century by an author living in the Sasanian Empire, who addressed it to his own Christian community. It separates the "upright", who keep the lesser commandments, from the "perfect", who follow the greater commandments of renunciation and celibacy. It also describes the visible church as working alongside a heavenly church. It is an important witness to early Syriac asceticism and spirituality.

The Life of Jacob of Serugh is an anonymous Syriac hagiography of Jacob of Serugh (c. 451–521), the Miaphysite poet, homilist and late in life bishop of Batnan. Its date is uncertain but is usually placed between the mid-sixth and seventh centuries. It opens by calling itself "another account" of the saint. It tells of his birth to a barren mother after prayer at a shrine, and of a childhood miracle in which he received divine inspiration at the Eucharist. It then follows his upbringing in Hawra, his hymn-writing as a visiting priest and his time as bishop.

The Life of Rabbula is an anonymous Syriac hagiography of Rabbula, bishop of Edessa from about 411 to 435/6. It was written by an unnamed member of the Edessene church, probably within a few decades of his death. It praises him as an ascetic champion of the faith. The work follows his conversion and ascetic life, then his time as bishop: his care for the poor, his strict discipline of clergy and monks, and his struggles against heretics and civil rulers. It is an important witness to Christianity in Edessa in the early fifth century.

This is a short anonymous Syriac martyr act, one of the Acts of the Persian Martyrs, which record Christians who died in the persecution under the Sasanian king Shapur II. It tells how Jacob, priest of the village of Tel Shlila, and his sister Mary, a "daughter of the covenant" (a consecrated woman), were arrested in the seventh year of the persecution. On the orders of Narses Tamshapur they were flogged for refusing to eat blood. A Christian layman named Mahdad then beheaded them at Tel Dara on the Great Zab, on 17 Adar.

An anonymous Syriac hagiography, one of the Persian martyr acts, about Miles, bishop of Susa, and his companions Aborsam the priest and Sinai the deacon. They were executed by the Sasanian authorities in 340 or 341, at the start of the persecution under Shapur II. The account opens with a rhetorical prologue in praise of the martyrs. Its date is uncertain. Sozomen summarized a Syriac account of Miles in the fifth century, but the fuller surviving Acts have been dated as late as the end of the sixth century.

The Memre on Joseph are a cycle of verse homilies (mēmrē) in Syriac by Jacob of Serugh (c. 451–521), the poet-theologian and late bishop of Batnan. They are written in the twelve-syllable metre linked with Jacob, and they retell the story of the patriarch Joseph from Genesis in a series of discourses. The first opens with a prayer to Christ as the source of all beauty. Jacob presents Joseph's beauty and virtue as a reflection of Christ, which fits the Syriac tradition of reading Old Testament figures as types of Christ.

On the Soul is a Syriac theological treatise by Moses bar Kepha (died 903), a Syriac Orthodox bishop and one of the most celebrated writers of his church in the ninth century. It begins by setting out the many senses of the word "soul" in Scripture and in ordinary usage. It can mean the divine nature, the whole human person, the body, the blood, or the life-giving power in plants. It then discusses the nature of the human soul. The work draws on earlier Greek patristic and philosophical thought, and it is a valuable witness to Syriac Christian anthropology.

The Memre are the verse homilies of Narsai (c. 399 – c. 502), a leading poet-theologian of the Church of the East who taught at the School of Edessa and later headed the School of Nisibis. About eighty-one survive. They are metrical sermons on biblical themes, feasts and doctrine. Many were linked to the liturgical year, for example a discourse on the revelations to Abraham for the first Sunday of the Annunciation. They reflect the exegetical tradition of Theodore of Mopsuestia and rank among the major works of classical Syriac preaching, alongside those of Jacob of Serugh.

The Bazaar (or Book) of Heracleides is a theological and autobiographical apology attributed to Nestorius, the archbishop of Constantinople deposed at the Council of Ephesus in 431. He wrote it in exile late in his life, around 451–452. The Greek original is lost, and the work survives only in a Syriac translation preserved by the Church of the East and rediscovered in the nineteenth century. In it Nestorius defends his Christology against Cyril of Alexandria and recounts the events of his condemnation. The work has prompted scholars to reassess his actual teaching.

The Odes of Solomon are a collection of 42 early Christian hymns. Their author is unknown, and the attribution to King Solomon is traditional, not historical. Most scholars date them to the late first or early second century, though some place them later. Whether they were first written in Greek or Syriac is also debated. The poems are lyrical and mystical. They celebrate union with the Lord through love, the gift of the Spirit, salvation and immortality, and each ends with "Hallelujah." They are among the oldest surviving Christian hymnbooks, and they share notable affinities with the Gospel of John.

This anonymous Syriac collection of letters is attributed to correspondence with Papa bar Aggai, bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon in the early fourth century, who is traditionally regarded as the first catholicos of the Church of the East. Writers such as Eusebius, called "patriarch of the Romans", and Judas Cyriacus of Jerusalem praise Papa and send gifts from Constantine and his mother. The letters are spurious and were probably composed between the sixth and eighth centuries. They likely served to support the dignity and apostolic standing of the see of Seleucia-Ctesiphon.

The Ascetic Discourses are a collection of thirteen Syriac discourses on the Christian and monastic life by Philoxenus of Mabbug (died 523), the Miaphysite bishop of Hierapolis. They were written in the late fifth or early sixth century, though the exact date is uncertain. The work sets out a gradual path of discipleship that starts from faith and simplicity and moves through the fear of God and renunciation of the world. It then turns to the struggle against gluttony and fornication, with spiritual love and perfection as the goal. It is among the most important works of early Syriac spirituality.

The Admonitions to Monks is a short set of disciplinary rules in Syriac attributed to Rabbula, bishop of Edessa (Urhay) from about 411 to 435/6. It governs life in the monasteries of his diocese. Its numbered precepts ban women from entering monasteries and limit monks' contact with villages and lay households to an appointed "Visitor". They also forbid drinking wine and restrict ascetic practices such as wearing long hair, iron chains or hair garments outside the monastery. The text is important evidence for early Syrian monasticism and for Rabbula's efforts to bring it under church discipline.

This polemical Syriac letter by Simeon of Beth Arsham, the early sixth-century Miaphysite bishop known as the "Persian Debater", sets out a hostile history of the Nestorian heresy and how it reached Persia. Simeon traces the belief that Christ was a mere man to Annas, Caiaphas and the Jews who rejected him, and then to Simon Magus. The chain continues through later teachers to Barsauma of Nisibis, the late fifth-century bishop who promoted Dyophysite doctrine in the Church of the East. The letter is an important witness to the Miaphysite–Nestorian conflict in the Persian Empire.

This is a Syriac prefatory letter by Simeon, abbot of the monastery of Mary, Mother of God, in Beth Liqnis. It is addressed to the priest Barlaha (Barlahe), a recluse living in the enclosure of Mar Elisha of Markabta. Simeon replies to Barlaha's repeated requests, carried by the deacon Damian, that he translate a book from Greek into Syriac. He professes himself unfit for the task but credits Barlaha's prayers with giving him the strength to attempt it. The letter's exact date and the identity of the translated work are uncertain.

The Testament of Adam is an anonymous Christian pseudepigraphon, preserved mainly in Syriac, in which Adam speaks to his son Seth. Its date is uncertain, but it is usually placed between the third and fifth centuries. It has three parts. The first is a horarium listing the worship offered by each creature at each hour of the night and day. The second is a prophecy of the Flood and of Christ's incarnation. The third describes the hierarchy of the angels. Versions also exist in Arabic, Ethiopic, Armenian and Georgian.

This Syriac treatise explains the feast of Christ's birth in the flesh. It was written by Thomas of Edessa (died c. 540), a theologian of the Church of the East, at the request of Mar Moses. Its chapters ask why the feast is celebrated and what benefits came through Christ. They also explain why God was revealed through a human being born of a virgin, and why the conception took place in Nisan. Reflecting the theology of Theodore of Mopsuestia, it is among the oldest surviving examples of the ʿelltā, or "cause", genre of feast explanations.

Against the Manichaeans is a polemical treatise in four books by Titus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia (died c. 378), written in Greek probably in the 360s or 370s. The Greek original survives only in part. The complete work is preserved in an early Syriac translation, attested in a manuscript of 411. Titus rejects Mani's doctrine of an eternal evil principle opposed to God. He defends divine providence and human free will as the source of sin, arguing first from reason and then from Scripture. It is a major early Christian source on Manichaean teaching.

The Travels of Peter is an anonymous Christian apocryphal narrative that survives in Syriac. Its date is uncertain, though it is generally placed somewhere between the fifth and eighth centuries. It tells of the apostle Simon Peter preaching baptism and the true faith from city to city. In its opening episode Peter meets a demon waiting to kill a newborn child, raises the dead infant to life and questions the demon about its attacks on children. That episode connects the text with traditions of protecting mothers and infants from demons. It is distinct from the Greek Pseudo-Clementine "Circuits of Peter."

The General Elementary Introduction is a Greek work in ten books by Eusebius of Caesarea. Its date is disputed: it may come from before the Great Persecution of 303 or from somewhat later. Only books six to nine survive, known as the Prophetic Extracts (Eclogae propheticae). They gather Old Testament prophecies about Christ, arranged by scriptural book and given brief commentary. They follow earlier books that argued for the faith without relying on Scripture. The work is an early source for Eusebius's exegesis and apologetic method.

The Ancoratus ("The Well-Anchored") is a Greek doctrinal treatise by Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia (Salamis) in Cyprus. He wrote it around 374 at the request of presbyters in Syedra in Pamphylia, whose letters stand at its beginning. It explains Christian teaching from Scripture and tradition: the consubstantiality of the Trinity, the full incarnation of Christ, and the resurrection and judgment. It argues against pagans, Jews and heretics, and lists the eighty heresies that Epiphanius later treated in the Panarion. It ends with two creeds, one of which closely resembles the creed associated with the Council of Constantinople of 381.

This is a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the Gospel of John, preserved in the catenae: medieval chains of excerpts from earlier commentators arranged verse by verse. They are attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253), whose large Commentary on John survives only in part. Catena attributions are often unreliable, so some passages may come from other writers or may have been reworded by later compilers. The fragments deal with themes such as the eternal Word, creation and the incarnation. They add to what is known of Origen's lost exegesis.

This is a collection of short Greek exegetical comments on the Book of Jeremiah, attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive as excerpts in the Byzantine catenae on the prophets, the chains of patristic comment arranged verse by verse. Some may come from Origen's lost homilies or notes on Jeremiah, though catena attributions are not always reliable. The fragments show his usual allegorical and moral reading, applying the prophet's images to sin, temptation and the soul's struggle, and they add to the Greek homilies on Jeremiah that survive in full.

These Greek exegetical fragments on the Book of Lamentations are attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive in the Byzantine catenae, or chains of commentary, on the prophets. They probably come from the commentary on Lamentations that Eusebius says Origen wrote at Alexandria and which is otherwise lost. The fragments discuss the alphabetic acrostic structure of Jeremiah's laments. They also read the Babylonian captivity allegorically, as the soul's captivity to hostile spiritual powers, from which Christ sets it free.

This is a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the whole Psalter, attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Most survive only as excerpts in later catenae, the Byzantine anthologies of biblical commentary. Origen wrote extensively on the Psalms, but compilers of catenae often confused or merged authors. Some material under his name is probably by others, such as Evagrius Ponticus, so the authenticity of individual fragments is doubtful. The comments read the Psalms morally and spiritually. Their opening reflection on Psalm 1 presents turning away from evil as the first step of the soul's progress toward God.

The Selecta in Psalmos are a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the Psalms attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive mainly as excerpts in later catenae, and their authenticity is doubtful in part because some passages may come from other writers, such as Evagrius Ponticus. The opening gathers philosophical definitions of "end" from Aristotle and Stoic sources to explain psalm titles. Even so, the fragments remain an important witness to Origen's lost commentaries and homilies on the Psalter.

The Lefafa Sedq ("Bandlet of Righteousness") is an anonymous Ethiopian funerary text in Ge'ez. It is a sequence of prayers that contain secret names of God and of Christ. According to tradition, Christ revealed it to the Virgin Mary to secure the salvation of believers. The text was copied onto a strip of parchment, often about the height of the dead person, and buried with the body. It was meant to protect the soul on its passage after death and gain it entry into heaven. Its date and origin are uncertain, and some scholars suggest Egyptian or Coptic influence.

Mysteries of Heaven and Earth is an anonymous apocryphal work that survives in Ge'ez, the classical language of Ethiopia. Its date and origin are uncertain. It is presented as mysteries that the apostle Peter revealed to his disciple Clement, which places it among the writings that circulated under Clement's name. The text gives an account of creation and a summary of biblical history down to the reign of King Jehoram. It also includes discourses on God's mercy toward humankind and on the role of Christ as Saviour.

The Sinodos is an anonymous Ethiopian collection of church order and canon law, counted among the books of the broader Ethiopian Orthodox biblical canon. It brings together earlier Christian material dating roughly from the third to the seventh centuries, including the Apostolic Tradition, the Apostolic Canons, and canons of councils such as Nicaea, Ancyra, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea and Chalcedon. It also includes letters of Constantine, Athanasius and Cyril of Alexandria, along with liturgical and baptismal texts. The Ge'ez text was translated from Arabic, and it remains an important source for church discipline and early liturgy.

The Ethiopian Synaxarion (Senkessar) is a liturgical collection of short commemorative notices of saints, martyrs, angels, prophets and church events. The notices are arranged day by day through the Ethiopian year, beginning with the month of Maskaram. It derives from the Arabic Synaxarion of the Coptic Church. Its preface attributes that work to Michael, bishop of Athribis and Malig, John, bishop of Burullus, and others, and dates it to the year 963 of the Martyrs (1246–47). It was probably translated into Ge'ez around 1400, later expanded with Ethiopian saints, and survives in more than one recension.

Contra Marcellum (Against Marcellus) is a polemical treatise in two books by Eusebius of Caesarea. It was written around 336–337, after Marcellus of Ancyra was deposed by a synod at Constantinople. Eusebius accuses Marcellus of attacking respected churchmen out of envy, among them Asterius the Sophist and Eusebius of Nicomedia. He charges him with Sabellianism for denying that the Son exists as a distinct person. Eusebius continued the argument in his Ecclesiastical Theology. Both works are important because they preserve many fragments of Marcellus's otherwise lost writings.

De ecclesiastica theologia ("On Ecclesiastical Theology") is a Greek theological treatise in three books written by Eusebius of Caesarea late in his life, probably around 337–338. It is dedicated to Flacillus, bishop of Antioch. It follows Eusebius's earlier two books Against Marcellus, which mostly quoted Marcellus of Ancyra's own words. Here Eusebius refutes Marcellus's teaching directly. Eusebius saw that teaching as Sabellian. Against it, he argues that the Son exists as a distinct being alongside the Father. The work is an important witness to the theological debates that followed the Council of Nicaea.

The Exhortation to Martyrdom is a Greek treatise by Origen of Alexandria, generally dated to about 235, during the persecution under the emperor Maximinus Thrax. It is addressed to his patron Ambrose and to Protoctetus, a presbyter of Caesarea, who were both facing arrest. Drawing heavily on Scripture, Origen urges them to stand firm, to reject idolatry and apostasy, and to see suffering for Christ as a contest that leads to glory. It is one of the most important early Christian writings on the meaning of martyrdom.

The Fragmenta are the surviving remains of the writings of Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra (died c. 374), a supporter of the Council of Nicaea and opponent of Arianism. Most come from his treatise against Asterius the Sophist, written around the early 330s. They survive almost entirely as quotations in Eusebius of Caesarea's polemical works against him, with a few more in Epiphanius's Panarion 72. The fragments set out Marcellus's theology of the Word, which his critics condemned as Sabellian, and they are central to the history of the Arian controversy.

On the Letters is a short Old Church Slavonic treatise attributed to Chernorizets Hrabar ("Hrabar the Monk"), a writer linked to the Preslav Literary School in the First Bulgarian Empire. It is usually dated to the late ninth or early tenth century. The work defends the Slavic alphabet created by Constantine-Cyril the Philosopher and argues that it is equal in dignity to the Hebrew, Greek and Latin scripts. It also describes how the letters were made in imitation of Greek. It is a key early witness to Slavic literacy and to the Cyrillo-Methodian mission.

The Euchologium Sinaiticum is an anonymous Old Church Slavonic prayer book (euchologion), mostly translated from Greek liturgical sources. It is preserved in a Glagolitic manuscript kept at Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai, usually dated to the eleventh century, though the translations may be older. Besides sacramental and penitential material, it contains many occasional blessings for daily life. Examples include prayers for planting a vineyard, blessing grapes and restoring wine that has turned sour. It is one of the most important witnesses to early Slavonic liturgical language and practice.

The Kiev Missal, also called the Kiev Folios, is an anonymous Old Church Slavonic manuscript written in Glagolitic script. It is usually held to be the oldest and most archaic Old Church Slavonic manuscript and is dated no later than the second half of the tenth century. Its seven small parchment folios contain Mass prayers of the Roman rite translated from a Latin sacramentary, among them propers for Saint Clement and Saint Felicity. It is important evidence for early Slavonic use of the Western liturgy.

The Demonstrations (Taḥwyātā) are twenty-three Syriac prose treatises by Aphrahat, the "Persian Sage," written in the Sasanian Empire between 337 and 345. Prefaced by a letter from an inquirer asking about the faith, the first twenty-two are arranged as an alphabetical acrostic. They address faith, love, fasting, prayer, humility, the "sons of the covenant," Passover, circumcision and the sabbath, often in debate with Jewish practice, and the persecution under Shapur II. They are the earliest major surviving works of Syriac Christianity, largely untouched by Greek theological influence.

De Decretis is a Greek treatise in the form of a letter by Athanasius of Alexandria, usually dated to the 350s. Athanasius answers the Arian objection that the Council of Nicaea (325) used unscriptural terms, "of the essence" and "one in essence" (homoousios). He argues that these words express the meaning of Scripture about the Son's true divinity. The work is a major early defence of the Nicene formula. It also preserves documents connected with the council.

The Fourth Discourse Against the Arians is a Greek theological treatise that has come down with the three Orations Against the Arians of Athanasius of Alexandria (4th century). Against Lying (Contra Mendacium) is a treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written around 420 in reply to Consentius, a Catholic layman in Spain. Consentius had suggested that Catholics could expose hidden Priscillianists by pretending to share their beliefs. Augustine rejects this: no lie is permissible, even to unmask heretics. Lying about the faith is especially grave, and good ends never justify deceit. The work takes up the themes of his earlier On Lying (De mendacio) and became a classic statement of his strict view that lying is always wrong.

Contra epistulam fundamenti is a Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated to about 396–397, early in his time as bishop. It refutes the "Fundamental Epistle", a foundational Manichaean letter attributed to Mani. Augustine quotes its opening passages and answers them one by one. Recalling his own years as a Manichaean hearer, he says he wants to heal his opponents, not crush them. The work contains his famous remark that he would not believe the Gospel unless moved by the authority of the Catholic Church. It also preserves fragments of the lost Manichaean text.

Against Two Letters of the Pelagians (Contra duas epistulas Pelagianorum) is a Latin treatise in four books by Augustine of Hippo, written about 420–421. It is addressed to Pope Boniface I, who had sent Augustine two Pelagian letters that slandered him. The first letter was attributed to Julian of Eclanum, and the second was issued by a group of Pelagian bishops. Augustine rejects their charge that he taught Manichaean doctrine. He also defends the Catholic teaching on original sin, grace, free will and the goodness of marriage. The work belongs to his later writings in the Pelagian controversy.

Answer to the Letters of Petilian (Contra litteras Petiliani) is a Latin polemical treatise in three books by Augustine of Hippo, written around 400–403 against Petilian, the Donatist bishop of Cirta (Constantina). Book I refutes the first part of a letter Petilian sent to his followers. Book II answers the whole letter point by point, and Book III replies to Petilian's response to Augustine. Augustine argues that the sacraments are valid whatever the holiness of the minister, and he defends the unity of the Catholic Church. The work is a major source for the Donatist controversy.

The City of God (De civitate Dei contra paganos) is a Latin apologetic and theological treatise in twenty-two books by Augustine of Hippo, written about 413–426. It was prompted by the Visigothic sack of Rome in 410 and dedicated to his friend Marcellinus. The first ten books answer pagan claims that Christianity caused Rome's misfortunes. The remaining twelve trace the origin, history and destiny of two cities: the earthly city, ruled by love of self, and the heavenly city, ruled by love of God. It deeply shaped Western theology and political thought.

The Confessions is an autobiographical work in thirteen books written in Latin by Augustine of Hippo between about 397 and 400. It is addressed to God as a long prayer. Books 1 to 9 tell the story of his restless youth, his attraction to Manichaeism and Neoplatonism, and his conversion to Christianity in 386. Book 10 examines memory, and the last three books are a commentary on the opening of Genesis. It is often called the first Western autobiography and has deeply shaped Christian spirituality and Western literature.

He describes the violence of the Circumcellions and closes with a discussion of the sin against the Holy Spirit.
